## Global Climate and Extreme Weather Report (Past 30 Days)

This report summarizes major climate and extreme weather events, their causes, and impacts reported in the past 30 days.

### **Global Weather Patterns and Drivers**

The strengthening El Niño phenomenon is significantly influencing global weather patterns, amplifying extreme events such as droughts, floods, and heatwaves. Its effects are projected to persist and strengthen through 2027. [source](https://www.bbc.com/weather/articles/c6dx07dznpyyo), [source](https://reliefweb.int/report/world/global-weather-hazards-summary-october-22-2026-october-28-2026), [source](https://www.yahoo.com/news/weather-news/articles/el-ni-o-rains-batter-205722211.html)

*   **El Niño Strengthening:** El Niño continues to strengthen, shaping global weather through 2027, and is expected to persist and strengthen further. [source](https://www.bbc.com/weather/articles/c6dx07dznpyyo), [source](https://reliefweb.int/report/world/global-weather-hazards-summary-october-22-2026-october-28-2026)
*   **Eastern Pacific Hurricane Activity:** The Eastern Pacific has seen above-average hurricane activity, with 22 named storms, 12 hurricanes, and 10 major hurricanes, including rapidly intensifying storms like Hurricane Polo, fueled by warm El Niño waters. [source](https://www.bbc.com/weather/articles/c6dx07dznpyyo)
*   **North Atlantic Hurricane Activity:** North Atlantic activity remains subdued, as El Niño tends to increase wind shear in the region, limiting hurricane formation (only one hurricane has made landfall in the U.S. so far). [source](https://www.bbc.com/weather/articles/c6dx07dznpyyo)

### **Regional Extreme Weather Events**

**Asia and the Pacific**

*   **Indonesia:** The country is experiencing its worst wildfire season since 2015, resulting in widespread land burning, school closures, and respiratory illnesses from toxic haze. [source](https://www.bbc.com/weather/articles/c6dx07dznpyyo)
*   **India:** Drier and hotter monsoon conditions are prevalent, with overall rainfall about 13% below average, impacting agriculture. The east/northeast is 26% drier, and southern states are 24% drier, with interrupted rain patterns increasing agricultural stress. [source](https://www.bbc.com/weather/articles/c6dx07dznpyyo)
*   **Western Pacific/East Asia:** China and Japan have experienced increased floods and landslides due to storms like Maysak and Dujuan. The Western Pacific has seen 10 tropical cyclones, the highest season count since 1966. [source](https://www.bbc.com/weather/articles/c6dx07dznpyyo)
*   **Nepal:** A catastrophic Langtang/Lirung glacier collapse on August 26, 2026, triggered a rock-ice avalanche and debris flood, killing over 1,451 people and affecting 1.6 million across five districts. This event is attributed to warming Himalayan temperatures. [source](https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/warming-himalayas-nepals-climate-justice-test)
*   **Nepal (Flooding):** Flooding in the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli corridor on August 26, 2026, killed over 1,000 people and damaged 1,800 hectares of crops (mostly paddy), with production losses of ~7,700 tonnes. [source](https://www.fao.org/newsroom/detail/nepal-floods-damage-1-800-hectares-of-crops-and-kill-thousands-of-livestock/en)

**Africa**

*   **East and Southern Africa:** Abnormal heat is forecasted for the eastern Sahel and parts of eastern/southern Africa. The Horn of Africa faces a high flood risk with heavy rainfall, while 90-day rainfall deficits are causing abnormal dryness across Chad and much of Eastern Africa. [source](https://reliefweb.int/report/world/global-weather-hazards-summary-october-22-2026-october-28-2026)
*   **South Sudan:** The Sudd wetlands are experiencing ongoing inundation. [source](https://reliefweb.int/report/world/global-weather-hazards-summary-october-22-2026-october-28-2026)
*   **Ethiopia and Somalia:** Recent heavy rains have caused flooding in southern Ethiopia and parts of Somalia, with ongoing heavy rainfall expected. [source](https://reliefweb.int/report/world/global-weather-hazards-summary-october-22-2026-october-28-2026)
*   **Central Africa:** Increased flood risk is present in southern Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, and east-central DRC due to recent and worsening rainfall. [source](https://reliefweb.int/report/world/global-weather-hazards-summary-october-22-2026-october-28-2026)

**Latin America**

*   **Widespread Flooding:** El Niño-driven storms are causing widespread flooding across the region. [source](https://www.yahoo.com/news/weather-news/articles/el-ni-o-rains-batter-205722211.html)
*   **Paraguay:** Flooding along the Parana River has affected approximately 4,200 families, caused two deaths, and displaced thousands. [source](https://www.yahoo.com/news/weather-news/articles/el-ni-o-rains-batter-205722211.html)
*   **Argentina:** Two farm workers were killed near Bella Vista while moving cattle from floodwaters, and hundreds were evacuated in Corrientes. [source](https://www.yahoo.com/news/weather-news/articles/el-ni-o-rains-batter-205722211.html)
*   **Mexico:** A luxury condo complex in San Pancho (Nayarit) collapsed its foundation due to pounding surf and eroded sand. [source](https://www.yahoo.com/news/weather-news/articles/el-ni-o-rains-batter-205722211.html)
*   **Peru:** The Pacific coast has been hit by storms, leading the government to approve 18 billion soles (~$5.2 billion) for 2027 to mitigate economic impact. [source](https://www.yahoo.com/news/weather-news/articles/el-ni-o-rains-batter-205722211.html)
*   **Chile:** Santiago experienced floods and a mudslide following a storm, with reports of hail and flooded streets. [source](https://www.yahoo.com/news/weather-news/articles/el-ni-o-rains-batter-205722211.html)

### **Impacts on Communities, Infrastructure, and Agriculture**

*   **Humanitarian Crisis:** The strong 2026-2027 El Niño is forecast to bring widespread droughts and floods, threatening food security, water access, and child health in affected regions. [source](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/10/1168537)
*   **Child Vulnerability:** UNICEF warns that over 347 million children in nearly 100 countries could experience unusually wet or dry conditions between October and December 2026, increasing risks of displacement, malnutrition, water shortages, disease, and schooling disruptions. [source](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/10/1168537)
*   **Agricultural Damage:** In Nepal, floods damaged 1,800 hectares of crops and killed thousands of livestock and 1.6 million poultry. [source](https://www.fao.org/newsroom/detail/nepal-floods-damage-1-800-hectares-of-crops-and-kill-thousands-of-livestock/en)
*   **Infrastructure Destruction:** The Nepal floods destroyed 41 bridges, damaged roads, markets, and fishponds, disrupting access and supply chains. [source](https://www.fao.org/newsroom/detail/nepal-floods-damage-1-800-hectares-of-crops-and-kill-thousands-of-livestock/en) The Langtang/Lirung glacier collapse in Nepal damaged 7,570 private homes, 48 public buildings, 18 schools, seven health facilities, and 30 cultural heritage sites. [source](https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/warming-himalayas-nepals-climate-justice-test)
*   **Economic Costs:** Reconstruction costs in Nepal following the glacier collapse exceed US $2.66 billion, with total needs for reconstruction and rehabilitation around US $4.72 billion. [source](https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/warming-himalayas-nepals-climate-justice-test) Peru's government approved $5.2 billion to mitigate economic impacts of El Niño storms. [source](https://www.yahoo.com/news/weather-news/articles/el-ni-o-rains-batter-205722211.html)
*   **Social and Psychosocial Impacts:** The Nepal glacier collapse resulted in profound social costs, including psychosocial harm to children, women, seniors, and marginalized groups, often underrepresented in official damage estimates. [source](https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/warming-himalayas-nepals-climate-justice-test)
*   **Displacement:** Ongoing displacement is reported in Nepal, with 1,743 people in 27 holding centers. [source](https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/warming-himalayas-nepals-climate-justice-test) Thousands have been displaced in Paraguay due to flooding. [source](https://www.yahoo.com/news/weather-news/articles/el-ni-o-rains-batter-205722211.html)

### **Response and Future Needs**

*   **Emergency Aid:** FAO has deployed emergency veterinary teams and provided medicines in Nepal, while the government is providing aid to displaced families. [source](https://www.fao.org/newsroom/detail/nepal-floods-damage-1-800-hectares-of-crops-and-kill-thousands-of-livestock/en), [source](https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/warming-himalayas-nepals-climate-justice-test)
*   **Climate Justice and Finance:** Nepal has urged the Loss and Damage Fund for reparations from polluters, seeking up to US $20 million in compensation, and civil society demands grants and climate justice rather than loans. [source](https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/warming-himalayas-nepals-climate-justice-test)
*   **Anticipatory Action:** Current humanitarian funding allocates less than 1% to anticipatory action, despite potential savings (up to $15 in recovery costs per $1 invested). [source](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/10/1168537)
*   **Resilience Building:** Immediate needs include seeds, feed, veterinary care, and basic necessities, while long-term recovery must address soil restoration, drainage/irrigation repair, and reestablishing market access. Priority is also on enhanced information sharing, early-warning systems, and institutional mechanisms. [source](https://www.fao.org/newsroom/detail/nepal-floods-damage-1-800-hectares-of-crops-and-kill-thousands-of-livestock/en), [source](https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/warming-himalayas-nepals-climate-justice-test)

## Semiconductor Industry: Past 30 Days Overview

This report summarizes key developments in the semiconductor industry over the past 30 days, categorized into Manufacturing & Capacity Expansion, Financial Performance & Market Trends, Product Announcements & Technological Advancements, and AI-Driven Developments.

### Manufacturing & Capacity Expansion

*   **GlobalFoundries Expansions**: GlobalFoundries is undertaking a significant $21 billion U.S.-Japan initiative to establish two new 300mm fabs in Malta, NY, with the first expected online by 2029. This is seen as a concrete push to boost U.S. domestic foundry capacity [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/), [originbrief.app](https://www.originbrief.app/en/reports/semiconductor-chip-industry/2026-10-19/weekly), [distillintelligence.com](https://www.distillintelligence.com/briefings/semiconductors-ai-chips-2026-10-16).
*   **Applied Materials R&D**: Applied Materials opened a new $5 billion, 600,000 sq ft EPIC Center R&D facility in Silicon Valley to advance semiconductor process and equipment technology [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/), [originbrief.app](https://www.originbrief.app/en/reports/semiconductor-chip-industry/2026-10-19/weekly), [distillintelligence.com](https://www.distillintelligence.com/briefings/semiconductors-ai-chips-2026-10-16).
*   **TSMC Capacity**: TSMC announced plans for a new 3nm manufacturing fab in Tainan, Taiwan, targeting mass production in H1 2028, expanding its 3nm capacity to four sites globally [vlsi.kr](https://www.vlsi.kr/en/daily-silicon-2026-10-20-en/), [distillintelligence.com](https://www.distillintelligence.com/briefings/semiconductors-ai-chips-2026-10-16).
*   **Equipment Spending Forecast**: SEMI forecasts a rise in 300mm equipment spending to $149 billion in 2026 and $227 billion by 2029, with the Americas projected to see the fastest growth [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/), [originbrief.app](https://www.originbrief.app/en/reports/semiconductor-chip-industry/2026-10-19/weekly).
*   **Nikon Lithography**: Nikon unveiled a new lithography system for advanced packaging, offering 40% higher throughput and supporting larger substrates, with availability slated for April 2027 [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/).
*   **Infineon & Wolfspeed Agreement**: Infineon and Wolfspeed signed a multi-year supply agreement for 200mm SiC wafers [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/).
*   **China's EUV Efforts**: China's Langdao Silex pitched a prototype EUV source with 90% local components, aiming for mass production in three to five years, though its output is still far from commercial EUV power [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/).

### Financial Performance & Market Trends

*   **Market Volatility and Rebound**: U.S. chip stocks experienced a significant selloff, with the PHLX Semiconductor Index (SOX) falling for seven straight sessions, wiping out roughly $2 trillion in market value, driven by oversupply fears (especially in memory), rising U.S. producer prices, and concerns over funding conditions for AI data centers [investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/us-chip-stocks-rise-after-steepest-weekly-selloff-in-months-4957420), [benzinga.com](https://www.benzinga.com/markets/tech/26/10/62389257/worst-15-chip-stocks-last-7-sessions-sk-hynix-arm-micron-sandisk), [gmt8press.com](https://www.gmt8press.com/flash/detail/1547508), [yahoo.com](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/chip-stocks-shrug-off-a-scary-morning-but-history-says-the-shakeout-isnt-over-154222842.html). However, stocks later rebounded due to easing government yields and oil prices, and dip buying [investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/us-chip-stocks-rise-after-steepest-weekly-selloff-in-months-4957420), [vlsi.kr](https://www.vlsi.kr/en/daily-silicon-2026-10-20-en/).
*   **TSMC & ASML Earnings**: TSMC reported Q3 revenue of approximately $46.7 billion, up 41% YoY, citing strong AI demand despite macroeconomic headwinds. ASML reported record Q3 sales of €11.7 billion and is evaluating additional capacity expansion beyond its current plans due to demand outpacing supply [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/), [distillintelligence.com](https://www.distillintelligence.com/briefings/semiconductors-ai-chips-2026-10-16).
*   **CXMT's Dramatic Growth**: China's ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) posted a dramatic Q3 rebound, with revenue estimated between 114.7–119.7 billion yuan (approx. $14–19B), a 589–619% YoY increase, turning a loss into a profit. CXMT's DRAM revenue share reached ~10% in Q2, making it the world's No. 4 DRAM supplier, driven by AI compute demand and supply tightness [vlsi.kr](https://www.vlsi.kr/en/daily-silicon-2026-10-18-en/).
*   **Startup Funding**: Q3 saw over $8.5 billion in chip-industry startup funding across approximately 80 companies, primarily focused on AI inference, memory alternatives, photonics, and data movement [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/).
*   **Qualcomm vs. Arm**: A jury awarded Qualcomm $2 in damages in a tech license dispute with Arm, concluding one phase of the lawsuit [distillintelligence.com](https://www.distillintelligence.com/briefings/semiconductors-ai-chips-2026-10-16).
*   **ESD and IP Revenue Growth**: The ESD industry revenue rose 12.2% YoY to $5.71 billion in Q2 2026, while IP revenue grew 20.4% to $2.199 billion [vlsi.kr](https://www.vlsi.kr/en/daily-silicon-2026-10-20-en/).

### Product Announcements & Technological Advancements

*   **Renesas MCUs**: Renesas launched RX74M and RX74N flagship 32-bit MCUs, the first RX family devices built on a 22nm process and featuring embedded MRAM. These target industrial automation and broader industrial equipment with high performance, security, and advanced connectivity (EtherCAT, TSN-capable Gigabit Ethernet) [renesas.com](https://www.renesas.com/en/about/newsroom/renesas-launches-rx74m-and-rx74n-flagship-32-bit-mcus-first-rx-family-built-22nm-process-and).
*   **Marvell Connectivity**: Marvell unveiled two new additions to its Alaska connectivity family for AI scale-up infrastructure: the Alaska E 3.2T protocol-aware retimer (3.2 Tbps bandwidth, 224G PAM4 lanes) and the Alaska A 1.6T second-generation AEC DSP (1.6T throughput over longer copper reaches). These aim to improve bandwidth, reach, and power efficiency for AI racks [investor.marvell.com](https://investor.marvell.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/1039/marvell-bolsters-connectivity-portfolio-with-new-3-2t-protocol-aware-retimer-and-second-generation-1-6t-aec-dsp).
*   **Microchip Space Converter**: Microchip expanded its space power portfolio with a new radiation-tolerant GaN-based Point-of-Load (POL) converter, the POL-05-20S-T, delivering up to 20A continuous current for space processing applications and specified up to 50 krad TID [ir.microchip.com](https://ir.microchip.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/1421/microchip-expands-space-power-portfolio-with-new-radiation-tolerant-gan-point-of-load-converter).
*   **BrainChip Neuromorphic AI**: BrainChip announced the AKD1500 SPI chip, a co-processor bringing Akida neuromorphic AI to microcontroller-based edge devices via SPI, enabling on-chip learning capabilities for wearables, smart homes, and sensors [brainchip.com](https://brainchip.com/press/brainchip-unveils-akd1500-spi-chip-bringing-neuromorphic-ai-to-everyday-edge-devices/).
*   **CXMT DDR5 for Servers**: CXMT is reportedly planning a DDR5 server RDIMM using 4F² DRAM cells by year-end to improve density and reduce costs [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/).
*   **Texas Instruments ADC**: TI introduced a nanosecond-level ADC designed for AI data centers [originbrief.app](https://www.originbrief.app/en/reports/semiconductor-chip-industry/2026-10-19/weekly).

### AI-Driven Developments

*   **Nvidia Capacity Expansion**: Nvidia announced partnerships with multiple suppliers, including Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Amkor Technology, Ibiden, Unimicron Technology, King Yuan Electronics, and Siliconware Precision, to significantly expand its chipmaking capacity for AI-related semiconductors to address high demand [wsj.com](https://www.wsj.com/livecoverage/stock-market-today-dow-sp-500-nasdaq-10-21-2026/card/S8kOVoeKXiwOVNvmToNv).
*   **AI Hardware Ecosystems**: There's a strong focus on AI inference accelerators and GPUs, with developments from Microsoft (AI inference accelerator), Intel (AI GPU), and Nvidia (high-speed optical modules). Marvell revealed multi-channel CXL 3.2 memory expanders [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/).
*   **Nvidia's China Shipments**: Nvidia's AI accelerator shipments in China were down 44% YoY in H1 2026, partly due to U.S. export controls and rising local competition, with Huawei holding a significant market share [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/), [distillintelligence.com](https://www.distillintelligence.com/briefings/semiconductors-ai-chips-2026-10-16).

*   **Thermal Management**: Thermal co-design is emerging as a critical constraint across chip design, packaging, and data centers due to increasing power density, with industry moves towards thermal co-simulation and thermal-aware design practices [originbrief.app](https://www.originbrief.app/en/reports/semiconductor-chip-industry/2026-10-19/weekly).

BrainChip announces AKD1500 SPI, a co-processor that brings Akida neuromorphic AI to microcontroller-based edge devices via SPI. Key points:

- Complementary to AKD1500 PCIe: SPI enables high-volume, low-power microcontroller applications, while PCIe serves higher-performance, multi-chip designs.
- Availability: now shipping via BrainChip Shop, DigiKey, or direct sales.

Summary:
- The McKinsey-sponsored SIA report maps US semiconductor upstream supply chains, showing that while equipment and materials suppliers are largely global (Europe, Japan, US account for ~95% of value), actual production inputs come from a multi-tier, highly global network with critical vulnerabilities deep in subtier layers.
- Three key findings:
  1) Semiconductor manufacturing relies on a precisely coordinated flow of specialized materials and equipment from Tier 1 and subtier suppliers worldwide.
  2) Resilience requires visibility beyond direct Tier 1 suppliers; risks often reside in subtier networks related to critical minerals, rare earths, engineered materials, and subcomponents, which can compound across the ecosystem.
  3) No single fix suffices. Strengthening resilience requires a multi-pronged approach: expanding domestic capacity, improving inventory management, securing supply chains, building strong international partnerships, and investing in sustained R&D in materials science, engineering, and recycling to reduce vulnerable inputs.
- Practical implication: Decisions now—through diversification, supply-chain visibility, and R&D investment—can reduce the risk of disruptive shortages and protect future manufacturing investments for decades.

## Semiconductor Industry Report: Past 30 Days

This report summarizes key developments in the semiconductor industry over the past 30 days, categorized into market trends, company earnings, manufacturing & technology, and supply chain updates.

### I. Market Trends & Outlook

The semiconductor market is experiencing a period of strong growth, driven primarily by demand for AI infrastructure, with expectations of continued expansion into 2026 and beyond.

*   **Overall Market Strength:** The semiconductor market is exceptionally strong, with positive momentum across equipment, materials, and overall semiconductor sales. Global semiconductor sales are projected to reach around $2 trillion in 2026, a significant increase from previous years [TechInsights](https://www.techinsights.com/blog/chip-insider-state-semiconductor-union).
*   **AI-Driven Demand:** AI and hyperscaler demand are the primary drivers of this growth, fueling investments in data centers and specialized chips [TechInsights](https://www.techinsights.com/blog/chip-insider-state-semiconductor-union), [FinVaulta](https://finvaulta.com/research/jp-morgan/semiconductors-and-semi-cap-equipment-3q26-sector-preview-2026-10-12). Wafer demand is projected to hit record levels through 2029 due to AI infrastructure needs [ChipNews](https://chipnews.io/).
*   **Silicon Wafer Shipments:** SEMI forecasts an 11.8% growth in silicon wafer shipments in 2026, reaching record highs through 2029 (17,034 MSI). This growth is attributed to strong AI-related demand for advanced wafers and a recovery in mature-node utilization [SEMI](https://www.semi.org/en/semi-press-release/semi-forecasts-11.8-percent-growth-in-silicon-wafer-shipments-in-2026-with-record-highs-expected-through-2029).
*   **Geopolitical and Macro Factors:** While the market is strong, geopolitical tensions, particularly between China and the U.S., and potential macro shifts (e.g., interest rates) remain factors to monitor [TechInsights](https://www.techinsights.com/blog/chip-insider-state-semiconductor-union). Tariffs and trade restrictions are creating a volatile business environment [TechInsights](https://www.techinsights.com/outlook-reports-2026/semiconductor-outlook-report).

### II. Company Earnings & Financials

Several major semiconductor companies have reported strong Q3 2026 earnings, indicating robust demand, particularly for advanced technologies and AI-related products.

*   **TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company):**
    *   Reported Q3 2026 revenue of US$46.72 billion (+50.9% YoY, +16.2% QoQ) and net income of US$4.60 per ADR (+68.7% YoY) [TSMC](https://pr.tsmc.com/english/news/3346).
    *   Advanced technologies (7nm and above) accounted for 79% of wafer revenue. 2nm process accounted for 8% of revenue and is expected to ramp further in Q4 [TSMC](https://pr.tsmc.com/english/news/3346).
    *   Q4 2026 revenue outlook is strong, projected at US$52.3–$54.3 billion [TSMC](https://pr.tsmc.com/english/news/3346).
*   **Lam Research:**
    *   Reported strong Q3 FY2026 revenue of $8.22 billion, up from $6.72 billion in the prior quarter. Net income was $2.75 billion ($2.19 per diluted share) [Lam Research](https://newsroom.lamresearch.com/2026-10-21-Lam-Research-Corporation-Reports-Financial-Results-for-the-Quarter-Ended-September-27,-2026).
    *   Q4 2026 revenue guidance is around $8.6 billion (+/- $0.4 billion) [Lam Research](https://newsroom.lamresearch.com/2026-10-21-Lam-Research-Corporation-Reports-Financial-Results-for-the-Quarter-Ended-September-27,-2026).
*   **Texas Instruments (TI):**
    *   Reported Q3 2026 revenue of $6.06 billion, up 28% YoY and 11% QoQ. Net income was $2.43 billion [TI](https://www.ti.com/about-ti/newsroom/news-releases/2026/2026-10-21-ti-reports-third-quarter-2026-financial-results-and-shareholder-returns.html).

Memory upcycle is continuing, driven by DRAM prices and HBM4 [TrendForce](https://insights.trendforce.com/p/weekly-radar-005).

### III. Manufacturing & Technology Advancements

Significant advancements are being made in fab expansion, lithography, advanced packaging, and AI hardware, indicating a rapid evolution in semiconductor manufacturing.

*   **Fab Expansion & Capex:**
    *   GlobalFoundries will operate two new fabs in Malta, NY, under a US-Japan initiative (up to $21B total; first fab by 2029) [SemiEngineering](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/).
    *   SEMI projects front-end 300mm fab equipment spending to reach $149B in 2026 and $227B by 2029 [SEMI](https://www.semi.org/en/news-media-press/newsroom), [SemiEngineering](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/).
    *   Applied Materials unveiled a $5B EPIC Center R&D facility in Silicon Valley [SemiEngineering](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/).
    *   Tokyo has 2nm foundry plans, indicating strategic investments in leading-edge process technology [ChipNews](https://chipnews.io/).
*   **Lithography & Advanced Packaging:**
    *   Nikon launched a lithography system for advanced packaging with 1.5 µm L/S and higher throughput, with mass production planned for 2027 [SemiEngineering](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/).
    *   Langdao Silex unveiled a prototype EUV light source with ~90% localized components, showing progress towards domestically sourced EUV in China [SemiEngineering](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/).
    *   Computational lithography, advanced packaging, photonics, and testing are increasingly interwoven with scaling strategies beyond traditional transistor scaling [InsideSemicon](https://www.insidesemicon.com/news).
*   **AI Hardware & Compute Systems:**
    *   Developments include new stackable 3D compute platforms, inference-first accelerators for memory-heavy AI workloads, and advancements in optical interconnects and compute cooling [SemiEngineering](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/).
    *   Nvidia is leading GPU supply-chain developments and has a chiplet-focused strategy [ChipNews](https://chipnews.io/). NVIDIA Cosmos provides new tools for training, evaluating, and deploying world models [InsideSemicon](https://www.insidesemicon.com/news).
    *   Alibaba has a RISC-V automotive roadmap [ChipNews](https://chipnews.io/). Tenstorrent, an AI chips-to-computers company, raised $1.5B in Series E funding [InsideSemicon](https://www.insidesemicon.com/news).
    *   Cloud-based AI continues to grow, driving datacenter investments for larger language models (LLMs) [TechInsights](https://www.techinsights.com/outlook-reports-2026/semiconductor-outlook-report).

### IV. Supply Chain Updates & Challenges

The semiconductor supply chain remains tight, particularly for memory and advanced components, with ongoing efforts to enhance resilience and mitigate vulnerabilities.

*   **Persistent Supply Bottlenecks:** Supply tightness continues, especially for leading-edge foundries, HBM (High Bandwidth Memory), advanced packaging, and power components. This is driving an acceleration in custom XPUs/ASICs [FinVaulta](https://finvaulta.com/research/jp-morgan/semiconductors-and-semi-cap-equipment-3q26-sector-preview-2026-10-12).
*   **Memory Market Tightness:** DRAM is "Very Tight" at ~20 weeks lead time (vs. 8-week balanced), with suppliers shifting bit supply from PC to server DRAM. CSPs are securing eSSD/HDD supply through 2027, with HDD lead times at ~50 weeks [TrendForce](https://insights.trendforce.com/p/weekly-radar-005). HBM4 is driving memory recovery [TechInsights](https://www.techinsights.com/outlook-reports-2026/semiconductor-outlook-report).
*   **Global Supply Chain Vulnerabilities:** The U.S. semiconductor supply chain is highly global, with critical vulnerabilities residing deep in subtier networks related to specialized materials, rare earths, engineered materials, and subcomponents [McKinsey](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/semiconductors/our-insights/strengthening-supply-chains-behind-us-semiconductors), [SIA](https://www.semiconductors.org/understanding-dependencies-in-the-u-s-semiconductor-supply-chain/).
*   **Mitigation Strategies:** Strengthening resilience requires expanding domestic capacity, improving inventory management, securing supply chains, building international partnerships, and investing in R&D for new materials and recycling technologies [McKinsey](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/semiconductors/our-insights/strengthening-supply-chains-behind-us-semiconductors), [SIA](https://www.semiconductors.org/understanding-dependencies-in-the-u-s-semiconductor-supply-chain/).
*   **Market Impact of Constraints:** Chip stocks declined after Lam Research indicated supply chain constraints affected its quarterly revenue guidance, causing a drop in the PHLX Semiconductor Index (SOXX) [Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/chip-stocks-fall-as-equipment-maker-lam-research-cites-supply-chain-constraints-130648719.html). Key companies like Nvidia, Qualcomm, and Intel saw significant declines [Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/chip-stocks-fall-as-equipment-maker-lam-research-cites-supply-chain-constraints-130648719.html).

sources.summary:
Summary:
- The McKinsey-sponsored SIA report maps US semiconductor upstream supply chains, showing that while equipment and materials suppliers are largely global (Europe, Japan, US account for ~95% of value), actual production inputs come from a multi-tier, highly global network with critical vulnerabilities deep in subtier layers.
- Three key findings:
  1) Semiconductor manufacturing relies on a precisely coordinated flow of specialized materials and equipment from Tier 1 and subtier suppliers worldwide.
  2) Resilience requires visibility beyond direct Tier 1 suppliers; risks often reside in subtier networks related to critical minerals, rare earths, engineered materials, and subcomponents, which can compound across the ecosystem.
  3) No single fix suffices. Strengthening resilience requires a multi-pronged approach: expanding domestic capacity, improving inventory management, securing supply chains, building strong international partnerships, and investing in sustained R&D in materials science, engineering, and recycling to reduce vulnerable inputs.
- Practical implication: Decisions now—through diversification, supply-chain visibility, and R&D investment—can reduce the risk of disruptive shortages and protect future manufacturing investments for decades.

Summary:
- The U.S. semiconductor supply chain is multi-tiered and globally dispersed. While about 95% of equipment and materials inputs to U.S. chip production are sourced from the U.S., Europe, and Japan, the actual manufacturing footprint is worldwide, creating vulnerabilities deep in upstream supply chains.
- Semiconductors are vital to the U.S. economy and national security, and recent disruptions highlight fragilities in critical materials, equipment, and subcomponents.
- Key vulnerabilities exist in Tier 1 and sub-tier inputs due to dependencies on raw materials and subcomponents, which can disrupt the broader ecosystem.
- Mitigation strategies require coordinated action across industry, government, and allies, including:
  - Onshoring and stockpiling of select inputs (prioritizing feasible near-term targets; full onshoring of all inputs is impractical).
  - Strengthening allied and partner supply chains to improve resilience.
  - Reducing dependence on unreliable sources of rare earths and critical minerals by expanding U.S. and partner mining/processing capacity and establishing long-term offtake agreements.
  - Increasing sustained funding for research and development in materials science, chemistry, and engineering to advance new semiconductor materials and recycling technologies.
- The path to stronger resilience involves sustained, coordinated efforts and targeted investments to expand domestic capabilities, secure strategic inventories, and foster international collaboration.

# Semiconductor Industry: One-Page Report

## Executive Summary

The semiconductor industry experienced significant growth and strategic developments in the past 30 days, largely driven by surging demand for AI chips and robust investment in advanced manufacturing. Global semiconductor sales topped $1 trillion through August 2026, with strong year-over-year increases across all regions. Major players like TSMC and ASML reported record revenues and are planning significant capacity expansions. Geopolitical factors continue to shape the industry, with the US and its allies investing heavily in domestic manufacturing and supply chain resilience to counter potential disruptions and reduce reliance on single-source suppliers, particularly from China. Stock market performance was mixed, with an initial sell-off due to inflation and AI financing concerns, followed by a rebound in AI-related equities as yields eased.

---

## Market Trends & Financial Performance

The semiconductor industry has seen unprecedented growth, with global sales reaching new highs and strong financial results from key companies.

*   **Record Sales Growth:** Global semiconductor sales hit $1 trillion through August 2026 for the first time. August 2026 sales were $159.7 billion, an 8% increase from July 2026 and a remarkable 144.3% jump year-over-year [source](https://www.semiconductors.org/year-to-date-global-semiconductor-sales-top-1-trillion-through-august/).
*   **Regional Growth:** All regions reported significant year-over-year gains: Americas (+180.9%), Asia Pacific/All Other (+143.0%), China (+131.3%), Europe (+98.5%), and Japan (+62.3%) [source](https://www.semiconductors.org/year-to-date-global-semiconductor-sales-top-1-trillion-through-august/).
*   **TSMC Q3 Performance:** TSMC reported a record Q3 net profit of NT$763.1 billion (+68.7% YoY) on revenue of NT$1.49 trillion (~$46.36 billion), beating expectations. Operating margin was 58.7%, driven by strong AI chip demand and advanced node contributions (3nm at 33%, 7nm+ at 79% of wafer revenue) [source](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/15/tsmc-third-quarter-profit-global-ai-.html), [source](https://www.vlsi.kr/en/daily-silicon-2026-10-19-en/). Q4 revenue guidance is $52.3–$54.3 billion [source](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/15/tsmc-third-quarter-profit-global-ai-.html).
*   **ASML Q3 Performance:** ASML posted Q3 net sales of €11.7 billion (+~55% YoY) and raised its 2026 outlook, citing strong demand outpacing supply, particularly for EUV lithography systems. They plan capacity expansion for 2027 (potentially 2028) [source](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/), [source](https://www.distillintelligence.com/briefings/semiconductors-ai-chips-2026-10-16/), [source](https://www.vlsi.kr/en/daily-silicon-2026-10-19-en/).
*   **Investment Outlook:** SEMI projects 300mm front-end fab equipment spending to reach $149 billion in 2026 (up 31%) and $227 billion by 2029, with Americas equipment spending growing from $18.1 billion (2026) to $40.6 billion (2029) [source](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/), [source](https://www.originbrief.app/en/reports/semiconductor-chip-industry/2026-10-19/weekly).
*   **AI-Driven Investment:** Top-10 semiconductor R&D spending runs at $67 billion/year, a 67% increase since 2021, driven by a structural AI-led investment surge [source](https://www.originbrief.app/en/reports/semiconductor-chip-industry/2026-10-19/weekly).
*   **Startup Funding:** Over $8.5 billion in Q3 startup funding across 80 companies, focusing on AI inference, memory alternatives, photonics, and networking [source](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/).

---

## Strategic Developments & Investments

Major investments in manufacturing facilities, R&D, and strategic partnerships highlight efforts to boost production capacity and technological advancements.

*   **GlobalFoundries US-Japan Initiative:** GlobalFoundries (GF) was selected to build and operate two new 300mm fabs in Malta, NY, under a US-Japan initiative with up to $21 billion in funding. The first fab is expected online in 2029, signaling a significant push for domestic foundry capacity. The US government will also take a ~4% equity stake in GF [source](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/), [source](https://www.originbrief.app/en/reports/semiconductor-chip-industry/2026-10-19/weekly), [source](https://www.distillintelligence.com/briefings/semiconductors-ai-chips-2026-10-16/).
*   **Applied Materials R&D Center:** Applied Materials opened the EPIC Center, a $5 billion, 600,000 sq.ft. R&D facility in Silicon Valley for semiconductor processing and equipment [source](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/), [source](https://www.distillintelligence.com/briefings/semiconductors-ai-chips-2026-10-16/).
*   **Infineon & Wolfspeed SiC Agreement:** Infineon and Wolfspeed signed a multi-year supply agreement for 200mm SiC wafers [source](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/).
*   **Nikon Lithography System:** Nikon unveiled a new lithography system for advanced packaging, offering 40% higher throughput and supporting large substrates, with availability expected April 2027 [source](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/).
*   **China’s Developments:** China-linked advancements include a 4F² DRAM cell (server RDIMM) for increased density and reduced costs, and Langdao Silex announced a prototype EUV light source with 90% localized components (output >15W), though mass production is 3-5 years away [source](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/).
*   **NVIDIA & AI Infrastructure:** NVIDIA, AMD, SK Hynix, and Intel unveiled major AI-infrastructure architectures at the OCP Global Summit, emphasizing a shift toward standardized next-gen AI factory design [source](https://www.originbrief.app/en/reports/semiconductor-chip-industry/2026-10-19/weekly). NVIDIA’s RTX Spark launched commercially, and the company is forming AI-defined fab partnerships, positioning itself as both a customer and critical infrastructure provider [source](https://www.originbrief.app/en/reports/semiconductor-chip-industry/2026-10-19/weekly).
*   **Samsung & NVIDIA HBM Collaboration:** Samsung is reportedly manufacturing NVIDIA’s NVHBM base dies on TSMC’s 3nm process, marking a rare collaboration between the two foundry giants for high-bandwidth memory [source](https://www.vlsi.kr/en/daily-silicon-2026-10-19-en/).
*   **Thermal Design Focus:** Thermal co-design and co-simulation are emerging as central to chip design, packaging, and data-center infrastructure due to increasing power density [source](https://www.originbrief.app/en/reports/semiconductor-chip-industry/2026-10-19/weekly).

---

## Supply Chain & Geopolitical Landscape

Supply chain resilience remains a critical focus, with reports highlighting vulnerabilities and advocating for strategic domestic and allied investments to mitigate risks, especially in response to geopolitical tensions.

*   **Supply Chain Vulnerabilities:** A joint report by McKinsey and the SIA emphasizes that the US semiconductor supply chain relies on a globally dispersed network of specialized materials and equipment. Critical risks often lie in "sub-tier" networks (minerals, rare earths, engineered materials) beyond direct Tier 1 suppliers [source](https://www.semiconductors.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SIA_2026_Supply-Chain-Report.pdf), [source](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/semiconductors/our-insights/strengthening-supply-chains-behind-us-semiconductors). About half of analyzed Tier-1 supply categories show "high" (11%) or "medium" (38%) vulnerability [source](https://www.semiconductors.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SIA_2026_Supply-Chain-Report.pdf).
*   **Strategic Recommendations:** Strategies to strengthen resilience include:
    *   **Onshoring:** Expanding domestic production and building strategic inventories for critical inputs, prioritizing targets for onshoring and stockpiling [source](https://www.semiconductors.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SIA_2026_Supply-Chain-Report.pdf), [source](https://www.semiconductors.org/sia-report-highlights-strategies-for-strengthening-supply-chains-supporting-the-u-s-chip-ecosystem/).
    *   **Allied Supply Chains:** Reinforcing trade relations and investing in complementary capabilities with partner nations to boost resilience and develop economic corridors [source](https://www.semiconductors.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SIA_2026_Supply-Chain-Report.pdf), [source](https://www.semiconductors.org/sia-report-highlights-strategies-for-strengthening-supply-chains-supporting-the-u-s-chip-ecosystem/).
    *   **Reduced Reliance on Critical Minerals:** Pursuing new mining/processing capacity in the US and allied countries, using long-term offtake agreements, and investing in R&D for next-generation materials and recycling [source](https://www.semiconductors.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SIA_2026_Supply-Chain-Report.pdf), [source](https://www.semiconductors.org/sia-report-highlights-strategies-for-strengthening-supply-chains-supporting-the-u-s-chip-ecosystem/).
*   **Geopolitical Risks:** China’s extensive export controls on heavy rare earths (imposed in 2025) highlight the risk of supply disruptions. Up to USD 6.5 trillion in annual sales across various sectors could be affected if controls expand [source](https://www.iea.org/commentaries/a-price-worth-paying-a-mineral-security-premium-as-insurance-against-supply-disruptions).
*   **Mineral Security Premium:** The IEA proposes a "mineral security premium" to value supply security in procurement and investment, acknowledging that supply diversification often incurs higher costs (e.g., 50% higher operating costs for new supply chains). A modest investment of ~$60 billion over a decade could diversify magnet rare earth supply chains outside China by 2035 [source](https://www.iea.org/commentaries/a-price-worth-paying-a-mineral-security-premium-as-insurance-against-supply-disruptions).
*   **NVIDIA China Shipments:** NVIDIA’s China AI-accelerator shipments declined 44% YoY in H1 2026 due to US export controls and rising local competition, with Huawei holding 28% of the data-center AI-accelerator market by units, compared to NVIDIA’s 34% [source](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/), [source](https://www.distillintelligence.com/briefings/semiconductors-ai-chips-2026-10-16/).

---

## Stock Performance & Investment Sentiment

The semiconductor sector experienced volatility, with an initial sell-off due to macroeconomic concerns, followed by a rebound driven by a positive outlook on AI demand.

*   **Initial Sell-off:** The PHLX Semiconductor Index (SOX) dropped about 10-11% over six down days and two months, influenced by CPI-driven rate repricing, AI financing concerns, and skepticism from some industry leaders [source](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/chip-stock-selloff-deepens-what-looks-attractive-and-names-to-avoid-93CH-4951092), [source](https://news.platform.elebank.com/post/1000606661/after-the-philadelphia-semiconductor-index-plunged-11-in-two-months). Key players like Nvidia (-5.2%), TSMC (-8.4%), and Broadcom (-7.8%) declined [source](https://www.morningstar.com/markets/markets-brief-chip-stocks-sell-off-investors-rotate-into-value-what-watch-big-tech-earnings).
*   **AI Stock Rebound:** AI-related equities bounced back as government yields fell and oil prices eased. Intel, Nvidia, AMD, and Broadcom saw modest gains after prior declines [source](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/us-chip-stocks-rise-after-steepest-weekly-selloff-in-months-4957420).
*   **Analyst Outlook:** Goldman Sachs maintains a constructive setup for US semis, expecting upward earnings revisions in Q3 for most segments. They are bullish on equipment, memory, and analog sectors, with top picks including AMD (target raised to $700, Buy) and Applied Materials (top pick, $670 target) [source](https://news.platform.elebank.com/post/1000606661/after-the-philadelphia-semiconductor-index-plunged-11-in-two-months).
*   **Valuation Concerns:** While the AI investment outlook remains buoyant (Morgan Stanley projects AI investment to reach $1.6T in 2027 and $1.8T in 2028), questions persist about whether investors will continue to pay premium valuations amid debt and rate concerns [source](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/us-chip-stocks-rise-after-steepest-weekly-selloff-in-months-4957420).
*   **Hyperscaler Capex:** Hyperscaler capital expenditure is vast (over $750 billion this year, double 2025), and upcoming earnings reports from major tech companies will provide insight into future AI spending expectations [source](https://www.morningstar.com/markets/markets-brief-chip-stocks-sell-off-investors-rotate-into-value-what-watch-big-tech-earnings).
*   **Companies to Watch:** On weakness, Astera Labs, Credo, MACOM, and Amkor are highlighted for strong fundamentals and improving estimates. Summary:

- The study compares write-heavy sysbench tests on a large server using modern Postgres versions (including Postgres 16.13, 18.3, and 19 beta1) versus MySQL 8.4.7 with InnoDB.
- Key finding: Postgres shows substantial throughput variance across tests, while MySQL/InnoDB is more stable.
- Overall throughput:
  - In 6 of 10 tests, InnoDB's average throughput is noticeably higher than Postgres.
  - In 1 test, results are similar between them.
  - In 3 tests, Postgres outperforms InnoDB.
- Per-test observations:
  - In tests where VMSTAT/iostat data are provided, Postgres tends to perform more write IO per operation than InnoDB.
  - InnoDB generally uses more CPU and experiences more context switches in several tests; Postgres may also see higher CPU in some cases.
- Specific results highlights:
  - update-index: InnoDB ~1.55x faster on average; Postgres shows high variance; Postgres writes more per operation.
  - update-zipf: InnoDB ~1.09x faster on average; Postgres higher write IO per operation; similar CPU usage overall with InnoDB more CPU-intensive in some measurements.
  - insert: Postgres ~2.06x faster than InnoDB on average; Postgres writes more per operation; InnoDB can be more CPU-intensive in some scenarios.
- Practical context:
  - The tests run for extended durations (2 hours per microbenchmark) with large tables that cannot be cached, and a vacuum is performed after each test to emulate real-world maintenance pressure.
  - The goal is to identify potential regressions associated with CPU overhead and MVCC/GC-related contention (Postgres vacuum vs InnoDB purge).
- Bottom line:
  - Throughput drops observed for Postgres across newer versions (not conclusively a regression yet).
  - InnoDB generally outperforms Postgres in the majority of tests, though Postgres outperforms InnoDB in some, and both systems vary by workload pattern (e.g., update-types vs insert-heavy workloads).

Essential results

- Postgres 17rc1 vs Postgres 15.8
  - Overall: Performance is mostly similar.
  - Writes: up to ~13% faster in some read-heavy/less IO-bound cases; one intermittently affected case (l.i2) exists.
  - Reads: largely unchanged or very close; small improvements in some read-heavy scenarios.

- MySQL 8.0.39 vs MySQL 5.6.51
  - Writes: dramatically faster (roughly 2.5x to 4x faster) in 8.0.39.
  - Reads: mixed – 8.0.39 slower, similar to, or faster than 5.6.51 depending on the context.
  - Point queries: substantially faster in 8.0.39.

- MySQL vs Postgres (relative performance)
  - Write-heavy and range queries: Postgres 17rc1 generally faster.
  - Point queries: MySQL 8.0.39 generally faster.
  - On average for point queries, MySQL and Postgres have comparable QPS in some cases; MySQL tends to excel on point lookups, while Postgres excels on writes and range scans.

- By workload category
  - Cached (small data, fits in memory):
    - Postgres: write-heavy gains up to ~11% (17rc1 vs 15.8); reads similar.
    - MySQL: write-heavy gains 2.5x–4x (8.0.39 vs 5.6.51); reads down ~12–27%.
  - Less IO-bound (moderate data, ~64M rows/table):
    - Postgres: write-heavy gains ~13% (17rc1 vs 15.8); reads similar.
    - MySQL: substantial write improvements; reads still weaker than 5.6.51 in some tests.
  - More IO-bound (large data, ~200M rows/table):
    - Postgres: write-heavy gains; reads mostly similar/slightly faster.
    - MySQL: continued strong write improvements; point queries remain faster overall; range queries show some slower performance vs older MySQL.

- Key takeaway
  - If your workload is write-heavy or involves many range queries, Postgres 17rc1 generally performs better.
  - If your workload emphasizes point queries, MySQL 8.0.39 tends to outperform older MySQL versions and can be competitive with Postgres on some point-query scenarios.
  - Overall, MySQL shows large gains in write performance from 5.6 to 8.0, but read throughput behavior is more variable depending on the workload.

- Study compares PostgreSQL and MySQL performance in a benchmarking framework geared toward large-scale behavioral data for continuous authentication.
- Core finding: PostgreSQL consistently outperforms MySQL in select operations, both with and without where clauses.

- Overall takeaway: PostgreSQL is more suitable for low-latency, high-concurrency scenarios typical of continuous authentication systems.

results.search_result:
Summary:
- In MySQL (InnoDB) vs PostgreSQL, writes are generally faster on PostgreSQL, especially for updates that require index maintenance.
- Binlog impact: 
  - With binlog disabled, MySQL insert throughput approaches PostgreSQL, but update throughput remains notably worse for MySQL; the gap widens when updates touch indexes.
  - With binlog enabled, MySQL throughput falls further (roughly 34–83% of binlog-off results depending on operation), with update-index the most affected.
- fsync impact: Enabling fsync widens the performance gap in favor of PostgreSQL. MySQL pays extra cost for binlog fsyncs and InnoDB redo fsyncs; PostgreSQL fsyncs only for WAL, plus other factors.
- Postgres optimizations: Full_page_writes=on can reduce performance for certain workloads if using pglz compression; using lz4 mitigates this. The fsync/WAL behavior remains more favorable to PostgreSQL overall.
- InnoDB doublewrite buffer options (off, on, DETECT_ONLY) show little impact in these results, though DETECT_ONLY is supported for workloads with heavier write-back.
- Bottom line: PostgreSQL generally outperforms MySQL for these configurations, especially for updates with index maintenance; disabling binlog improves MySQL performance relative to its binlog-on baseline but typically does not close the gap to PostgreSQL.

results.search_result:
Summary:
- Problem: Web apps often see fast responses in development but multi-second latency under production due to PostgreSQL bottlenecks; database work frequently drives overall latency.
- Diagnostic workflow: Use EXPLAIN (and EXPLAIN ANALYZE) to inspect query plans and runtimes, compare estimated costs, actual times, and row counts to spot inefficiencies.
- Key outputs to watch: startup_cost and total_cost, actual time (first_row/last_row) with ANALYZE, estimated vs. actual rows, and the scan type (Sequential Scan vs. Index Scan).
- Indexing guidance:
  - B-tree indexes for common sortable/equality/range queries on typical data types (integers, timestamps, strings, UUIDs).
  - GIN indexes for JSONB, array containment, and full-text-like searches.
  - Partial indexes to cover queries that target a subset of rows (e.g., status = 'active') to reduce index size and maintenance.
- Storage vs. performance trade-offs: Indexes speed reads but increase storage and slow writes; choose types based on query patterns.
- Load and connections:
  - PostgreSQL uses a backend process per connection; high concurrent requests require appropriate memory and connection limits.
  - If you exceed limits, new connections fail.
  - Connection pooling is recommended; Render supports PgBouncer for transaction-level pooling. Note: enabling pooling restarts the DB and causes brief downtime.
- Practical setup on Render:
  - Enable PgBouncer via the database Info page; pooled connections use port 6432, direct connections use 5432.
  - Pooling reduces connection overhead and helps with latency under load but plan downtime for the switch.
- Maintenance and monitoring cycle:
  - Continuously monitor slow queries, run EXPLAIN plans, implement targeted indexes or query rewrites, re-measure, and iterate.
  - Consider integrating Datadog or similar tools to correlate Postgres metrics with request traces and identify latency sources quickly.

Takeaway: To maintain responsive production performance, regularly analyze queries with EXPLAIN/ANALYZE, apply targeted indexing (including partial and GIN where appropriate), use connection pooling (PgBouncer) to manage concurrent connections, and adopt an iterative workflow with monitoring to detect and address bottlenecks before user impact.

runs.report:
## PostgreSQL vs. MySQL for Write-Heavy Web Applications

This report summarizes key findings and considerations when choosing between PostgreSQL and MySQL for web applications with a high volume of write operations.

### Performance Benchmarks

*   **Mixed Workloads and General Performance**
    *   PostgreSQL 17rc1 generally shows better performance for write-heavy and range queries [source](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2024/09/mysql-and-postgres-vs-insert-benchmark.html).
    *   MySQL 8.0.39 generally performs faster for point queries and can be competitive with PostgreSQL in some point-query scenarios [source](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2024/09/mysql-and-postgres-vs-insert-benchmark.html).
    *   In a study comparing PostgreSQL and MySQL for large-scale behavioral data for continuous authentication, PostgreSQL consistently outperformed MySQL in select operations (fetch all records, select with `WHERE` clauses) and showed near parity with a slight edge in insert performance [source](https://www.mdpi.com/1999-5903/16/10/382).
    *   During complex, simultaneous operations (mixed inserts and selects), PostgreSQL remained stable, while MySQL's performance degraded [source](https://www.mdpi.com/1999-5903/16/10/382).
    *   A study using sysbench tests on a large server showed that in 6 out of 10 tests, InnoDB's (MySQL) average throughput was noticeably higher than PostgreSQL. PostgreSQL showed substantial throughput variance across tests, while MySQL/InnoDB was more stable. PostgreSQL outperformed InnoDB in 3 tests, and results were similar in 1 test [source](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2026/06/write-heavy-sysbench-tests-large-server.html).
    *   Specifically, for `update-index` and `update-zipf` workloads, InnoDB was faster, while for `insert` workloads, PostgreSQL was approximately 2.06x faster on average [source](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2026/06/write-heavy-sysbench-tests-large-server.html).
    *   PostgreSQL tends to perform more write IO per operation than InnoDB in tests where VMSTAT/iostat data are available [source](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2026/06/write-heavy-sysbench-tests-large-server.html).

*   **Version-Specific Performance Changes**
    *   PostgreSQL 17rc1 showed performance mostly similar to 15.8, with writes up to ~13% faster in some read-heavy/less IO-bound cases [source](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2024/09/mysql-and-postgres-vs-insert-benchmark.html).
    *   MySQL 8.0.39 demonstrated dramatically faster writes (roughly 2.5x to 4x faster) compared to MySQL 5.6.51 [source](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2024/09/mysql-and-postgres-vs-insert-benchmark.html).

### Write Performance Tuning Strategies

*   **MySQL Specifics**
    *   Disabling the binlog in MySQL can significantly improve insert throughput to approach PostgreSQL levels, but update throughput (especially with index maintenance) remains worse than PostgreSQL [source](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2024/09/configuration-options-that-make-writes.html).
    *   Enabling the binlog further reduces MySQL throughput (34–83% of binlog-off results), with `update-index` being the most affected operation [source](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2024/09/configuration-options-that-make-writes.html).
    *   MySQL incurs extra costs for `fsync` operations due to both binlog `fsync`s and InnoDB redo `fsync`s [source](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2024/09/configuration-options-that-make-writes.html).

*   **PostgreSQL Specifics**
    *   PostgreSQL generally outperforms MySQL for writes, particularly for updates requiring index maintenance [source](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2024/09/configuration-options-that-make-writes.html).
    *   PostgreSQL's `fsync`/WAL behavior is generally more favorable, as it primarily `fsync`s for WAL [source](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2024/09/configuration-options-that-make-writes.html).
    *   `full_page_writes=on` in PostgreSQL can reduce performance for certain workloads if `pglz` compression is used; `lz4` compression can mitigate this [source](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2024/09/configuration-options-that-make-writes.html).

*   **General Optimization Practices (Applicable to both, but often highlighted for PostgreSQL)**
    *   **Query Analysis:** Use `EXPLAIN` and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to inspect query plans, identify inefficiencies, and compare estimated vs. actual costs and row counts [source](https://render.com/articles/postgresql-performance-optimization-for-web-applications), [source](https://www.dbgorilla.com/learn/).
    *   **Indexing:**
        *   B-tree indexes are suitable for common sortable/equality/range queries [source](https://render.com/articles/postgresql-performance-optimization-for-web-applications).
        *   GIN indexes are beneficial for JSONB, array containment, and full-text searches [source](https://render.com/articles/postgresql-performance-optimization-for-web-applications).
        *   Partial indexes can be used for queries targeting a subset of rows to reduce index size and maintenance [source](https://render.com/articles/postgresql-performance-optimization-for-web-applications).
        *   Understand the trade-offs: indexes speed reads but increase storage and slow writes [source](https://render.com/articles/postgresql-performance-optimization-for-web-applications).
        *   Create indexes concurrently (`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`) to avoid downtime [source](https://www.dbgorilla.com/learn/).
    *   **Connection Management:**
        *   PostgreSQL uses a backend process per connection; manage high concurrent requests with appropriate memory and connection limits [source](https://render.com/articles/postgresql-performance-optimization-for-web-applications).
        *   Connection pooling (e.g., PgBouncer) is recommended to reduce connection overhead and manage latency under load [source](https://render.com/articles/postgresql-performance-optimization-for-web-applications), [source](https://www.dbgorilla.com/learn/).
    *   **Maintenance:** Regularly address table bloat (MVCC dead tuples) using `VACUUM` and `pg_repack` [source](https://www.dbgorilla.com/learn/). Tune `autovacuum` parameters [source](https://www.dbgorilla.com/learn/).
    *   **Monitoring:** Continuously monitor slow queries, correlate database metrics with request traces, and adopt an iterative workflow to detect and address bottlenecks [source](https://render.com/articles/postgresql-performance-optimization-for-web-applications).

### Conclusion

For write-heavy web applications, the choice between PostgreSQL and MySQL depends heavily on the specific workload patterns. PostgreSQL generally excels in `INSERT`-heavy scenarios and complex mixed operations, especially when range queries or non-point lookups are frequent. It also exhibits more stable performance under concurrent stress with mixed workloads. MySQL (InnoDB) can show higher throughput for certain `UPDATE` workloads and is generally faster for point queries. Tuning configurations like binlog and `fsync` are critical, with PostgreSQL often having a performance advantage due to its WAL architecture. Regardless of the choice, robust query analysis, strategic indexing, and effective connection management are crucial for maintaining performance in production environments.

Summary:
- In MySQL (InnoDB) vs PostgreSQL, writes are generally faster on PostgreSQL, especially for updates that require index maintenance.
- Binlog impact: 
  - With binlog disabled, MySQL insert throughput approaches PostgreSQL, but update throughput remains notably worse for MySQL; the gap widens when updates touch indexes.
  - With binlog enabled, MySQL throughput falls further (roughly 34–83% of binlog-off results depending on operation), with update-index the most affected.
- fsync impact: Enabling fsync widens the performance gap in favor of PostgreSQL. MySQL pays extra cost for binlog fsyncs and InnoDB redo fsyncs; PostgreSQL fsyncs only for WAL, plus other factors.
- Postgres optimizations: Full_page_writes=on can reduce performance for certain workloads if using pglz compression; using lz4 mitigates this. The fsync/WAL behavior remains more favorable to PostgreSQL overall.
- InnoDB doublewrite buffer options (off, on, DETECT_ONLY) show little impact in these results, though DETECT_ONLY is supported for workloads with heavier write-back.
- Bottom line: PostgreSQL generally outperforms MySQL for these configurations, especially for updates with index maintenance; disabling binlog improves MySQL performance relative to its binlog-on baseline but typically does not close the gap to PostgreSQL.

PostgreSQL (the Elephant) generally outperforms MySQL (the Dolphin) across 17 tested scenarios, with higher throughput and lower latency.

Key results by workload (PostgreSQL vs MySQL, approximate ranges):
- Overall throughput (QPS): PostgreSQL up to 3.72x higher in mixed workloads; generally 2–4x higher in many tests.
- Latency: PostgreSQL latency substantially lower across all tests (mean and 99th percentile reductions commonly 2–11x, depending on workload).
- Specific workloads:
  - Inserts: PostgreSQL ~1.05–4.87x throughput advantage; 3.5–11x lower mean latency; 4.2–10.7x lower 99th percentile latency. Single-row inserts: 21,338 QPS (4.009 ms 99th) vs MySQL 4,383 QPS (42.729 ms 99th).
  - Selects: PostgreSQL ~1.04–1.67x higher throughput; latency 1.25–4.51x better at 99th percentile. Single-row selects by id: 55,200 QPS (5.446 ms 99th) vs MySQL 33,469 QPS (12.721 ms 99th).
  - Updates: PostgreSQL ~4.2–4.82x higher throughput; latency 6.0–10.6x lower (mean) and 7.5–8.5x lower (99th). By-id multi-column updates: 18,046 QPS (4.704 ms 99th) vs MySQL 3,747 QPS (39.774 ms 99th).
  - Deletes: PostgreSQL ~3.27–4.65x higher throughput; latency ~6–10x lower (mean) and ~9–10x lower (99th). By-id deletes: 18,285 QPS (4.661 ms 99th) vs MySQL 5,596 QPS (43.039 ms 99th).

Overall takeaway: PostgreSQL delivers superior performance in most scenarios, with notably better throughput and significantly lower latency across inserts, selects, updates, deletes, and mixed workloads.

- Bottom line: For 2026 SaaS transactional workloads, Postgres 17 is the clear winner for 80% of use cases, with MySQL 8.4 remaining preferable mainly for batch-heavy or MySQL-centric scenarios. Start new SaaS projects with Postgres 17 and test migrations from MySQL 8.x if write constraints exist.

- The article argues that MySQL has several advantages over PostgreSQL for certain workloads, especially write-heavy and deployment scenarios.
- Key points:
  - Storage and writes: MySQL’s clustered index storage and undo logging can yield better write performance and lower write amplification than PostgreSQL’s heap storage with MVCC and heavier WAL/VACUUM needs. It notes that PostgreSQL improvements like HOT updates help but don’t fully close the gap.
  - Replication and failover: MySQL Group Replication offers built-in single- and multi-primary replication with automatic failover and conflict handling. PostgreSQL relies on external tools (e.g., Patroni, pg_auto_failover) with higher operational overhead.
  - Invisible indexes: MySQL supports invisible indexes to test or temporarily disable index usage without affecting live queries, aiding optimization.
  - Online schema changes: MySQL has mature, production-ready online schema-change tooling (e.g., gh-ost, pt-online-schema-change); PostgreSQL lacks a comparable, widely adopted solution.
  - Connection handling: PostgreSQL uses a process-per-connection model with strong isolation but higher memory and context-switch overhead; MySQL’s thread-per-connection model is more scalable but risks entire-server crashes from a single long-running query.
- Context: The piece underscores ongoing PostgreSQL challenges (e.g., transaction ID wraparound, MultiXact exhaustion) and suggests OrioleDB as a future option, while highlighting MySQL’s enduring architectural advantages and ecosystem maturity (replication, online DDL tools, invisible indexes).

If you’re deciding between PostgreSQL and MySQL for a write-heavy or highly available deployment, this article leans toward MySQL as the more mature, scalable choice today, particularly for replication, online schema changes, and optimization workflows.

results.search_result:
Here’s a concise summary of the article’s essential results:

- Storage models:
  - MySQL (InnoDB): Uses a clustered B+Tree where the table data lives in leaf nodes; secondary indexes point to primary keys. Updates are often in-place; undo logs support MVCC for reads of old versions.
  - PostgreSQL: Uses a heap storage model with a separate B-Tree index structure containing CTIDs that point to heap locations. Updates create new full rows (no in-place overwrite) to maintain MVCC.

- Update behavior and costs:
  - MySQL (InnoDB): In-place updates when size doesn’t increase; uses Undo Log for MVCC. If the updated column isn’t indexed, index structures remain untouched. Writes are generally more space-efficient for small changes.
  - PostgreSQL: Every UPDATE is effectively a delete + insert of a new row. Leads to write amplification (new full row written). All relevant index pointers may need updating even if the change doesn’t affect indexed columns, since CTIDs point to heap rows.

- Deletion handling and space reclamation:
  - MySQL (InnoDB): Deleted rows are marked and placed on a free list within the leaf page; space is reused by subsequent inserts.
  - PostgreSQL: Deleted rows become Dead Tuples, tracked with transaction IDs. Space is reclaimed later by VACUUM; poor autovacuum tuning can cause table bloat and higher I/O.

- Practical guidance:
  - For append-only/static data with heavy analytical queries and complex data types, PostgreSQL is the stronger all-in-one option.
  - For write-heavy workloads with frequent updates on a small set of rows, InnoDB (MySQL) tends to offer more stable I/O and lower write amplification.

- Bottom line:
  - If your app prioritizes write efficiency and update-heavy patterns, MySQL/InnoDB is preferable.
  - If your app prioritizes complex queries, data diversity, and fewer but bulk updates, PostgreSQL is preferable.

Summary:

- Overall: PostgreSQL and MySQL (InnoDB) are both mature, ACID-relational DBs suitable for most web apps. Choose based on architectural differences and team needs.

Key takeaways:
- When to choose PostgreSQL (default recommendation):
  - No constraints backing you: richer type system, diverse index types, transactional DDL, and strong extensions cover more needs in one system.
  - Useful features: jsonb, partial indexes, GIN/BRIN/GiST indexes, materialized views, richer data types.
- When to choose MySQL (InnoDB):
  - Team already proficient with MySQL.
  - Workload dominated by primary-key lookups and simple writes.
  - You want built-in high-availability (Group Replication, InnoDB Cluster) without extra tooling.
  - You plan to shard at scale (Vitess ecosystem).
- Core architectural differences (highlights):
  - Storage and MVCC: PostgreSQL stores old row versions in-table with VACUUM cleanup; MySQL uses undo logs and purge threads.
  - Isolation: PostgreSQL defaults to Read Committed; MySQL defaults to Repeatable Read.
  - DDL: PostgreSQL supports transactional DDL; MySQL DDL statements are atomic but commit implicitly.
  - Replication: PostgreSQL offers physical streaming (WAL) and logical replication; MySQL uses binary log with Group Replication.
  - Failover: PostgreSQL requires external tools or managed services for automatic failover; MySQL provides built-in options (Group Replication, InnoDB Cluster).
  - Extensibility: PostgreSQL through extensions; MySQL via plugins/components.
  - Licensing: PostgreSQL (permissive) vs MySQL Community (GPLv2) with Oracle licenses for commercial options.
- Decision guide:
  1) No constraints → PostgreSQL.
  2) If you’re already on MySQL → stay with MySQL.
  3) High-volume PK reads/writes → InnoDB’s clustered index is advantageous.
  4) Need automatic failover out-of-the-box → MySQL offers built-in options; PostgreSQL needs tooling.
  5) Planning to shard → consider Vitess (MySQL) vs. Citus (PostgreSQL).
  6) Manage connection/transaction practices (set deliberate isolation, keep transactions short, plan pooling).

If you want a quick pick:
- Choose PostgreSQL for broader capabilities and fewer external tools.
- Choose MySQL if you’re existing with it and want built-in HA or Vitess-based sharding.

runs.report:
## PostgreSQL vs. MySQL for Write-Heavy Web Applications

This report compares PostgreSQL and MySQL, specifically focusing on their performance and features relevant to write-heavy web applications.

### Performance Benchmarks

**PostgreSQL generally shows superior performance in many write-heavy scenarios, but MySQL (InnoDB) can have advantages in specific update and batch insert workloads.**

*   **Overall Throughput and Latency**
    *   PostgreSQL generally achieves higher throughput and significantly lower latency across a range of workloads (inserts, selects, updates, deletes, mixed workloads) [binaryigor.com](https://binaryigor.com/mysql-vs-postgresql-performance.html).
    *   One benchmark indicated PostgreSQL outperformed MySQL in 16 out of 17 scenarios, with throughput up to 3.72x higher in mixed workloads and latency reductions commonly 2–11x [binaryigor.com](https://binaryigor.com/mysql-vs-postgresql-performance.html).

*   **Insert Performance**
    *   PostgreSQL demonstrates a significant throughput advantage for single-row inserts (e.g., 21,338 QPS vs. MySQL's 4,383 QPS, with substantially lower 99th percentile latency) [binaryigor.com](https://binaryigor.com/mysql-vs-postgresql-performance.html).
    *   PostgreSQL also shows higher throughput for single-row inserts (11,240 vs 9,870 writes/sec) and JSON writes (8,120 vs 6,540 writes/sec) with lower p99 latency (12ms vs 18ms) on ARM architecture [johal.in](https://johal.in/postgres-17-vs-mysql-84-write-throughput-benchmarks).
    *   However, MySQL 8.4 shows better performance for batch INSERTs, outperforming PostgreSQL 17 by approximately 2.5% (10,120 vs 9,870 writes/sec) due to its InnoDB change buffer [johal.in](https://johal.in/postgres-17-vs-mysql-84-write-throughput-benchmarks).

*   **Update Performance**
    *   PostgreSQL often shows higher throughput (e.g., 4.2–4.82x higher) and significantly lower latency (e.g., 6.0–10.6x lower mean latency) for updates (e.g., 18,046 QPS vs MySQL's 3,747 QPS) [binaryigor.com](https://binaryigor.com/mysql-vs-postgresql-performance.html).
    *   Conversely, some write-heavy Sysbench tests found InnoDB to outperform Postgres in update-related tests, with InnoDB throughput being about 1.55x higher on average, although Postgres exhibited notable variance across versions [smalldatum.blogspot.com](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2026/06/write-heavy-sysbench-tests-large-server.html).

*   **Delete Performance**
    *   PostgreSQL generally has higher throughput (e.g., 3.27–4.65x higher) and lower latency (e.g., 6–10x lower mean latency) for deletes (e.g., 18,285 QPS vs MySQL's 5,596 QPS) [binaryigor.com](https://binaryigor.com/mysql-vs-postgresql-performance.html).

### Architectural and Feature Differences

**Key architectural differences influence write performance and operational overhead, with MySQL often lauded for its built-in HA and online schema change tools, while PostgreSQL offers richer features and extensibility.**

*   **Storage and MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control)**
    *   **PostgreSQL:** Uses a heap storage model where updates create new full rows ("dead tuples") to maintain MVCC. Space is reclaimed by `VACUUM`, which can lead to write amplification, table bloat, and higher I/O if not tuned correctly [dev.to](https://dev.to/quangpv/how-the-two-most-popular-open-source-databases-mysql-postgresql-handle-insert-update-delete-4klf), [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
    *   **MySQL (InnoDB):** Uses a clustered B+Tree where data resides in leaf nodes. Updates are often in-place, using undo logs for MVCC. This can lead to more stable I/O and lower write amplification, especially for frequent updates on a small set of rows [dev.to](https://dev.to/quangpv/how-the-two-most-popular-open-source-databases-mysql-postgresql-handle-insert-update-delete-4klf), [bytebase.com](https://www.bytebase.com/blog/features-i-wish-postgres-had-but-mysql-already-has/).

*   **Replication and High Availability (HA)**
    *   **PostgreSQL:** Relies on external tools (e.g., Patroni, pg_auto_failover) for automatic failover and built-in HA, requiring higher operational overhead [bytebase.com](https://www.bytebase.com/blog/features-i-wish-postgres-had-but-mysql-already-has/), [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
    *   **MySQL:** Offers built-in solutions like Group Replication and InnoDB Cluster for single- and multi-primary replication with automatic failover and conflict handling, making it a more mature and scalable choice for HA out-of-the-box [bytebase.com](https://www.bytebase.com/blog/features-i-wish-postgres-had-but-mysql-already-has/), [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).

*   **Online Schema Changes (DDL)**
    *   **PostgreSQL:** Lacks a widely adopted, production-ready solution for online schema changes, which can be a challenge for write-heavy applications that need frequent schema updates without downtime [bytebase.com](https://www.bytebase.com/blog/features-i-wish-postgres-had-but-mysql-already-has/).
    *   **MySQL:** Has mature tools like `gh-ost` and `pt-online-schema-change` that are production-ready for online DDL, providing significant operational advantages [bytebase.com](https://www.bytebase.com/blog/features-i-wish-postgres-had-but-mysql-already-has/).

*   **Connection Handling**
    *   **PostgreSQL:** Uses a process-per-connection model, offering strong isolation but potentially higher memory and context-switch overhead [bytebase.com](https://www.bytebase.com/blog/features-i-wish-postgres-had-but-mysql-already-has/).
    *   **MySQL:** Uses a thread-per-connection model, which is generally more scalable but carries a risk of server-wide crashes if a single long-running query misbehaves [bytebase.com](https://www.bytebase.com/blog/features-i-wish-postgres-had-but-mysql-already-has/).

*   **Other Features**
    *   **PostgreSQL:** Offers a richer type system, diverse index types (GIN, BRIN, GiST), transactional DDL, JSONB support, partial indexes, and strong extensibility, making it suitable for complex data models and analytical queries [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter), [johal.in](https://johal.in/postgres-17-vs-mysql-84-write-throughput-benchmarks). PostgreSQL 17 also features parallel WAL writing, reducing full-page write overhead [johal.in](https://johal.in/postgres-17-vs-mysql-84-write-throughput-benchmarks).
    *   **MySQL:** Supports invisible indexes for testing optimization, and offers strong native sharding capabilities through ecosystems like Vitess [bytebase.com](https://www.bytebase.com/blog/features-i-wish-postgres-had-but-mysql-already-has/), [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).

### Recommendations

*   **Choose PostgreSQL for:**
    *   Most new SaaS transactional workloads, especially those involving complex data types, JSON-heavy applications, multi-tenant partitioning, or a need for a richer feature set out of the box [johal.in](https://johal.in/postgres-17-vs-mysql-84-write-throughput-benchmarks), [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
    *   Applications prioritizing broader capabilities and fewer external tools for core database features [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).

*   **Consider MySQL for:**
    *   Workloads dominated by batch-heavy inserts [johal.in](https://johal.in/postgres-17-vs-mysql-84-write-throughput-benchmarks).
    *   Existing teams proficient with the MySQL ecosystem [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
    *   Applications requiring built-in high-availability solutions (Group Replication, InnoDB Cluster) without needing to integrate external tooling [bytebase.com](https://www.bytebase.com/blog/features-i-wish-postgres-had-but-mysql-already-has/), [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
    *   Workloads with frequent updates on a small set of rows, where InnoDB's in-place updates and lower write amplification can be beneficial [dev.to](https://dev.to/quangpv/how-the-two-most-popular-open-source-databases-mysql-postgresql-handle-insert-update-delete-4klf).
    *   Scenarios needing mature online schema change tools or native sharding via ecosystems like Vitess [bytebase.com](https://www.bytebase.com/blog/features-i-wish-postgres-had-but-mysql-already-has/), [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
