- Overall: PostgreSQL and MySQL (InnoDB) are both mature, ACID-relational DBs suitable for most web apps. Choose based on architectural differences and team needs.

Key takeaways:
- When to choose PostgreSQL (default recommendation):
  - No constraints backing you: richer type system, diverse index types, transactional DDL, and strong extensions cover more needs in one system.
  - Useful features: jsonb, partial indexes, GIN/BRIN/GiST indexes, materialized views, richer data types.
- When to choose MySQL (InnoDB):
  - Team already proficient with MySQL.
  - Workload dominated by primary-key lookups and simple writes.
  - You want built-in high-availability (Group Replication, InnoDB Cluster) without extra tooling.
  - You plan to shard at scale (Vitess ecosystem).
- Core architectural differences (highlights):
  - Storage and MVCC: PostgreSQL stores old row versions in-table with VACUUM cleanup; MySQL uses undo logs and purge threads.
  - Isolation: PostgreSQL defaults to Read Committed; MySQL defaults to Repeatable Read.
  - DDL: PostgreSQL supports transactional DDL; MySQL DDL statements are atomic but commit implicitly.
  - Replication: PostgreSQL offers physical streaming (WAL) and logical replication; MySQL uses binary log with Group Replication.
  - Failover: PostgreSQL requires external tools or managed services for automatic failover; MySQL provides built-in options (Group Replication, InnoDB Cluster).
  - Extensibility: PostgreSQL through extensions; MySQL via plugins/components.
  - Licensing: PostgreSQL (permissive) vs MySQL Community (GPLv2) with Oracle licenses for commercial options.
- Decision guide:
  1) No constraints → PostgreSQL.
  2) If you’re already on MySQL → stay with MySQL.
  3) High-volume PK reads/writes → InnoDB’s clustered index is advantageous.
  4) Need automatic failover out-of-the-box → MySQL offers built-in options; PostgreSQL needs tooling.
  5) Planning to shard → consider Vitess (MySQL) vs. Citus (PostgreSQL).
  6) Manage connection/transaction practices (set deliberate isolation, keep transactions short, plan pooling).

If you want a quick pick:
- Choose PostgreSQL for broader capabilities and fewer external tools.
- Choose MySQL if you’re existing with it and want built-in HA or Vitess-based sharding.

Here’s a concise summary of the article’s essential results:

- Storage models:
  - MySQL (InnoDB): Uses a clustered B+Tree where the table data lives in leaf nodes; secondary indexes point to primary keys. Updates are often in-place; undo logs support MVCC for reads of old versions.
  - PostgreSQL: Uses a heap storage model with a separate B-Tree index structure containing CTIDs that point to heap locations. Updates create new full rows (no in-place overwrite) to maintain MVCC.

- Update behavior and costs:
  - MySQL (InnoDB): In-place updates when size doesn’t increase; uses Undo Log for MVCC. If the updated column isn’t indexed, index structures remain untouched. Writes are generally more space-efficient for small changes.
  - PostgreSQL: Every UPDATE is effectively a delete + insert of a new row. Leads to write amplification (new full row written). All relevant index pointers may need updating even if the change doesn’t affect indexed columns, since CTIDs point to heap rows.

- Deletion handling and space reclamation:
  - MySQL (InnoDB): Deleted rows are marked and placed on a free list within the leaf page; space is reused by subsequent inserts.
  - PostgreSQL: Deleted rows become Dead Tuples, tracked with transaction IDs. Space is reclaimed later by VACUUM; poor autovacuum tuning can cause table bloat and higher I/O.

- Practical guidance:
  - For append-only/static data with heavy analytical queries and complex data types, PostgreSQL is the stronger all-in-one option.
  - For write-heavy workloads with frequent updates on a small set of rows, InnoDB (MySQL) tends to offer more stable I/O and lower write amplification.

- Bottom line:
  - If your app prioritizes write efficiency and update-heavy patterns, MySQL/InnoDB is preferable.
  - If your app prioritizes complex queries, data diversity, and fewer but bulk updates, PostgreSQL is preferable.

Summary:

- The article argues that MySQL has several advantages over PostgreSQL for certain workloads, especially write-heavy and deployment scenarios.
- Key points:
  - Storage and writes: MySQL’s clustered index storage and undo logging can yield better write performance and lower write amplification than PostgreSQL’s heap storage with MVCC and heavier WAL/VACUUM needs. It notes that PostgreSQL improvements like HOT updates help but don’t fully close the gap.
  - Replication and failover: MySQL Group Replication offers built-in single- and multi-primary replication with automatic failover and conflict handling. PostgreSQL relies on external tools (e.g., Patroni, pg_auto_failover) with higher operational overhead.
  - Invisible indexes: MySQL supports invisible indexes to test or temporarily disable index usage without affecting live queries, aiding optimization.
  - Online schema changes: MySQL has mature, production-ready online schema-change tooling (e.g., gh-ost, pt-online-schema-change); PostgreSQL lacks a comparable, widely adopted solution.
  - Connection handling: PostgreSQL uses a process-per-connection model with strong isolation but higher memory and context-switch overhead; MySQL’s thread-per-connection model is more scalable but risks entire-server crashes from a single long-running query.
- Context: The piece underscores ongoing PostgreSQL challenges (e.g., transaction ID wraparound, MultiXact exhaustion) and suggests OrioleDB as a future option, while highlighting MySQL’s enduring architectural advantages and ecosystem maturity (replication, online DDL tools, invisible indexes).

If you’re deciding between PostgreSQL and MySQL for a write-heavy or highly available deployment, this article leans toward MySQL as the more mature, scalable choice today, particularly for replication, online schema changes, and optimization workflows.

results.search_result:
Summary of essential results

- Postgres (recent versions 16–19 beta) shows significant throughput variation (high variance) across tests.
- MySQL with InnoDB generally outperforms Postgres in 6 of 10 tests, performs similarly in 1 test, and Postgres is better in 3 of 10 tests.

Test specifics and key takeaways
- Workload: write-heavy sysbench tests with large tables that cannot be cached; each test runs 2 hours; after each test a vacuum is performed.
- IO and CPU patterns:
  - Postgres tends to do more write I/O per operation than InnoDB.
  - In some tests InnoDB consumes more CPU and context switches; in others the opposite.
- Regression signal:
  - Overall, Postgres throughput declines relative to its 15.17 baseline in several tests, suggesting possible regressions in newer versions, though the author is not definitive.
- Test categories with results:
  - update-index: InnoDB about 1.55× higher throughput on average; Postgres has higher per-op write IO; InnoDB uses more CPU.
  - update-zipf: InnoDB about 1.09× higher throughput on average; Postgres higher per-op write IO; InnoDB uses more CPU.
  - insert: Postgres about 2.06× higher throughput on average; Postgres higher per-op write IO; Postgres uses more CPU.
- Overall conclusion: InnoDB delivers stronger throughput in most tests, but Postgres can outperform in insert-heavy scenarios; allocations of hardware IO and CPU vary by test, explaining some fluctuations in observed throughput.

If you want, I can extract the exact per-test figures or contrast specific versions (16 vs 19) for a particular workload.

results.search_result:
Summary:

- Overall finding: PostgreSQL (the Elephant) outperforms MySQL (the Dolphin) across 14 of 17 test cases, with 1 draw. PostgreSQL delivers higher throughput (QPS) and lower latency in most scenarios, including mixed workloads.

Key throughput vs latency results (PostgreSQL vs MySQL):
- Mixed workload (1:1 writes:reads): PostgreSQL ~23,441 QPS vs MySQL ~6,300 QPS; PostgreSQL latency ~4.63 ms 99th vs MySQL ~40.64 ms.
- Inserts:
  - Single-row inserts: PostgreSQL ~21,338 QPS @ 99th ~4.009 ms vs MySQL ~4,383 QPS @ 99th ~42.729 ms.
  - 100-row batch inserts: PostgreSQL ~3,535 QPS @ 99th ~34.779 ms vs MySQL ~1,883 QPS @ 99th ~146.497 ms.
- Selects:
  - Single-row selects by id: PostgreSQL ~55,200 QPS @ 99th ~5.446 ms vs MySQL ~33,469 QPS @ 99th ~12.721 ms.
  - Multi-row sorted selects: PostgreSQL ~4,745 QPS @ 99th ~9.146 ms vs MySQL ~4,559 QPS @ 99th ~41.294 ms.
- Updates:
  - By id of multiple columns: PostgreSQL ~18,046 QPS @ 99th ~4.704 ms vs MySQL ~3,747 QPS @ 99th ~39.774 ms.
- Deletes:
  - By id: PostgreSQL ~18,285 QPS @ 99th ~4.661 ms vs MySQL ~5,596 QPS @ 99th ~43.039 ms.

Additional notes:
- For read-heavy vs write-heavy patterns, PostgreSQL generally achieves higher throughput and lower latency across most scenarios.
- The study used 8 CPUs with connection pool strategies favoring PostgreSQL for mixed workloads and writes, contributing to observed differences.

Bottom line: If you prioritize overall throughput and latency across diverse workloads, PostgreSQL offers stronger performance than MySQL in the tested scenarios.

results.search_result:
Essential results summary:

- Scope: CPU-bound Insert Benchmark comparing MySQL across versions (5.6 to 9.5) on 24-core and 32-core servers with a cached database (primarily CPU-bound, with some write IO steps). Tests use medium/high concurrency (8 clients on 24-core, 12 on 32-core).

- Overall trend across modern MySQL:
  - Write-heavy steps: Large performance improvements over older versions due to reduced mutex contention. Modern MySQL shows less CPU overhead and fewer context switches on certain write steps (notably l.i1 on both 24-core and 32-core).
  - Read-heavy steps: Performance regressions relative to older versions due to higher CPU usage per query; CPU per query and context switches are higher for range and point queries (qr*, qp*) with modern MySQL vs 5.6.51.

- MySQL vs MySQL across versions:
  - On write-heavy steps, modern MySQL generally performs better (lower cpupq and cspq on l.i1; cz13a with reduced mutex contention compares favorably to cz12a).
  - On read-heavy steps, modern MySQL tends to use more CPU per query (cpupq increases by up to ~1.4–1.5x; cspq increases as well).

- MySQL vs PostgreSQL:
  - PostgreSQL beats MySQL on read-heavy steps (qr*, qp*) in CPU efficiency and fewer context switches.
  - PostgreSQL shows more variance and occasional write stalls on write-heavy steps (l.i1 and especially l.i2), with l.i2 generally more write-stall prone.
  - On write-heavy steps, PostgreSQL has somewhat favorable variance properties but higher write-stall risk compared to MySQL on some configurations.

- Configs and variance:
  - cz12a vs cz12a_nocb (config variations) show little difference when the dataset is cached, due to minimal change buffering activity.
  - Read/write balance highlights: modern MySQL reduces mutex contention for writes but incurs higher CPU for reads; PostgreSQL excels on reads but can stall on heavy writes.

Bottom line:
- If your workload is write-heavy, modern MySQL versions offer notable gains over older versions.
- If your workload is read-heavy, PostgreSQL tends to be faster than MySQL, though MySQL may catch up or stall less on some write-heavy scenarios depending on configuration.

results.search_result:
Summary of essential results:

- Both PostgreSQL and MySQL (InnoDB) are mature, ACID-relational databases suitable for web apps; the best choice depends on architectural differences and workload.
- Key architectural differences:
  - Data storage and indexing: PostgreSQL uses heap storage with pointers from all indexes; MySQL uses a clustered B-tree by primary key with secondary indexes storing the primary key.
  - Old row versions: PostgreSQL keeps old versions in the table and vacuum removes them; MySQL uses undo logs and purge threads.
  - Isolation: PostgreSQL defaults to Read Committed; MySQL defaults to Repeatable Read.
  - DDL: PostgreSQL supports transactional DDL; MySQL DDL statements are atomic but commit implicitly.
  - Index types: PostgreSQL offers rich options (B-tree, hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN, BRIN, plus partial/expression indexes); MySQL supports B-tree, full-text, spatial, functional keys, invisible indexes.
  - JSON: PostgreSQL supports json/jsonb with GIN indexes; MySQL uses a JSON type with indexing via generated columns and functional/multi-valued indexes.
  - Materialized views: PostgreSQL has materialized views; MySQL does not.

- Decision guidance:

  3) Workload with heavy primary-key lookups and simple updates: MySQL/InnoDB may fit better.

runs.report:
## PostgreSQL vs. MySQL for Write-Heavy Web Applications

This report summarizes the comparison between PostgreSQL and MySQL, with a focus on their performance, features, and scalability for write-heavy web applications.

### Performance Benchmarks

*   **Mixed Workloads:**
    *   One study found PostgreSQL to significantly outperform MySQL in mixed workloads (1:1 writes:reads), achieving ~23,441 QPS and ~4.63 ms 99th percentile latency compared to MySQL's ~6,300 QPS and ~40.64 ms latency [binaryigor.com](https://binaryigor.com/mysql-vs-postgresql-performance.html).
    *   This study generally concluded that PostgreSQL delivered higher throughput and lower latency across 14 of 17 test cases, including mixed workloads [binaryigor.com](https://binaryigor.com/mysql-vs-postgresql-performance.html).

*   **Write-Heavy Operations:**
    *   **Inserts:**
        *   PostgreSQL showed superior performance in insert-heavy scenarios. In one benchmark, it achieved ~21,338 QPS for single-row inserts and ~3,535 QPS for 100-row batch inserts, compared to MySQL's ~4,383 QPS and ~1,883 QPS respectively [binaryigor.com](https://binaryigor.com/mysql-vs-postgresql-performance.html).
        *   Another benchmark indicated that modern MySQL versions offer notable performance gains over older versions for write-heavy steps due to reduced mutex contention [smalldatum.blogspot.com](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2026/01/cpu-bound-insert-benchmark-vs-mysql-on.html).
        *   However, a separate sysbench test found PostgreSQL to have about 2.06x higher throughput on average for inserts, though with higher per-operation write I/O and CPU usage [smalldatum.blogspot.com](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2026/06/write-heavy-sysbench-tests-large-server.html).
    *   **Updates:**
        *   PostgreSQL achieved ~18,046 QPS for updates by ID of multiple columns, while MySQL reached ~3,747 QPS [binaryigor.com](https://binaryigor.com/mysql-vs-postgresql-performance.html).
        *   In `update-index` and `update-zipf` sysbench tests, MySQL with InnoDB generally had higher throughput (1.55x and 1.09x respectively) compared to PostgreSQL, with PostgreSQL exhibiting higher per-operation write I/O [smalldatum.blogspot.com](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2026/06/write-heavy-sysbench-tests-large-server.html).
    *   **Deletes:** PostgreSQL showed higher throughput for deletes by ID, at ~18,285 QPS compared to MySQL's ~5,596 QPS [binaryigor.com](https://binaryigor.com/mysql-vs-postgresql-performance.html).

*   **Read Operations:**
    *   PostgreSQL generally performed better in read-heavy scenarios, showing higher CPU efficiency and fewer context switches [smalldatum.blogspot.com](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2026/01/cpu-bound-insert-benchmark-vs-mysql-on.html).
    *   For single-row selects by ID, PostgreSQL achieved ~55,200 QPS versus MySQL's ~33,469 QPS [binaryigor.com](https://binaryigor.com/mysql-vs-postgresql-performance.html).
    *   However, a more recent benchmark (PostgreSQL 18 vs MySQL 9.7) indicated that MySQL and MariaDB were 10-35% faster in reads than PostgreSQL [melonslab.com](https://www.melonslab.com/guides/postgresql-vs-mysql-vs-mariadb).

*   **Performance Variability:**
    *   PostgreSQL (recent versions 16-19 beta) exhibited significant throughput variation across write-heavy sysbench tests [smalldatum.blogspot.com](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2026/06/write-heavy-sysbench-tests-large-server.html).
    *   PostgreSQL can also experience more variance and occasional write stalls on write-heavy steps compared to MySQL on some configurations [smalldatum.blogspot.com](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2026/01/cpu-bound-insert-benchmark-vs-mysql-on.html).

### Key Features and Architectural Differences

*   **Data Storage and Indexing:**
    *   PostgreSQL uses heap storage with pointers from all indexes. It offers a wide array of index types (B-tree, hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN, BRIN, partial/expression indexes) [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
    *   MySQL uses a clustered B-tree by primary key, with secondary indexes storing the primary key. It supports B-tree, full-text, spatial, functional keys, and invisible indexes [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
*   **Transaction and Concurrency:**
    *   PostgreSQL defaults to Read Committed isolation; MySQL defaults to Repeatable Read [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
    *   PostgreSQL supports transactional DDL, allowing schema changes to be rolled back; MySQL DDL statements are atomic but commit implicitly [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
    *   PostgreSQL keeps old row versions in the table, cleaned by a `VACUUM` process; MySQL uses undo logs and purge threads [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
*   **JSON Support:** PostgreSQL offers `json` and `jsonb` types with GIN indexes, while MySQL uses a `JSON` type with indexing via generated columns and functional/multi-valued indexes [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
*   **Materialized Views:** PostgreSQL has built-in materialized views, a feature absent in MySQL [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
*   **Extensibility and Licensing:** PostgreSQL is highly extensible under a permissive license. MySQL relies on plugins and components, with GPLv2 and commercial licenses [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
*   **Memory and Disk Footprint:** PostgreSQL generally uses less idle memory and has a smaller data footprint compared to MySQL and MariaDB [melonslab.com](https://www.melonslab.com/guides/postgresql-vs-mysql-vs-mariadb).

### Scalability and Replication

*   **Replication and Failover:**
    *   PostgreSQL uses physical streaming and logical replication, but built-in failover requires external tooling (e.g., Patroni) or managed services [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
    *   MySQL uses binary logs with GTIDs and Group Replication, offering native built-in failover capabilities (e.g., InnoDB Cluster) [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
*   **Sharding Strategies:**
    *   Both databases can scale to very large workloads using various tools and architectures [howtheyscaled.com](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/postgresql-vs-mysql/).
    *   MySQL teams commonly leverage Vitess for sharding and online migrations [howtheyscaled.com](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/postgresql-vs-mysql/).
    *   PostgreSQL teams often use PgBouncer, read replicas, caching, and application-layer or custom sharding [howtheyscaled.com](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/postgresql-vs-mysql/).
*   **Real-world Scale:**
    *   Companies like OpenAI use PostgreSQL with a single primary and ~50 read replicas for ChatGPT [howtheyscaled.com](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/postgresql-vs-mysql/).
    *   GitHub handles ~5.5 million QPS across 50+ MySQL clusters, and Shopify uses Vitess for sharding [howtheyscaled.com](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/postgresql-vs-mysql/).
    *   The success of scaling largely depends on tooling and architecture rather than the inherent technology alone [howtheyscaled.com](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/postgresql-vs-mysql/).

### Conclusion

For a write-heavy web application, the choice between PostgreSQL and MySQL depends on specific workload patterns and architectural preferences:

*   **Choose PostgreSQL if:**
    *   You prioritize overall throughput and lower latency across diverse workloads, including mixed and insert-heavy scenarios [binaryigor.com](https://binaryigor.com/mysql-vs-postgresql-performance.html).
    *   You need advanced features like transactional DDL, a rich variety of index types, native JSONB support with GIN indexes, and materialized views [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
    *   You require strong data integrity rules and efficient restore operations [melonslab.com](https://www.melonslab.com/guides/postgresql-vs-mysql-vs-mariadb).
    *   You are comfortable implementing failover and sharding solutions with external tooling or managed services [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).

*   **Choose MySQL if:**
    *   Your workload involves frequent primary-key lookups and simple updates where InnoDB may perform well [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
    *   Your team already has extensive experience and tooling for MySQL [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
    *   You value vendor-provided automatic failover solutions like MySQL InnoDB Cluster [dpkdb.com](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
    *   You expect a higher throughput on `update-index` or `update-zipf` type workloads as observed in some benchmarks [smalldatum.blogspot.com](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2026/06/write-heavy-sysbench-tests-large-server.html).

- Both PostgreSQL and MySQL scale to very large workloads in real companies.
- PostgreSQL (examples: OpenAI, Figma, Notion, Atlassian, GitLab, etc.)
  - OpenAI runs ChatGPT on a single primary with ~50 read replicas.
  - Other teams use PgBouncer, read replicas, and application-layer sharding or custom proxies.

  - GitHub handles ~5.5 million QPS across 50+ clusters.
  - Slack ~2.3 million QPS; Shopify’s Shop app shards with Vitess; TAO caches a graph stored in sharded MySQL.
  - Shopify moved inventory reservations to MySQL with a bounded per-item row pool and transactional optimizations; PlanetScale benchmarks show up to ~1 million QPS with Vitess.
- Key takeaway (Verdict):
  - No inherent winner by technology alone. The success comes from scaling tooling and architecture.
  - MySQL teams commonly use Vitess for sharding; PostgreSQL teams lean on PgBouncer, read replicas, caching, and application-layer or custom sharding.
- Notable scale figures mentioned:
  - Postgres: 350 TB+ datasets, 800M users (OpenAI), 4M databases (Atlassian).
  - MySQL: hundreds of millions of users (Canva), $5.1M per minute peak during Black Friday (Shopify), 5.5M QPS (GitHub). TAO handles over a billion reads/sec for the graph cache.
- Sharding strategies covered:
  - PostgreSQL: custom proxies, logical sharding, selective replication, and caching.
  - MySQL: Vitess-based sharding, online migrations, and targeted uses of Skip Locked reads; Ghostferry for cross-shard moves.

results.search_result:
Summary:

- Topic: Assessing backup fuel options for electrically heated homes in cold climates, focusing on heat pump systems with electric or natural gas backup versus new conventional furnaces.

- Method: Hourly techno-economic model for 6,000 Canadian homes to compare space heating/cooling demand, emissions, household costs, marginal abatement costs, and electricity demand profiles under different backup configurations.

- Key findings:
  - Fully electrified heating (heat pumps with electric backup) can reduce annual space heating and cooling energy use by over 59% and cut national residential greenhouse gas emissions by up to 21 million tonnes CO2e per year vs. new conventional furnace replacements.
  - Economic outcome is mixed: without supportive policy, only about 9% of households save money with fully electric heating.
  - Fully electric systems tend to increase peak electricity demand.
  - Hybrid systems using natural gas backup have smaller impacts on peak demand and greenhouse gas reductions than fully electric systems.

- Implications:
  - Electrification can significantly lower energy use and emissions but may require policy measures (pricing, incentives, grid planning) to ensure broad household affordability and to manage peak load.
  - The choice of backup (electric vs. gas) materially affects peak demand and decarbonization outcomes.

results.search_result:
Summary of essential results

- Objective: Compare a gas absorption heat pump (GAHP) and an electric air-source heat pump (ASHP) for space heating (and cooling) in nine Canadian cities, using climate-based metrics: SCOP (seasonal performance), energy use, annual fuel costs, and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.

- Key performance: GAHP’s SCOP is lower than that of the electric ASHP in all nine cities, meaning GAHP is less energy-efficient overall for heating.

- Cost findings:
  - Heating-only operation: GAHP yields 13%–83% lower annual fuel costs than a electric ASHP across the nine cities.
  - Including cooling: GAHP remains more cost-effective in seven of the nine cities, but the magnitude of fuel cost savings is smaller.

- Emissions findings:
  - GAHP emits fewer GHGs than the electric ASHP in two of the nine cities; in the others, emissions are not consistently lower.
  - Overall, GAHPs can offer emissions benefits when the electricity grid has higher emission intensity.

- Influencing factors:
  - GAHP advantage grows in regions with lower natural gas prices relative to electricity prices.
  - Emissions benefits improve when the electrical grid is relatively high-emission.

- Practical tool: A screening method is developed to extend the findings beyond the nine Canadian cities. By using heating/cooling degree days and the local electricity-to-gas price ratio, the method helps determine, for any city, whether GAHP or electric ASHP is more advantageous.

- Implications for designers/owners: In colder climates or areas with high electricity costs, or where the grid is high-emission, GAHPs can be economically favorable and may offer emissions benefits; electric ASHPs may be preferable where electricity is cheap and cleaner, or gas is expensive.

- Publication details: Journal of Building Engineering, 2026; open for access under a non-commercial license.

results.search_result:
Summary: Essential results on cold-climate heat pumps (from the page)

- Real-world performance: Field studies show heat pumps work in cold winters, but running costs depend on fuel alternatives. PNNL found a median COP of 1.9 in 0–5°F; NREL found some cases where resistance heat dominated even when the heat pump was present. A correctly sized/commissioned unit delivered heat as advertised; poorly configured systems can use more electricity than the replaced resistance heat.
- Relative economics by fuel:
  - Against natural gas (in cold states): running cost is usually worse. A COP of 3.4 or higher is needed to break even, which no northern-market unit reliably achieves across the winter.
  - Against oil or propane: heat pumps are generally advantageous. A COP between 1.1 and 2.8 suffices to beat oil/propane for most of the heating season with a good cold-climate unit.
- Key guidance for homeowners (priority actions):
  1) Use actual electricity and fuel bills (not averages) to estimate costs.
  2) Check the unit’s COP at typical winter temperatures (e.g., 47°F, 17°F, 5°F) against your fuel cost—if it can’t clear the targeted COP at your main heating hours, running costs may be weak.
  3) For gas heating, consider dual-fuel strategy (heat pump plus furnace for extreme cold) and ensure crossover settings are computed correctly.
  4) Demand a proper load calculation (avoid oversizing; prevents short cycling and extra backup heat).

runs.report:
## Heat Pumps vs. Gas Furnaces in Cold Climates: A Cost Analysis

This report summarizes recent research comparing the running costs of heat pumps and gas furnaces in cold climates. The findings highlight the complex interplay of energy efficiency, fuel prices, emissions, and policy in determining cost-effectiveness.

### Cost-Effectiveness and Running Costs

The economic outcome of choosing between heat pumps and gas furnaces in cold climates is mixed and highly dependent on various factors, including local fuel prices and the specific type of heat pump.

*   **Heat Pumps vs. Natural Gas Furnaces**
    *   In cold states, the running cost of a heat pump is generally worse than natural gas. A Coefficient of Performance (COP) of 3.4 or higher is typically needed to break even against natural gas, which most northern-market units do not reliably achieve across the winter [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   Using 2025 U.S. averages (electricity at 17.30 cents/kWh and gas at $15.34/Mcf), the break-even COP for a heat pump to be cheaper than a 95% efficient gas furnace is approximately 3.25 [source](https://electricconsumer.org/guides/heat-pump-vs-gas-cost.html).
    *   In 17 of 45 states, a COP of 3.0 or higher makes heat pumps cheaper than gas furnaces at specified prices [source](https://electricconsumer.org/guides/heat-pump-vs-gas-cost.html).
    *   An Empire Center estimate for heating an average home from October to March suggested natural gas costs around $790, a heat pump $1,100, and electric resistance heating $3,300, without accounting for installation [source](https://www.empirecenter.org/publications/switching-to-electric-home-heating-could-add-thousands-to-energy-bills/).
    *   Nationwide, natural gas is typically cheaper, but heat pumps win in about 9 of 41 states with published winter gas prices when compared to an 80% gas furnace [source](https://homecostsbystate.com/en/heat-pump-vs-furnace/).
    *   A gas absorption heat pump (GAHP) can yield 13%–83% lower annual fuel costs than an electric air-source heat pump (ASHP) for heating-only operation across nine Canadian cities, and remains more cost-effective in seven cities when cooling is included [source](https://harvest.usask.ca/items/135e690b-94bb-43f0-b469-8f42bd69166d/full).
*   **Heat Pumps vs. Oil or Propane Furnaces**
    *   Heat pumps are generally more advantageous against oil or propane. A COP between 1.1 and 2.8 is sufficient to outperform oil/propane for most of the heating season with a good cold-climate unit [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   In Ohio, an 80% gas furnace costs $892/year, a heat pump (HSPF2 7.5) costs $1,299/year, while propane and oil furnaces are more expensive at $1,836 and $1,756 respectively [source](https://homecostsbystate.com/en/heat-pump-vs-furnace/).
*   **Factors Influencing Cost**
    *   The advantage of gas absorption heat pumps grows in regions with lower natural gas prices relative to electricity prices [source](https://harvest.usask.ca/items/135e690b-94bb-43f0-b469-8f42bd69166d/full).
    *   Performance heavily relies on correct sizing, proper commissioning, and effective management of backup heat [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   Policy measures, such as pricing, incentives, and grid planning, are crucial for widespread household affordability of fully electric heating [source](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enbuild.2026.116963).
    *   The choice of backup (electric vs. gas) significantly impacts peak electricity demand and decarbonization outcomes [source](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enbuild.2026.116963).
    *   Cold weather can cause heat pumps to deliver less heat per kWh, potentially leading to increased reliance on resistance heating, which sharply lowers seasonal efficiency [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).

### Energy Efficiency and Performance

Heat pumps demonstrate varying levels of energy efficiency depending on the type and operating conditions, with implications for overall energy consumption.

*   **Overall Efficiency**
    *   Fully electrified heating (heat pumps with electric backup) can reduce annual space heating and cooling energy use by over 59% compared to new conventional furnace replacements [source](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enbuild.2026.116963).
    *   Gas absorption heat pumps (GAHP) have a lower Seasonal Coefficient of Performance (SCOP) than electric air-source heat pumps (ASHP) in all nine Canadian cities studied, indicating lower energy efficiency for heating [source](https://harvest.usask.ca/items/135e690b-94bb-43f0-b469-8f42bd69166d/full).
    *   Field studies show that while heat pumps work in cold winters, running costs are highly dependent on fuel alternatives. A median COP of 1.9 was found at 0–5°F [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   Correctly sized and commissioned heat pump units deliver heat as advertised, while poorly configured systems can use more electricity than replaced resistance heat [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
*   **Key Performance Metrics**
    *   The Coefficient of Performance (COP) of a heat pump is not fixed; it varies with temperature. It's important to use the model's seasonal COP and a cold-climate figure for freezing conditions [source](https://electricconsumer.org/guides/heat-pump-vs-gas-cost.html).
    *   Colder climates can widen the dollar gap in favor of heat pumps, even if the COP ratio remains similar [source](https://electricconsumer.org/guides/heat-pump-vs-gas-cost.html).

### Environmental Impact

Electrification through heat pumps offers significant potential for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, though the extent of this benefit is influenced by the electricity grid's emission intensity.

*   **Greenhouse Gas Emissions**
    *   Fully electric heating can cut national residential greenhouse gas emissions by up to 21 million tonnes CO2e per year compared to new conventional furnace replacements [source](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enbuild.2026.116963).
    *   Gas absorption heat pumps emit fewer GHGs than electric air-source heat pumps in only two out of nine Canadian cities; overall emissions benefits improve when the electricity grid has higher emission intensity [source](https://harvest.usask.ca/items/135e690b-94bb-43f0-b469-8f42bd69166d/full).

### Practical Guidance for Homeowners

To optimize the cost-effectiveness and performance of heating systems in cold climates, homeowners should consider several practical steps.

*   **Assessment and Planning**
    *   Use actual electricity and fuel bills to estimate costs, rather than averages [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   Check the heat pump unit’s COP at typical winter temperatures (e.g., 47°F, 17°F, 5°F) against local fuel costs. If the unit cannot achieve the target COP during main heating hours, running costs may be high [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   For homes with natural gas, consider a dual-fuel strategy, using a heat pump for moderate cold and a furnace for extreme cold, and ensure crossover settings are calculated correctly [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   Demand a proper load calculation to avoid oversizing, which can lead to short cycling and increased reliance on backup heat [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   Understand the auxiliary heat lockout setting, as even small dependence on resistance heat can significantly reduce seasonal efficiency [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).

### Policy and Market Considerations

Policy choices and market conditions play a significant role in the viability and adoption of heat pump technologies.

*   **Economic Implications of Electrification**
    *   Without supportive policy, only about 9% of households may save money with fully electric heating [source](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enbuild.2026.116963).
    *   Fully electric systems tend to increase peak electricity demand, which hybrid systems with natural gas backup have smaller impacts on [source](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enbuild.2026.116963).
    *   The Empire Center suggests that replacing natural gas heating with electricity could raise bills by hundreds to thousands of dollars for New Yorkers due to higher electricity prices (63% above national average) [source](https://www.empirecenter.org/publications/switching-to-electric-home-heating-could-add-thousands-to-energy-bills/).
*   **Regulations and Incentives**
    *   New split heat pumps must meet 14.3 SEER2 and 7.5 HSPF2 efficiency standards, while new non-weatherized gas furnaces must reach 80% AFUE (moving to 95% by 2028) [source](https://homecostsbystate.com/en/heat-pump-vs-furnace/).
    *   Federal tax credits for heat pumps/furnaces expired for purchases after 2025; rebates vary by utility and region [source](https://homecostsbystate.com/en/heat-pump-vs-furnace/).

- Breakeven COP formula (example values): Breakeven COP = (293.07 × $/kWh) ÷ (gas $/therm ÷ 1.037 ÷ AFUE). If your heat pump’s average COP meets or exceeds this, it will cost less to heat than the furnace.
- Regional and fuel caveats: Climate zone affects achievable COP; in zones 1–3 and 4, heat pumps are favorable or breakeven favorable, while zones 5–8 often favor gas unless you have a cold-climate heat pump or dual-fuel setup.
- Other considerations: Ductwork, electrical work, and whether you already have AC impact total costs. Dual-fuel systems (heat pump with gas furnace) switch to gas when cold lowers COP. 
- Financials and incentives: The 25°C (30%, up to $2,000) federal tax credit ended for heat pumps placed after 12/31/2025; state/util rebates may apply. DOE rule: new gas furnaces post-12/18/2028 must be 95% AFUE (subject to judicial review/delay).
- Practical takeaway: Run a breakeven COP calculation using your local electricity and gas rates to decide, and consider climate suitability, existing infrastructure, and potential rebates.

## Heat Pumps vs. Gas Furnaces in Cold Climates: A Cost Analysis

This report summarizes the findings from recent research comparing the running costs of heat pumps and gas furnaces in cold climates. The analysis highlights that the cheaper option depends heavily on various factors, including fuel prices, grid intensity, system efficiency, and local policies.

### Running Cost Comparisons

The cost-effectiveness of heat pumps versus gas furnaces in cold climates varies significantly based on the type of fuel they are compared against and the specific local economic and environmental conditions.

*   **Against Natural Gas:**
    *   **Generally More Expensive:** In many cold states, heat pumps generally have higher running costs than natural gas furnaces. To break even with a gas furnace, a heat pump typically needs to maintain a Coefficient of Performance (COP) between 3.4 and 5.4, which is challenging for common units to sustain throughout a northern winter [heatpumpmath.com](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   **Break-even COP Varies:** Using 2025 U.S. averages, a heat pump requires a COP of 3.25 to be cheaper than a 95% efficient gas furnace. This break-even COP can range from 1.73 (Florida) to 5.81 (Alaska) across states [electricconsumer.org](https://electricconsumer.org/guides/heat-pump-vs-gas-cost.html). At 2026 EIA winter averages, the break-even COP against a 95% gas furnace is approximately 3.92, and against an 80% furnace, it's about 3.30 [gladewick.com](https://gladewick.com/heat-pump-vs-furnace-cost/).
    *   **Dual-Fuel Systems:** Dual-fuel setups, which use a heat pump for milder temperatures and switch to a gas furnace for the coldest hours, can be a cost-effective strategy [heatpumpmath.com](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   **Gas Absorption Heat Pumps (GAHP) vs. Electric Air-Source Heat Pumps (ASHP):** GAHP can offer lower annual fuel costs for heating in Canadian cities, with fuel costs 13%–83% lower than electric ASHP, especially when natural gas prices are cheaper relative to electricity [harvest.usask.ca](https://harvest.usask.ca/items/135e690b-94bb-43f0-b469-8f42bd69166d/full).

*   **Against Oil or Propane:**
    *   **Typically Cheaper:** Heat pumps are generally cheaper to run than furnaces using oil or propane. A COP of roughly 1.1 to 2.8 is often sufficient for a heat pump to beat oil/propane for most of the heating season, which good cold-climate units can achieve [heatpumpmath.com](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   **Significant Savings:** In an Ohio sample, an 80% AFUE propane furnace cost $1,836 annually, and an oil furnace cost $1,756, while a heat pump (HSPF2 7.5) cost $1,299 [homecostsbystate.com](https://homecostsbystate.com/en/heat-pump-vs-furnace/).

*   **Against Electric Resistance Heating:**
    *   **Always Cheaper:** Heat pumps are significantly more cost-effective than electric resistance heating, which is typically the most expensive option [homecostsbystate.com](https://homecostsbystate.com/en/heat-pump-vs-furnace/).

### Factors Influencing Costs

Several key factors determine the actual running costs and the most economical choice.

*   **Energy Prices:**
    *   The relative prices of natural gas and electricity are the most critical drivers. Heat pumps are more favorable when electricity is cheaper or gas is expensive, while gas furnaces are favored when gas prices are low [harvest.usask.ca](https://harvest.usask.ca/items/135e690b-94bb-43f0-b469-8f42bd69166d/full).
    *   Using actual electricity and fuel bills for comparison, rather than state averages, is crucial for accurate cost assessment [heatpumpmath.com](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).

*   **System Efficiency and Installation:**
    *   Proper sizing and commissioning are vital for heat pump performance. Mis-sized or poorly installed systems can lead to much higher energy use due to excessive reliance on auxiliary heat [heatpumpmath.com](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   Heat pump performance (COP) declines in very cold weather. Actual efficiency and output can drop, so lower HSPF2 values should be considered for harsh winters [homecostsbystate.com](https://homecostsbystate.com/en/heat-pump-vs-furnace/).
    *   Minimizing reliance on resistance heat, especially auxiliary heat lockout settings, can significantly impact seasonal energy use [heatpumpmath.com](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).

*   **Climate and Grid Intensity:**
    *   Cold climate heat pumps (CCHPs) do work in freezing temperatures, delivering heat with a median COP around 1.9 in the 0–5°F range in real cold winters [heatpumpmath.com](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   Grid electricity emission intensity affects the environmental and economic conclusions; higher emissions favor GAHP over electric ASHP [harvest.usask.ca](https://harvest.usask.ca/items/135e690b-94bb-43f0-b469-8f42bd69166d/full).
    *   In Canada, fully electrified heating can reduce annual space heating and cooling energy use by over 59% [doi.org/10.1016/j.enbuild.2026.116963](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enbuild.2026.116963).

### Policy and Incentives

Government policies and incentives play a significant role in making fully electric heating systems economically viable.

*   **Policy Support:** Electrification of residential heating offers substantial energy and emissions benefits but requires policy or mechanism support to keep costs favorable for most households. Without supportive policy, only about 9% of households might save money with fully electric heating [doi.org/10.1016/j.enbuild.2026.116963](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enbuild.2026.116963).
*   **Tax Credits and Rebates:** The federal 30% tax credit for heat pumps expired for improvements made after December 31, 2025. State and utility rebates may still apply and vary by location [homecostsbystate.com](https://homecostsbystate.com/en/heat-pump-vs-furnace/).

### Implications for Decision Making

*   **Personalized Calculation:** It is essential to perform a break-even COP calculation using local electricity and gas rates to make an informed decision [gladewick.com](https://gladewick.com/heat-pump-vs-furnace-cost/).
*   **Holistic View:** The comparison should include equipment and duct costs, potential rebates, fixed gas charges, and cooling costs, which are often omitted from simple running cost analyses [electricconsumer.org](https://electricconsumer.org/guides/heat-pump-vs-gas-cost.html).
*   **Backup Fuel Choice:** The choice of backup fuel (electric vs. natural gas) materially affects peak electricity load and greenhouse gas emissions, with gas-backup presenting different trade-offs than full electric backup [doi.org/10.1016/j.enbuild.2026.116963](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enbuild.2026.116963).

Essential results:

- Field data show air-source heat pumps (ASHPs) are significantly more efficient than fossil-fuel or electric-resistance heating, even when outdoor temperatures are below 0°C.
- At 5°C to −10°C, mean COP is 2.74 (median 2.62), meaning ASHPs can meet heating loads with much higher efficiency than alternatives.

- A key strategy to maintain performance is delivering heat at lower temperatures (lowering delivery temperature).
- Back-up heating may be used in the coldest conditions, but is typically engaged only when outside temperatures fall past around −10°C.
- For colder climates, ground-source heat pumps or hybrid systems may offer additional value.
- Overall policy takeaway: ASHPs are effective for most climates with proper design and installation; widespread deployment is viable for decarbonization in regions with space heating demand.

Summary of essential results from the Heat Pump Assessment Study (EPRI)

- Systems compared for a 2,600 sq ft Albany, NY home: gas furnace, electric furnace with resistance heating, and an air source heat pump (ASHP) with supplemental electric resistance heat.

  - ASHP (including supplemental heat) uses about 65% less total heating energy than natural gas furnaces and 59% less than electric resistance heating.

  - To meet winter loads, either larger ASHP equipment or supplemental heat (electric resistance or fossil fuel) is needed.
- Peak demand and energy use:
  - Heat pumps are less effective at reducing winter peak demand.
  - Supplemental heat accounts for a substantial portion of winter peak load; at peak hour, the distribution observed was approximately 67% supplemental heat vs 33% from the heat pump itself.
- System characteristics:
  - Heat pump supply air temperature is cooler (92°F) than gas furnace supply (135°F) while maintaining indoor setpoint (70°F in winter).
  - Primary energy varies with technology efficiency (COP) and defrost/fan energy considerations.
- Key takeaways:
  - Air source heat pumps offer significant energy savings overall compared with gas and electric resistance heating.
  - Their effectiveness declines at low outdoor temperatures, increasing reliance on supplemental heat and reducing peak-shaving benefits.
  - Meeting cold-season loads reliably may require system oversizing, supplemental heat, or both.

This report summarizes the recent findings on the operational cost and efficiency of heat pumps compared to gas furnaces in cold climates, aiming to inform our team's understanding and decision-making.

### I. Operating Cost Comparison

*   **Natural Gas:**
    *   In most northern winters, heat pumps typically cost more to run than natural gas furnaces [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   A heat pump would need a Coefficient of Performance (COP) between 3.4 and 5.4 to break even with natural gas, which is generally not achieved by units in northern winters [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   The "break-even COP" (where a heat pump costs the same as a 95% efficient gas furnace) averages 3.25 across the U.S. in 2025 (with electricity at 17.30 cents/kWh and gas at $15.34/Mcf). However, in many cold states, a significantly higher COP is required for a heat pump to be cheaper to run [source](https://electricconsumer.org/guides/heat-pump-vs-gas-cost.html).
    *   For example, break-even COPs in cold states range from 5.81 in Alaska, 5.29 in Michigan, and 4.88 in Wisconsin [source](https://electricconsumer.org/guides/heat-pump-vs-gas-cost.html).
    *   Some analyses indicate that in Midwestern climates, a high-efficiency gas furnace often remains superior for economics in the near term [source](https://www.mwalliance.org/sites/default/files/Furnaces-vs-ASHPs-Sept18.pdf).
    *   **Practical Guidance for Gas Users:** Consider dual-fuel strategies, keeping the gas furnace for extreme cold and using the heat pump otherwise [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
*   **Oil and Propane:**
    *   Heat pumps are generally cheaper to run than oil and propane heating in cold climates [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   A COP between 1.1 and 2.8 is often sufficient for a heat pump to beat oil/propane for most of the heating season [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
*   **General Operating Cost Findings (Typical Values):**
    *   Annual heating costs can range from $180–$320 for heat pumps vs. $300–$500 for gas furnaces [source](https://jouleio.com/blog/heat-pump-operating-cost-by-climate/).
    *   Total yearly costs (heating + cooling) for heat pumps are estimated at $780–$1,420, compared to $950–$1,700 for a gas furnace plus AC [source](https://jouleio.com/blog/heat-pump-operating-cost-by-climate/).
    *   **Break-Even Factors:** Heat pumps become more cost-effective when electricity prices are less than approximately three times the price of gas (per BTU) [source](https://jouleio.com/blog/heat-pump-operating-cost-by-climate/).
    *   **Calculation:** To compare costs, calculate dollars per MMBtu delivered, using 293.1 kWh per MMBtu for electricity and accounting for gas price and furnace efficiency [source](https://electricconsumer.org/guides/heat-pump-vs-gas-cost.html).

### II. Efficiency and Performance in Cold Climates

*   **Heat Pump Technology:**
    *   Heat pumps move heat rather than generate it, delivering 2–4 units of heat per 1 unit of electricity, while gas furnaces are 80–96% efficient [source](https://jouleio.com/blog/heat-pump-operating-cost-by-climate/).
    *   Cold-climate models with variable-speed compressors are most effective and can rival or beat gas costs even in harsh winters [source](https://jouleio.com/blog/heat-pump-operating-cost-by-climate/).
*   **Coefficient of Performance (COP) in Cold:**
    *   Field data show Air-Source Heat Pumps (ASHPs) are significantly more efficient than fossil-fuel heating even below 0°C [source](https://www.cell.com/joule/fulltext/S2542-4351(23)00351-3).
    *   Mean COP is 2.74 (median 2.62) at 5°C to -10°C [source](https://www.cell.com/joule/fulltext/S2542-4351(23)00351-3).
    *   Even in extreme cold (down to -30°C), cold-climate ASHPs can achieve COPs between 1.5 and 2 (e.g., Mitsubishi units) [source](https://www.cell.com/joule/fulltext/S2542-4351(23)00351-3).
    *   A PNNL study found a median COP of 1.9 in the 0–5°F band from 22 units in occupied homes [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   In Albany, NY, an ASHP's seasonal COP (without supplemental heat) was 2.44, dropping to 1.43 at -3°F [source](https://www.nyiso.com/documents/20142/35104194/2022%20LFTF%20Dec%2019%20-%20EPRI%20Heat%20Pump%20Assessment%20Study.pdf/171575b4-3329-17b1-feb2-07dea7770092).
*   **Supplemental Heat:**
    *   Heat pump performance declines as outdoor temperatures fall, increasing the need for supplemental heat (often electric resistance) to meet heating loads [source](https://www.nyiso.com/documents/20142/35104194/2022%20LFTF%20Dec%2019%20-%20EPRI%20Heat%20Pump%20Assessment%20Study.pdf/171575b4-3329-17b1-feb2-07dea7770092).
    *   Backup heating is often not needed until temperatures drop below -10°C [source](https://www.cell.com/joule/fulltext/S2542-4351(23)00351-3).
    *   Poorly installed systems or incorrect auxiliary heat lockout settings can lead to excessive use of expensive resistance heat [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   At peak winter hours, supplemental heat can account for approximately 67% of the load, with the heat pump contributing 33% [source](https://www.nyiso.com/documents/20142/35104194/2022%20LFTF%20Dec%2019%20-%20EPRI%20Heat%20Pump%20Assessment%20Study.pdf/171575b4-3329-17b1-feb2-07dea7770092).
*   **System Design and Installation:**
    *   Installation quality and correct sizing are crucial for heat pump performance and cost-effectiveness, often more so than climate alone [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   Proper load calculations and understanding auxiliary heat lockout settings are essential to minimize expensive resistance heat [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   Oversizing the heat pump system or relying on supplemental heat is often needed to meet cold-season loads reliably [source](https://www.nyiso.com/documents/20142/35104194/2022%20LFTF%20Dec%2019%20-%20EPRI%20Heat%20Pump%20Assessment%20Study.pdf/171575b4-3329-17b1-feb2-07dea7770092).

### III. Other Considerations

*   **Upfront Costs and Incentives:**
    *   Heat pumps generally have higher upfront installation and equipment costs, especially for cold-climate models [source](https://jouleio.com/blog/heat-pump-operating-cost-by-climate/).
    *   Rebates (e.g., from the IRA) and rising gas prices can help offset these higher initial costs [source](https://jouleio.com/blog/heat-pump-operating-cost-by-climate/).
*   **Additional Benefits of Heat Pumps:**
    *   Heat pumps provide both heating and cooling, often eliminating the need for a separate AC unit [source](https://jouleio.com/blog/heat-pump-operating-cost-by-climate/).
    *   They offer environmental benefits, which are enhanced when powered by renewable electricity [source](https://jouleio.com/blog/heat-pump-operating-cost-by-climate/).
*   **Location-Specific Factors:**
    *   Electricity prices vary significantly by utility and within states, directly impacting cost outcomes [source](https://heatpumpmath.com/cold-climate-heat-pump-cost/).
    *   The decision between a heat pump and a gas furnace is complex and location-specific, considering local electric grid mixes, energy costs, and equipment efficiencies [source](https://www.mwalliance.org/sites/default/files/Furnaces-vs-ASHPs-Sept18.pdf).
    *   Studies on Midwest cities show mixed results, with ASHPs sometimes offering CO2 benefits but often with higher life-cycle costs and lower source energy efficiency compared to high-efficiency gas furnaces [source](https://www.mwalliance.org/sites/default/files/Furnaces-vs-ASHPs-Sept18.pdf).
*   **Tools:**
    *   It is recommended to use heat pump and electricity cost calculators to tailor comparisons to specific climates and rates [source](https://jouleio.com/blog/heat-pump-operating-cost-by-climate/).

**Bottom Line:** While cold-climate heat pumps offer significant energy savings overall compared to gas furnaces and are generally more cost-effective than oil/propane, they often cost more to run than natural gas in cold winter conditions. Their performance and cost-effectiveness are highly dependent on proper sizing, high-quality installation, minimizing reliance on expensive auxiliary resistance heat, and the relative prices of electricity and natural gas in a specific location. Dual-fuel systems may be a strategic option for natural gas users in very cold climates.

sources.summary:
Summary:
- Cold-climate heat pumps can work in real winters, but their operating cost depends on the fuel they replace.
- Relative performance (cost) by fuel:
  - Natural gas: typically worse. Needs a COP between 3.4 and 5.4 to break even, which no northern-winter unit achieves; thus heat pumps usually cost more to run than gas in cold states.
  - Oil and propane: usually better. A COP between 1.1 and 2.8 is sufficient to beat oil/propane for most of the heating season; a good unit often achieves this.
- Real-world findings from field studies:
  - PNNL: median COP of 1.9 in the 0–5°F band (22 units in occupied homes).
  - NREL: at two sites, resistance backup heat sometimes used more energy than the compressor.
  - Overall: a properly sized, commissioned cold-climate heat pump performs close to its rated efficiency; poorly installed systems can consume more electricity than the reduced-backup heat they replace.
- Important factors influencing cost:
  - Installation quality and correct sizing matter more than climate alone (large variability across households).
  - Electricity prices vs. fuel prices drive outcomes; utilities within a state vary, so actual costs should be calculated from individual bills.
- Practical guidance:
  - Compute your actual electricity and current fuel costs.
  - Check unit COP at 47°F, 17°F, and 5°F against your target COP for your fuel.
  - For gas users, consider dual-fuel strategies (keep furnace for extreme cold, use heat pump otherwise).
  - Ensure proper load calculations (avoid oversizing) and know the auxiliary heat lockout settings to minimize expensive resistance heat.
- Bottom line: Cold climate heat pumps can offer cost savings against oil/propane, but against natural gas they often cost more to run in cold winters; performance hinges on proper sizing, commissioning, and low reliance on auxiliary resistance heat.

Summary:
- The analysis compared replacing an existing gas furnace with a high-efficiency gas furnace vs. an electric air source heat pump (ASHP) in five Midwest cities (CZs 4–7) with varying electric grids and energy costs.

- CO2 emissions from heating could be significantly reduced with an ASHP in some cities (notably Chicago, Madison, Minneapolis) due to cleaner electric generation, but this often comes with higher life-cycle cost and lower source energy efficiency.
- In St. Louis (warmer climate), ASHPs are only slightly less cost-effective than a high-efficiency furnace but are worse for source energy efficiency and would increase long-term CO2 emissions.
- Table 1 (not shown) indicates which criteria favor an ASHP vs. furnace for each city.
- Overall takeaway: Midwest climates, electric-generation mixes, energy costs, and equipment efficiencies yield mixed results; the decision is complex and location-specific. The study suggests periodic reanalysis as technologies and grid mixes evolve. In many Midwest locations, a full replacement with an ASHP is not favored when considering efficiency, cost, and CO2 emissions together, though ASHPs can offer CO2 benefits in some cases.

Summary:
- Objective: Examine how cell-level properties and chemistries translate to battery pack characteristics in electric vehicles using statistical correlations on benchmark data.
- Key pack-level finding: Energy densities at the pack level are broadly comparable across cell formats (prismatic, cylindrical, pouch) despite format differences; this is due to higher pack-level factors for prismatic cells balancing other formats.
- Chemistry insight: NMC and NCA cells exhibit higher gravimetric energy density than LFP at both cell and pack levels, but LFP’s favorable cell-to-pack factors mitigate these advantages, narrowing pack-level differences.
- Cell-to-pack dynamics: Increases in cell-level volumetric and gravimetric energy density yield smaller gains at the pack level, especially for prismatic cells, where the volumetric cell-to-pack factor declines markedly with higher cell energy density. This is attributed to the growing share of passive components in the pack.
- Pack geometry: No significant influence of cell chemistry on the battery pack’s vertical (z) dimension; pack height is more strongly linked to cell format, with prismatic cells associated with taller packs and cylindrical cells with shorter packs.
- Practical implication: Lower-energy-density cells (e.g., some LFP CtP configurations) can achieve favorable pack-level performance due to advantageous cell-to-pack factors, challenging assumptions that higher cell energy density always scales to higher pack energy density.
- Emerging tech: The study touches on sodium-ion and assesses pack-level energy densities derived from cell properties, contributing to understanding of how alternative chemistries may perform at the pack level.
- Overall contribution: Provides empirical, correlation-based insights into cell-to-pack relationships to guide R&D and optimization of EV energy storage, balancing cell chemistry, format, and pack design.

- Key findings:

  - NMC: High specific energy with strong overall performance; adaptable via various derivatives to meet different EV needs.

Summary: The guide compares NMC and LFP lithium-ion chemistries for EV batteries. Key takeaways:

- Performance priorities:
  - NMC: higher energy density and better cold-weather range; preferred for long-range or premium vehicles.
  - LFP: longer life, safer chemistry, lower cost, and charging flexibility; preferred for budget, high-cycle usage, or standard-range/urban use.

- Practical metrics:
  - Energy density: NMC 150-220 Wh/kg (cell) vs LFP 90-200 Wh/kg.
  - Cycle life (80% SOH): NMC 1,500-3,000 cycles; LFP 4,000-10,000 cycles (premium cells >10,000).
  - Thermal stability: LFP onset ~270 °C vs NMC 150-210 °C; LFP releases less energy and gas in thermal runaway.
  - Cost: Pack cost ~$95/kWh (LFP) vs $130-150/kWh (NMC); cell-level LFP cheaper by ~20-30%.
  - Charging: LFP can be charged to 100% daily; NMC often recommended to 80% in daily use.

- Temperature and climate guidance:
  - Hot climates: LFP shows less lifespan loss.
  - Cold climates: NMC retains more usable power at -20 °C (70-80%).

- User-type recommendations:
  - Long-range/premium vehicle or cold-weather use: choose NMC.
  - City/high-cycle use, cost-conscious, or 100% daily charging: choose LFP.
  - Fleets or taxi/dense charging: LFP offers lower total cost of ownership.

Bottom line: If you prioritize energy density and range, go NMC; if you prioritize lifespan, safety, charging flexibility, and lower cost, go LFP.

Key takeaways: LiFePO4 (LFP) and NMC each excel in different use cases.

- Energy density: NMC is higher (roughly 250–300 Wh/kg) vs LFP (160–180 Wh/kg). This drives longer range and lighter weight NEEDS for EVs and weight-critical devices.
- Cycle life and durability: LFP lasts much longer (3,000–6,000+ cycles @ 80% DoD; ~10–15+ years calendar life) vs NMC (1,000–2,000 cycles; ~8–10 years). Better for high-cycle storage and hot climates.
- Safety and thermal: LFP has superior thermal stability and safer in indoor/storage contexts; NMC is more prone to thermal risk.
- Cost and economics: Pack price (2025 data) ≈ $81/kWh for LFP vs $128/kWh for NMC (lower upfront cost for LFP; better levelized cost in many stationary/deep-cycle roles). Overall LCOS favors LFP in many stationary scenarios.
- Cobalt/nickel and supply risk: LFP contains no cobalt/nickel; less exposure to supply volatility.
- Best fit by application:
  - LFP: stationary storage, RV/marine/golf carts, hot climates, high-cycle use, indoor/low-risk environments, budget EVs with shorter range.
  - NMC: long-range EVs, drones/eVTOL/weight-critical devices, high-energy-density needs, cold environments where certain performance is required.
- Verdict pattern: No universal winner. Choose by application:
  - Long-range, weight-sensitive, or flight/drones: NMC.
  - Storage, intra-vehicle living spaces, hot climates, high cycle life, cost sensitivity: LFP.

Bottom line: For storage and non-traction uses, LFP is typically the rational default; for range-critical EVs, drones, and weight-constrained designs, NMC is the premium option due to energy density.

The article reviews five common Li-ion chemistries used in electric vehicles, comparing their electrochemical performance and practical applications:

- LiMn2O4 (LMO): Pros — low cost, good high-rate performance due to spinel structure; Cons — poor high-temperature cyclability and limited cycle life.

- LiFePO4 (LFP): Pros — long life, low cost, excellent thermal stability; Cons — relatively low specific energy and higher self-discharge; performance drops at low temperatures.
- Li4Ti5O12 (LTO): Pros — best thermal stability, cyclability, safety; supports fast charging with no lithium plating at high currents. Cons — very low specific energy and high cost.

- LFP offers safety and longevity for cost-sensitive applications, though energy density is lower.

runs.report:
## LFP vs. NMC Lithium-Ion Batteries for Electric Vehicles

This report compares Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) and Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC) lithium-ion batteries, highlighting their key characteristics, market trends, and suitability for electric vehicles (EVs).

### Performance Characteristics

*   **Energy Density & Range**
    *   **NMC:** Generally exhibits higher gravimetric energy density (150-220 Wh/kg at cell level, up to 250-300 Wh/kg for higher-end cells) than LFP, making it suitable for longer-range and premium EVs where weight is critical [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries), [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/).
    *   **LFP:** Has a lower energy density (90-200 Wh/kg at cell level, 160-180 Wh/kg for top-selling models by 2023) compared to NMC, but pack-level improvements and advantageous cell-to-pack factors can significantly narrow this gap, making them increasingly viable for longer ranges [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/automotive-and-assembly/our-insights/the-battery-chemistries-powering-the-future-of-electric-vehicles), [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries), [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/), [doi.org/10.3390/wevj16090484).
*   **Cycle Life & Durability**
    *   **LFP:** Offers a significantly longer cycle life (4,000-10,000+ cycles to 80% SOH, 3,000-6,000+ cycles at 80% DoD) and calendar life (10-15+ years), making it ideal for high-cycle usage, such as urban driving, fleets, or taxi services, and better performance in hot climates [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries), [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/).
    *   **NMC:** Typically provides 1,500-3,000 cycles to 80% SOH (1,000-2,000 cycles for general NMC) and 8-10 years calendar life [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries), [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/).
*   **Thermal Stability & Safety**
    *   **LFP:** Demonstrates superior thermal stability with a higher onset temperature for thermal runaway (~270 °C) and releases less energy and gas during a thermal event, leading to safer overall behavior [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries), [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/), [doi.org/10.1016/j.etran.2023.100305), [doi.org/10.3390/wevj16030153).
    *   **NMC:** Has a lower thermal runaway onset temperature (150-210 °C) and is more prone to violent reactions (sparks and flames) during thermal runaway, requiring more extensive safety measures and system integration [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries), [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/), [doi.org/10.1016/j.etran.2023.100305), [doi.org/10.3390/wevj16030153).
*   **Charging Capabilities**
    *   **LFP:** Can be safely charged to 100% daily without significant degradation, offering greater flexibility in daily use [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries).
    *   **NMC:** Often recommended to be charged only to 80% for daily use to preserve battery lifespan [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries).
*   **Temperature Performance**
    *   **NMC:** Generally retains more usable power in cold climates (e.g., 70-80% at -20 °C) [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries).
    *   **LFP:** Performance can drop at very low temperatures, though it shows less lifespan loss in hot climates [eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/134354/1/The%20Electrochemical%20Performance%20and%20Applications%20of%20Several%20Popular%20Lithium-ion%20Batteries%20for%20Electric%20Vehicles%20-%20A%20Review.pdf), [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries).

### Economic & Market Aspects

*   **Cost**
    *   **LFP:** Is significantly cheaper per kWh than NMC. Cell-level LFP is about 20-30% lower in cost, with pack costs around $95/kWh (LFP) vs. $130-150/kWh (NMC) [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/automotive-and-assembly/our-insights/the-battery-chemistries-powering-the-future-of-electric-vehicles), [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries), [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/). This cost advantage contributes to a lower total cost of ownership for LFP in many applications [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries).
    *   **NMC:** Higher material costs, especially for cobalt and nickel, contribute to its higher price per kWh [media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs44406-026-00044-6/MediaObjects/44406_2026_44_MOESM1_ESM.pdf).
*   **Material Sourcing & Sustainability**
    *   **LFP:** Contains no cobalt or nickel, reducing exposure to supply chain volatility and ethical concerns associated with these materials [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/), [insideevs.com](https://insideevs.com/news/784963/lfp-overtakes-nickel-battery-chemistry/).
    *   **NMC:** Relies on cobalt and nickel, which can have higher material costs and potential supply risks [media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs44406-026-00044-6/MediaObjects/44406_2026_44_MOESM1_ESM.pdf).
*   **Market Share & Adoption**
    *   **LFP Dominance:** LFP became the dominant global EV battery chemistry in 2025, accounting for over half of global EV battery deployments and more than 90% of battery storage globally [insideevs.com](https://insideevs.com/news/784963/lfp-overtakes-nickel-battery-chemistry/), [iea.org](https://www.iea.org/commentaries/global-battery-markets-are-growing-strongly-and-so-are-the-supply-risks).
    *   **Regional Trends:** China leads LFP deployment, with LFP sharing rising to 60% of passenger EVs by 2023 and 81.2% of China's EV battery market in 2025 [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/automotive-and-assembly/our-insights/the-battery-chemistries-powering-the-future-of-electric-vehicles), [electrive.com](https://www.electrive.com/2026/01/19/chinas-ev-battery-market-grows-by-40-percent/), [chinaevhome.com](https://chinaevhome.com/2026/01/21/chinas-2025-nev-power-battery-installations-hit-714-4-gwh-up-35-5yoy-1/). Europe and North America, while historically NMC-dominant, are increasingly adopting LFP for entry-level and cost-conscious models [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/automotive-and-assembly/our-insights/the-battery-chemistries-powering-the-future-of-electric-vehicles).
    *   **Major Players:** CATL is the leading LFP supplier globally, followed by BYD, Gotion High-Tech, LG Energy Solution, Panasonic, and Samsung SDI [electrive.com](https://www.electrive.com/2026/01/19/chinas-ev-battery-market-grows-by-40-percent/), [congruencemarketinsights.com](https://www.congruencemarketinsights.com/report/li-ion-battery-for-aevs-market).
*   **Market Outlook**
    *   Both NMC and LFP demand are expected to grow, with LFP potentially capturing the largest global market share before 2030, driven by affordability and improving energy density [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/automotive-and-assembly/our-insights/the-battery-chemistries-powering-the-future-of-electric-vehicles).
    *   The market for Li-ion batteries in AEVs is projected to reach $46.51B by 2033, with LFP dominating demand for its cost and durability benefits [congruencemarketinsights.com](https://www.congruencemarketinsights.com/report/li-ion-battery-for-aevs-market).

### System Integration & Design

*   **Cell-to-Pack (CtP) & Cell-to-Body (CtB) Designs**
    *   Advances in CtP and CtB integration allow LFP batteries to achieve comparable pack-level energy densities to NMC, mitigating LFP's cell-level energy density disadvantage [doi.org/10.3390/wevj16090484), [reneweconomy.com.au](https://reneweconomy.com.au/batteries-and-cells-whether-on-wheels-or-the-grid-its-all-about-chemistry-and-cost/). This reduces costs and improves packaging efficiency, offering 10-20% gains [congruencemarketinsights.com](https://www.congruencemarketinsights.com/report/li-ion-battery-for-aevs-market).
*   **Pack Geometry**
    *   Pack height is more strongly linked to cell format than chemistry, with prismatic cells (often used for LFP) associated with taller packs and cylindrical cells (often used for NMC) with shorter packs [doi.org/10.3390/wevj16090484).
*   **Safety Integration**
    *   NMC requires significantly more extensive safety measures due to its faster thermal runaway propagation, influencing overall pack architecture and thermal management systems [doi.org/10.1016/j.etran.2023.100305).
    *   LFP allows for potentially simpler safety designs, contributing to better integration opportunities at the pack level [doi.org/10.1016/j.etran.2023.100305).

### Conclusion

The choice between LFP and NMC batteries for EVs involves balancing trade-offs. NMC offers higher energy density, suiting long-range and premium vehicles, especially in cold climates. LFP excels in cost-effectiveness, superior safety, longer cycle life, and charging flexibility, making it ideal for urban, entry-level, and high-cycle use cases. The rapid advancements in LFP technology, particularly in energy density and cell-to-pack integration, along with its cost advantages and material sustainability, are driving its dominance in the global EV battery market, especially in China. While NMC will retain its niche for performance-driven applications, LFP is reshaping the EV landscape towards more affordable, durable, and safer electric transportation. OEMs and battery manufacturers must adapt their portfolios to these evolving market dynamics to remain competitive [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/automotive-and-assembly/our-insights/the-battery-chemistries-powering-the-future-of-electric-vehicles), [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries), [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/).

Summary: The guide compares NMC and LFP lithium-ion chemistries for EV batteries. Key takeaways:

- Performance priorities:
  - NMC: higher energy density and better cold-weather range; preferred for long-range or premium vehicles.
  - LFP: longer life, safer chemistry, lower cost, and charging flexibility; preferred for budget, high-cycle usage, or standard-range/urban use.

- Practical metrics:
  - Energy density: NMC 150-220 Wh/kg (cell) vs LFP 90-200 Wh/kg.
  - Cycle life (80% SOH): NMC 1,500-3,000 cycles; LFP 4,000-10,000 cycles (premium cells >10,000).
  - Thermal stability: LFP onset ~270 °C vs NMC 150-210 °C; LFP releases less energy and gas in thermal runaway.
  - Cost: Pack cost ~$95/kWh (LFP) vs $130-150/kWh (NMC); cell-level LFP cheaper by ~20-30%.
  - Charging: LFP can be charged to 100% daily; NMC often recommended to 80% in daily use.

- Temperature and climate guidance:
  - Hot climates: LFP shows less lifespan loss.
  - Cold climates: NMC retains more usable power at -20 °C (70-80%).

- User-type recommendations:
  - Long-range/premium vehicle or cold-weather use: choose NMC.
  - City/high-cycle use, cost-conscious, or 100% daily charging: choose LFP.
  - Fleets or taxi/dense charging: LFP offers lower total cost of ownership.

Bottom line: If you prioritize energy density and range, go NMC; if you prioritize lifespan, safety, charging flexibility, and lower cost, go LFP.
