Summary: The guide compares NMC and LFP lithium-ion chemistries for EV batteries. Key takeaways:

- Performance priorities:
  - NMC: higher energy density and better cold-weather range; preferred for long-range or premium vehicles.
  - LFP: longer life, safer chemistry, lower cost, and charging flexibility; preferred for budget, high-cycle usage, or standard-range/urban use.

- Practical metrics:
  - Energy density: NMC 150-220 Wh/kg (cell) vs LFP 90-200 Wh/kg.
  - Cycle life (80% SOH): NMC 1,500-3,000 cycles; LFP 4,000-10,000 cycles (premium cells >10,000).
  - Thermal stability: LFP onset ~270 °C vs NMC 150-210 °C; LFP releases less energy and gas in thermal runaway.
  - Cost: Pack cost ~$95/kWh (LFP) vs $130-150/kWh (NMC); cell-level LFP cheaper by ~20-30%.
  - Charging: LFP can be charged to 100% daily; NMC often recommended to 80% in daily use.

- Temperature and climate guidance:
  - Hot climates: LFP shows less lifespan loss.
  - Cold climates: NMC retains more usable power at -20 °C (70-80%).

- User-type recommendations:
  - Long-range/premium vehicle or cold-weather use: choose NMC.
  - City/high-cycle use, cost-conscious, or 100% daily charging: choose LFP.
  - Fleets or taxi/dense charging: LFP offers lower total cost of ownership.

Bottom line: If you prioritize energy density and range, go NMC; if you prioritize lifespan, safety, charging flexibility, and lower cost, go LFP.

Key takeaways: LiFePO4 (LFP) and NMC each excel in different use cases.

- Energy density: NMC is higher (roughly 250–300 Wh/kg) vs LFP (160–180 Wh/kg). This drives longer range and lighter weight NEEDS for EVs and weight-critical devices.
- Cycle life and durability: LFP lasts much longer (3,000–6,000+ cycles @ 80% DoD; ~10–15+ years calendar life) vs NMC (1,000–2,000 cycles; ~8–10 years). Better for high-cycle storage and hot climates.
- Safety and thermal: LFP has superior thermal stability and safer in indoor/storage contexts; NMC is more prone to thermal risk.
- Cost and economics: Pack price (2025 data) ≈ $81/kWh for LFP vs $128/kWh for NMC (lower upfront cost for LFP; better levelized cost in many stationary/deep-cycle roles). Overall LCOS favors LFP in many stationary scenarios.
- Cobalt/nickel and supply risk: LFP contains no cobalt/nickel; less exposure to supply volatility.
- Best fit by application:
  - LFP: stationary storage, RV/marine/golf carts, hot climates, high-cycle use, indoor/low-risk environments, budget EVs with shorter range.
  - NMC: long-range EVs, drones/eVTOL/weight-critical devices, high-energy-density needs, cold environments where certain performance is required.
- Verdict pattern: No universal winner. Choose by application:
  - Long-range, weight-sensitive, or flight/drones: NMC.
  - Storage, intra-vehicle living spaces, hot climates, high cycle life, cost sensitivity: LFP.

Bottom line: For storage and non-traction uses, LFP is typically the rational default; for range-critical EVs, drones, and weight-constrained designs, NMC is the premium option due to energy density.

- Objective: Evaluate and compare SOH diagnosis and forecasting for LFP vs. NMC Li-ion batteries in EVs under realistic cycling across 25–65°C.
- Key finding: Both chemistries degrade faster with higher temperature, but NMC ages much more rapidly above 50°C.

Summary:
- The review maps how cell form factor (cylindrical, prismatic, pouch) and electrode architecture (jelly-roll, stacked, blade) together with chemistry (LFP, NMC, NCA, LCO) determine performance, safety, and manufacturability across modern LIBs.
- Key trade-offs:
  - Gravimetric vs volumetric energy density: pouch cells offer high energy per weight; prismatic/blade designs with LFP optimize volume utilization and thermal stability.
  - Thermal safety and cycle life: LFP provides superior thermal stability and longer cycle life, suitable for prismatic and blade formats in EVs and stationary storage, despite lower nominal voltage.
  - Energy/power and manufacturability: NMC/NCA benefit from jelly-roll type architectures (often with tabless or multi-tab current collection) to improve current distribution and ease manufacturing.
  - LCO is confined largely to small electronics due to safety, cobalt cost, and limited cycle life; not ideal for high-power or large-scale needs.
- Form factor implications by chemistry:
  - LFP excels in safety and cost; fits prismatic and blade geometries for compact packaging.
  - NMC/NCA achieve higher specific energy and power in jelly-roll configurations, supporting scalable EV/vectorized applications.
  - Cylindrical cells offer mechanical stability and automation but limit packing efficiency; less favorable for volumetric density in large modules.
  - Pouch cells provide high energy-to-weight and flexible packaging but require precise mechanical compression and stacking.
  - LCO remains for small devices due to safety and cost constraints.
- Emerging options: LiMnFePO4 (LMFP) as a path to higher voltage/energy with maintained cycle life and cost, though optimum form factor and electrode architecture need further exploration.
- Practical takeaway: an application-driven framework is needed to select feasible combinations of form factor and electrode design tailored to chemistry, performance targets, safety requirements, and manufacturability, acknowledging clear interdependencies among geometry, architecture, and system integration.

runs.report:
## LFP vs. NMC Lithium-Ion Batteries for Electric Vehicles: A Team Report

This report summarizes the current state and future outlook of Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) and Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC) lithium-ion batteries in electric vehicles (EVs), based on recent research.

### Battery Chemistry and Performance

This section compares LFP and NMC batteries across key performance metrics, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses.

*   **Energy Density & Range**
    *   NMC batteries currently offer higher energy density, enabling longer EV ranges [10.47392/irjaeh.2026.0139, insideevs.com/news/782685/all-ev-battery-chemistries-explained/].
    *   LFP batteries have a lower energy density, which typically translates to shorter ranges [10.47392/irjaeh.2026.0139, insideevs.com/news/782685/all-ev-battery-chemistries-explained/].
    *   Emerging variants like LMFP (adding manganese to LFP) aim to boost energy density and range while maintaining LFP's advantages [10.3390/batteries11120450, insideevs.com/news/782685/all-ev-battery-chemistries-explained/].
    *   Energy density for NMC rose over 50% from 2020-2024, and for LFP, it rose approximately 65% in the same period [iea.org/commentaries/how-can-innovation-help-secure-future-battery-markets-and-mineral-supplies].
*   **Lifespan & Durability**
    *   LFP batteries generally offer a longer cycle life compared to NMC [10.47392/irjaeh.2026.0139, 10.3390/batteries11120450, iea.org/commentaries/how-can-innovation-help-secure-future-battery-markets-and-mineral-supplies].
    *   At 60°C, LFP retains approximately 80% State of Health (SOH) for roughly twice as many cycles as NMC, showing lower internal resistance growth and higher coulombic efficiency across all temperatures [10.53375/ijecer.2025.489].
    *   While LFP's longer lifetime is an advantage, it does not fully offset its higher resource and environmental burdens compared to NMC in certain circularity evaluations [10.1016/j.resconrec.2024.107833].
*   **Safety & Thermal Stability**
    *   LFP batteries are considered safer and exhibit higher thermal stability, making them suitable for high-temperature conditions and commercial vehicles [10.47392/irjaeh.2026.0139, 10.3390/batteries11120450, insideevs.com/news/782685/all-ev-battery-chemistries-explained/].
    *   NMC batteries are challenged by thermal safety and require stricter thermal management, as they degrade much more rapidly above 50°C [10.47392/irjaeh.2026.0139, 10.53375/ijecer.2025.489].
    *   NMC also exhibits greater degradation variability and higher failure risk under thermal stress [10.53375/ijecer.2025.489].
*   **Charging Characteristics**
    *   Fast charging capabilities have advanced significantly, with both chemistries seeing improvements. For instance, BYD/CATL in early 2025 achieved 400–500 km range added in about 5 minutes [iea.org/commentaries/how-can-innovation-help-secure-future-battery-markets-and-mineral-supplies].

### Cost and Market Adoption

This section examines the cost implications and market trends for LFP and NMC batteries, including regional adoption and future projections.

*   **Cost**
    *   LFP batteries are generally cheaper due to abundant and lower-cost raw materials, making them attractive for mass-market and commercial EVs [10.47392/irjaeh.2026.0139, insideevs.com/news/782685/all-ev-battery-chemistries-explained/, mckinsey.com/features/mckinsey-center-for-future-mobility/our-insights/the-future-of-affordable-evs-breakthroughs-in-battery-pack-costs].
    *   Chinese OEMs achieve significant cost advantages (up to ~40%) for battery packs, with LFP packs around €64/kWh and NMC packs around €82/kWh [mckinsey.com/features/mckinsey-center-for-future-mobility/our-insights/the-future-of-affordable-evs-breakthroughs-in-battery-pack-costs].
    *   NMC batteries are typically more costly, partly due to the reliance on cobalt [10.47392/irjaeh.2026.0139, insideevs.com/news/782685/all-ev-battery-chemistries-explained/].
    *   Average lithium-ion battery prices fell about 30% between 2020-2024, driven by scale and manufacturing improvements [iea.org/commentaries/how-can-innovation-help-secure-future-battery-markets-and-mineral-supplies].
*   **Market Share & Trends**
    *   LFP is increasingly dominating the market, especially in China, with 85.5% market share of traction batteries in September 2026 [latestevnews.com/articles/chinas-battery-market-lfp-reaches-855percent].
    *   Globally, LFP's share of EV cathode shipments reached 65.4% by August 2026, widening its lead over NMC/ternary materials [biz.heraldcorp.com/article/10899351].
    *   In non-China markets, LFP's share rose to 34.9% by August 2026 [biz.heraldcorp.com/article/10899351].
    *   The overall EV battery mix in 2024 was roughly 50% LFP and 50% NMC, with LFP growing fastest due to lower cost and longer cycle life [iea.org/commentaries/how-can-innovation-help-secure-future-battery-markets-and-mineral-supplies].
    *   In China's electric car market, LFP held approximately 57.24% share in 2025, with NMC/NCM expected to grow at about 8.03% CAGR to 2031 [mordorintelligence.com/industry-reports/china-electric-car-market].
*   **Strategic Adoption by OEMs**
    *   LFP batteries are gaining traction in the U.S. for cost reduction and reduced reliance on nickel/cobalt. Ford is building a $3B BlueOval Battery Park for LFP production using CATL technology, and GM is pursuing U.S.-based LFP production via LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI [insideevs.com/news/780869/ev-battery-stories-of-2025/].
    *   Korean and Japanese battery suppliers are seeing their shares decline as LFP-focused momentum strengthens, with SK On expanding LFP linkages [biz.heraldcorp.com/article/10899351].
    *   Many major automakers are developing cost-effective battery designs, standardizing platforms, and implementing design-for-cost measures to reduce capital expenditure and footprint [mckinsey.com/features/mckinsey-center-for-future-mobility/our-insights/the-future-of-affordable-evs-breakthroughs-in-battery-pack-costs].

### Sustainability and Environmental Impact

This section addresses the sustainability aspects of LFP and NMC batteries, including material sourcing, recycling, and environmental footprints.

*   **Material Sourcing & Dependency**
    *   NMC batteries rely on cobalt, nickel, and manganese, with cobalt being a significant concern due to its cost volatility and concentrated supply chains [10.47392/irjaeh.2026.0139, iea.org/commentaries/how-can-innovation-help-secure-future-battery-markets-and-mineral-supplies].
    *   LFP batteries use abundant and less costly materials like iron and phosphate, reducing reliance on critical minerals like cobalt and nickel [10.47392/irjaeh.2026.0139, insideevs.com/news/780869/ev-battery-stories-of-2025/].
    *   Both chemistries have geographically concentrated supply chains, raising security concerns [iea.org/commentaries/how-can-innovation-help-secure-future-battery-markets-and-mineral-supplies].
*   **Recycling and Circularity**
    *   Recycling is crucial for both chemistries to recover materials from manufacturing scrap and end-of-life batteries, potentially cutting lithium and nickel demand by ~25% and cobalt by ~40% by 2050 [iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/e75c9a13-3753-4677-933f-c7f9ae38cfdb/EVBatterySupplyChainSustainability.pdf].
    *   NMC batteries are estimated to be 6–25% more circular than LFP, with higher material recovery ratios (+13–24%) [10.1016/j.resconrec.2024.107833].
    *   Achieving circularity, especially for cobalt and nickel, requires substantial investments in both primary and secondary supply infrastructure and policies that prioritize smaller, LFP-promoted, and technology-selective second-life battery usage [10.1016/j.resourpol.2024.105160].
    *   Cobalt is identified as a bottleneck material for recycling capacity in Europe [10.1016/j.resourpol.2024.105160].
*   **Environmental Footprint**
    *   NMC batteries can deliver 3–6% lower Global Warming Potential (GWP) and 12–16% lower Abiotic Depletion Potential of minerals (ADPm) than LFP, particularly with hydrometallurgical recycling (HyR) [10.1016/j.resconrec.2024.107833].
    *   Battery-related emissions are a meaningful portion of EV life cycle emissions but are expected to decline as production processes electrify, energy density improves, and recycled materials are used [iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/e75c9a13-3753-4677-933f-c7f9ae38cfdb/EVBatterySupplyChainSustainability.pdf].

### Emerging Technologies and Future Outlook

This section briefly touches on advancements beyond current LFP and NMC chemistries.

*   **LMFP (Lithium Manganese Iron Phosphate)**
    *   LMFP is emerging as a path to higher voltage/energy with maintained cycle life and cost, building on LFP's foundation [10.3390/batteries11120450, insideevs.com/news/782685/all-ev-battery-chemistries-explained/].
*   **Solid-State Batteries**
    *   Solid-state batteries offer potential for ultra-high energy density, improved safety, and faster charging, but face challenges in cost and manufacturing scalability [10.47392/irjaeh.2026.0139, insideevs.com/news/782685/all-ev-battery-chemistries-explained/].
    *   Solid-state and sodium-ion batteries currently have limited manufacturing bases (1% and 4% of total capacity, respectively), primarily in China, limiting their near-term potential [iea.org/commentaries/how-can-innovation-help-secure-future-battery-markets-and-mineral-supplies].
*   **Sodium-Ion Batteries**
    *   Sodium-ion batteries are cheaper, use abundant raw materials, and offer good safety, but have lower energy density, making them more suitable for short-range or entry-level EVs [10.47392/irjaeh.2026.0139].
*   **LMR (Lithium-Manganese-Rich) Batteries**
    *   LMR batteries are being positioned by Ford and GM between LFP and NCM in terms of cost and energy, but commercialization and market impact are still pending verifiable data post-2028 [staranx.com/blog/equipment/lmr-battery-market-impact/].

Summary:
- Study investigates how liquid nitrogen (LN2) cooling can suppress thermal runaway in lithium-ion batteries, focusing on chemistry-dependent boundaries between safe/unsafe regimes for NCM (nickel–c manganese–cobalt oxide) and LFP (lithium iron phosphate) chemistries.
- Key finding: LN2 cooling can effectively halt or slow thermal runaway propagation, but the effectiveness and boundary conditions depend strongly on battery chemistry, cell design, and confinement.
- For NCM cells, LN2 interacts with higher energy density and more exothermic reactions; suppression requires tailored LN2 delivery, sufficient cooling capacity, and rapid heat transfer to prevent propagation.
- For LFP cells, which have different thermal behavior and lower voltage/energy density, LN2 can provide rapid cooling with potentially easier boundary control, but overcooling or rapid phase changes can induce mechanical/structural stresses.
- Boiling heat transfer dynamics of LN2 play a crucial role: nucleate boiling, film boiling onset, and local boiling regimes determine how quickly heat is removed and how effectively thermal runaway is suppressed.
- The work defines chemistry-dependent boundaries (operating conditions under which LN2 cooling prevents propagation) and analyzes how boiling heat transfer regimes influence suppression effectiveness.
- Practical implications: LN2-based suppression strategies may be feasible for battery packs, but require chemistry-specific protocols, controlled LN2 dosing, and attention to confinement effects and heat transfer surfaces.
- Context: Builds on prior work showing LN2 and other extinguishing agents can inhibit propagation, extending understanding to precise boundary conditions and heat transfer mechanisms for NCM and LFP chemistries.

- Main finding: An LFP-dominant battery strategy, complemented by recycling and remanufacturing, markedly reduces critical metal demand and life-cycle carbon emissions for China’s EV fleet.

- Goal: Assess strategies for achieving circularity in lithium, cobalt, and nickel supply for European EVs, and quantify mining, recycling, costs, and emissions under different pathways.

runs.report:
## LFP vs. NMC Lithium-Ion Batteries for Electric Vehicles: A Comparative Report

This report summarizes the performance, cost, safety, market trends, and environmental impact of Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) and Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC) lithium-ion batteries for electric vehicles (EVs).

### Performance Characteristics

**Energy Density & Range**
*   **NMC** offers higher cell energy density (250–300 Wh/kg) compared to LFP (160–180 Wh/kg), making it preferable for weight-critical, long-range EVs, drones, and portable power applications [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/).
*   At a system level, performance depends on both chemistry and cell format, with 21700 cells showing a favorable balance of higher energy and lower peak surface temperatures for automotive use [intechopen.com](https://www.intechopen.com/online-first/1257182).

**Charging Speed & Thermal Behavior**
*   **LFP** batteries consistently demonstrated a unique advantage in fast-charging, reaching 100% state of charge (SOC) in less than half the time of other chemistries (NMC, NCA) under tested ~3C conditions [papers.ssrn.com](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7466288).
*   **NMC** cells generally deliver higher power output and better rapid charging performance but generate more heat [intechopen.com](https://www.intechopen.com/online-first/1257182).
*   **LFP** cells run cooler with more consistent temperature profiles and exhibit lower heat generation [intechopen.com](https://www.intechopen.com/online-first/1257182).
*   Fast charging (0.5C to 2C) reduces charging time but increases internal and external heat, demanding effective thermal management [intechopen.com](https://www.intechopen.com/online-first/1257182).
*   Despite wide differences in energy density, fast-charging and heat-generation characteristics among cells are converging, highlighting the importance of thermal management [papers.ssrn.com](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7466288).

**Lifespan & Durability**
*   **LFP** batteries offer a significantly longer cycle life (3,000–6,000+ cycles at 80% Depth of Discharge) compared to NMC (1,000–2,000 cycles) [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/).
*   **LFP** also has a longer calendar life (10–15+ years vs. ~8–10 years for NMC) [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/).
*   Both chemistries degrade faster with rising temperature, but **NMC** aging accelerates more quickly above 50°C, leading to faster loss of State of Health (SOH) and greater internal resistance growth compared to LFP [doi.org/10.53375/ijecer.2025.489](https://doi.org/10.53375/ijecer.2025.489).
*   At 60°C, **LFP** retains about 80% SOH for nearly twice as many cycles as NMC [doi.org/10.53375/ijecer.2025.489](https://doi.org/10.53375/ijecer.2025.489).
*   **LFP** demonstrates superior thermal resilience, slower capacity fade, and more stable efficiency, making it suitable for hot climates or high-duty/high-temperature charging [doi.org/10.53375/ijecer.2025.489](https://doi.org/10.53375/ijecer.2025.489).

### Cost, Safety & Supply Chain

**Cost**
*   **LFP** battery packs are significantly cheaper (around $81/kWh) than **NMC** packs (around $128/kWh) in 2025 [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/).
*   For stationary storage, LFP averages around $70/kWh [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/).
*   The price gap between chemistries is becoming a smaller share of the car's total price in premium vehicles [reneweconomy.com.au](https://reneweconomy.com.au/batteries-and-cells-whether-on-wheels-or-the-grid-its-all-about-chemistry-and-cost/).

**Safety & Thermal Runaway**
*   **LFP** has better thermal safety and is less prone to thermal runaway compared to NMC [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/).
*   NMC's thermal safety degrades with higher nickel content [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/).
*   Liquid nitrogen (LN2) cooling can suppress thermal runaway in both chemistries, but effectiveness and boundary conditions are chemistry-dependent, with LFP potentially having easier boundary control due to different thermal behavior and lower energy density [doi.org/10.1016/j.energy.2026.142762](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.energy.2026.142762).

**Supply Chain & Materials**
*   **LFP** batteries do not contain cobalt or nickel, avoiding related supply-chain risks associated with these geopolitically sensitive materials [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/).
*   Global battery production is increasing, with gigafactories, particularly in China, playing a leading role [doi.org/10.5599/jese.3120](https://doi.org/10.5599/jese.3120).
*   The value chain is tightening, with increasing integration of feedstock control, cathode production, cell manufacturing, and long-term off-take contracts [thebatterymagazine.com](https://www.thebatterymagazine.com/lithium-ion-battery-materials-in-2026-scale-supply-chains-and-system-gaps/).
*   Non-Chinese LFP capacity remains limited outside China, posing a challenge for diversification [thebatterymagazine.com](https://www.thebatterymagazine.com/lithium-ion-battery-materials-in-2026-scale-supply-chains-and-system-gaps/).

### Market Adoption & Future Outlook

**Current Trends & Market Share**
*   **LFP** is experiencing significant growth and dominance, particularly in China's battery market. In September 2026, LFP captured 85.5% of traction battery installations in China, with year-to-date share at 82.8% [latestevnews.com](https://www.latestevnews.com/articles/chinas-battery-market-lfp-reaches-855percent).
*   Global EV cathode shipments from January–August 2026 show LFP's share jumping to 65.4% (up 5.0 percentage points), while ternary (NCM/others) declined [biz.heraldcorp.com](https://biz.heraldcorp.com/article/10899351).
*   LFP is expanding beyond China into Europe, Asia, and other overseas markets, with its overseas share climbing to 34.9% [biz.heraldcorp.com](https://biz.heraldcorp.com/article/10899351).
*   **NMC** is primarily favored in premium vehicles for higher energy density [reneweconomy.com.au](https://reneweconomy.com.au/batteries-and-cells-whether-on-wheels-or-the-grid-its-all-about-chemistry-and-cost/).

**Application Best Fits**
*   **LFP** is best suited for stationary storage, RV/marine/indoor use (due to safety), hot climates, high cycle requirements, budget/fleet use, and short-range EVs [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/). Electric heavy trucks also predominantly use LFP due to cost and duty cycles [itkservices3.com](https://itkservices3.com/posts/battery_technology).
*   **NMC** is ideal for long-range EVs, drones/eVTOL/weight-critical portable power, and scenarios where energy density justifies a higher cost [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/).
*   Deep-cold sites may favor NMC (or sodium-ion) with good thermal management [ljyenergy.com](https://ljyenergy.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery/).

**General Outlook**
*   Global EV sales continue to rise, with projections of passenger EV penetration reaching 50% by 2035 [woodmac.com](https://www.woodmac.com/blogs/the-edge/nextgen-batteries-could-be-transformational/).
*   The industry focuses on manufacturability, producing safe, consistent, and economical cells at scale rather than just theoretical performance gains [thebatterymagazine.com](https://www.thebatterymagazine.com/lithium-ion-battery-materials-in-2026-scale-supply-chains-and-system-gaps/).
*   Battery management systems (BMS) are crucial for extracting maximum performance and safety from LIBs [doi.org/10.5599/jese.3120](https://doi.org/10.5599/jese.3120).
*   The future of battery development will emphasize high energy density, faster charging, longer cycle life, and safer chemistries, with solid-state batteries and cobalt-free formulations being promising directions [doi.org/10.5599/jese.3120](https://doi.org/10.5599/jese.3120).

### Environmental Impact & Sustainability

**Circularity & Resource Depletion**
*   **NMC** batteries are 6–25% more circular than LFP batteries across various metrics, primarily due to better material recovery in recycling [doi.org/10.1016/j.resconrec.2024.107833](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.resconrec.2024.107833).
*   An **LFP-dominant** battery strategy, combined with recycling and remanufacturing, significantly reduces critical metal demand (lithium, cobalt, nickel) for EV fleets, particularly alleviating import dependency for cobalt and nickel [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-86250-1).
*   Achieving circularity requires reducing overall material demand in parallel with scaling recycling capacity; relying solely on recycling is insufficient [doi.org/10.1016/j.resourpol.2024.105160](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.resourpol.2024.105160).
*   Optimal strategies for Europe include slower EV battery growth, smaller battery sizes, selective reuse, and widespread LFP adoption, which can reduce primary material demand by 60–64% for lithium, cobalt, and nickel [doi.org/10.1016/j.resourpol.2024.105160](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.resourpol.2024.105160).
*   Recycling is pivotal from the 2030s, potentially reducing lithium and nickel demand by ~25% and cobalt demand by ~40% by 2050 [IEA](https://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/e75c9a13-3753-4677-933f-c7f9ae38cfdb/EVBatterySupplyChainSustainability.pdf).

**Carbon Emissions**
*   Environmentally, **NMC** shows a lower impact than LFP, with Global Warming Potential (GWP) 3–6% lower and Abiotic Depletion of minerals (ADPm) 12–16% lower per kWh delivered, mainly due to better material recovery in recycling [doi.org/10.1016/j.resconrec.2024.107833](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.resconrec.2024.107833).
*   Battery recycling plus reuse can cut life-cycle carbon emissions by about 36.0–37.9% [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-86250-1).
*   The optimal strategy for circularity in Europe, combining reduced material demand and expanded recycling, could lower cumulative CO2-eq emissions by about 78% [doi.org/10.1016/j.resourpol.2024.105160](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.resourpol.2024.105160).
*   A medium-size battery EV typically emits about half as much as an equivalent ICE vehicle over 15 years, with the advantage varying by country based on the electricity mix [IEA](https://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/e75c9a13-3753-4677-933f-c7f9ae38cfdb/EVBatterySupplyChainSustainability.pdf).

Summary:

- Purpose: Benchmark comparing Rust vs Go HTTP servers under high load on Kubernetes, using identical workload (100 SHA256 iterations per request) across three iterations with varying setups.
- Workload and test setup: Up to 15,000 virtual users, 2-minute ramp-up, 15-minute sustained load, 30-second ramp-down. Load tested with k6.
- Key results across iterations:
  - Iteration 1 (musl Go, Rust baseline): Go had faster latencies at P50/P99, Rust had lower throughput.
  - Iteration 2 (glibc, more resources): Go outperformed Rust in both latency (P50-P99) and throughput; Go had zero failures, Rust had a small number of failures.
  - Iteration 3 (Rust optimization: eliminate Vec allocations; dedicated load generators): Rust’s median latency improved significantly (P50 from ~0.376ms to ~0.203ms), Go’s tail latency remained better, but overall throughput for Rust surged to be comparable to Go (28.8M vs 28.6M total requests). Rust memory usage dropped dramatically (224MB vs 521MB), with slightly higher CPU.
- Concrete highlights:
  - Go generally faster for latency (P50–P99) across iterations.
  - Rust achieved higher throughput in Iteration 3 after removing per-request heap allocations, closing the gap with Go.
  - Tail latency: Go retains better P99; Rust improves but still trails in some percentiles.
  - Reliability: Go had zero failures in Iterations 2 and 3; Rust had a small number of timeouts/failures (though still low overall, especially after optimizations).
  - Memory efficiency: Rust 3rd iteration uses ~57% less memory than Go.
- Takeaway: Unnecessary allocations in Rust’s hot path historically masked its potential; eliminating heap allocations in the critical path yielded substantial throughput gains and improved median latency, demonstrating Rust’s performance potential when allocations are removed. Go remains favorable for tail latency and throughput in early iterations, with higher memory usage.

Summary:
- A side-by-side test compared a Go gateway and a Rust gateway under 3,000 requests/s (4 vCPU) for an AI inference workflow.
- Latency (excluding backend token delays): Go p99 = 9.4 ms; Rust p99 = 2.7 ms; p99.9: Go 27.8 ms vs Rust 4.6 ms. Median gaps are small, but Go shows heavy tail with spikes tied to GC cycles.
- Memory usage (RSS at 3,000 req/s): Go ~148 MB; Rust ~34 MB (Rust is far more memory-efficient here).
- GC/Pause behavior (Go): most latency impact comes from mutator assist during GC; with tuning, Go’s p99 and p99.9 improve but at the cost of memory. Different Go GC tuning (GOGC values, GOMEMLIMIT) reduces pauses but increases RSS.
- Rust (with tuned settings) achieves similar or better latency with far lower memory use and fewer GC-related spikes.
- Throughput comparison: at 6,000 req/s, Go is CPU-saturated (3.9/4 cores) with p99 ~31.6 ms (node queueing, not GC); Rust reaches 6,000 req/s with ~2.7 cores and much lower p99 (4.8 ms). This implies Rust uses far fewer vCPUs per throughput at high load.
- Practical takeaways:
  - For overall SLOs that cover the entire request, Go’s added latency at p99 (~9.4 ms) is a small fraction of typical 90 ms-time-to-first-token, so Go often wins on user-perceived latency.
  - If the gateway’s own SLO is strict or you need maximum throughput with lower memory, Rust performs better in latency tail and uses far less memory, but at the cost of longer initial build times and more complex toolchain.
- Decision: They deployed Rust for the shared multi-tenant tier and kept Go for the internal, single-model tier, balancing latency, memory, and operational familiarity.

runs.report:
# Rust vs Go for Network Services: Performance and Developer Productivity Trade-offs

This report summarizes the performance and developer productivity trade-offs between Rust and Go for network services, based on various benchmarks and real-world team experiences.

## Performance

### Throughput and Latency

*   **Go often demonstrates strong throughput and lower tail latency (P99) in initial benchmarks.**
    *   In a Kubernetes HTTP server benchmark, Go consistently showed faster latencies at P50/P99 in early iterations, and maintained better tail latency even after Rust optimizations [source](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
    *   One experiment found Go's HTTP server outperformed Rust in all measured timings for sorting input data, with significantly lower average request round-trip and server processing times across various data sizes [source](https://jmkopper.github.io/posts/2023/04/go-rust/).
    *   For HTTP/2 multiplexed workloads, Go showed lower P99 latency (≈9 ms) compared to Rust (~12 ms) [source](https://johal.in/language-benchmark-rust-185-vs-go-123-vs).
    *   In an AI inference gateway scenario, Go had a P99 latency of 9.4 ms and P99.9 of 27.8 ms, with spikes tied to Garbage Collection (GC) cycles [source](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/go-vs-rust-ai-inference-gateway-latency-memory/).
*   **Rust can achieve comparable or superior throughput and significantly better median latency with optimizations, excelling in latency-critical workloads without GC pauses.**
    *   After eliminating per-request heap allocations, Rust's median latency significantly improved (P50 from ~0.376ms to ~0.203ms), and its overall throughput surged to be comparable to Go (28.8M vs 28.6M total requests) in a Kubernetes HTTP server benchmark [source](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
    *   For a TCP echo server with 1KB payload and 10 clients, Rust achieved higher throughput at 142k req/s compared to Go's 116k req/s [source](https://johal.in/language-benchmark-rust-185-vs-go-123-vs).
    *   In an AI inference gateway, Rust achieved a P99 of 2.7 ms and P99.9 of 4.6 ms, demonstrating far better tail latency due to the absence of GC [source](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/go-vs-rust-ai-inference-gateway-latency-memory/).
    *   Rust's ability to avoid GC pauses makes it suitable for latency-sensitive workloads like Discord Read States rewrite and Cloudflare Pingora [source](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).

### Resource Utilization (Memory & CPU)

*   **Rust generally offers superior memory efficiency, especially under high load, but can have slightly higher CPU usage.**
    *   In the Kubernetes HTTP server benchmark, Rust's memory usage dropped dramatically to ~57% less than Go (224MB vs 521MB) after optimizations, with slightly higher CPU [source](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
    *   For an AI inference gateway at 3,000 req/s, Go used ~148 MB RSS, while Rust used ~34 MB, making Rust far more memory-efficient [source](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/go-vs-rust-ai-inference-gateway-latency-memory/).
    *   At 6,000 req/s, Go was CPU-saturated using 3.9/4 cores, while Rust handled the same load with ~2.7 cores, indicating Rust uses fewer vCPUs per throughput at high load [source](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/go-vs-rust-ai-inference-gateway-latency-memory/).
    *   Rust eliminates garbage collection entirely with ownership and deterministic deallocation, while Go relies on a GC, which can lead to memory footprint growth under heavy allocations [source](https://oscave.com/blog/rust-vs-go-for-microservices-architecture-trade-offs).
*   **Go's memory usage is typically higher than Rust's, particularly when GC tuning is used to reduce pauses.**
    *   Go's memory usage was midway compared to Zig (least) and Rust (highest) in some benchmarks [source](https://johal.in/language-benchmark-rust-185-vs-go-123-vs).
    *   Tuning Go's GC (GOGC values, GOMEMLIMIT) to reduce pauses often comes at the cost of increased memory usage (RSS) [source](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/go-vs-rust-ai-inference-gateway-latency-memory/).

### Reliability

*   **Go generally shows better reliability with zero failures in several benchmark iterations.**
    *   In the Kubernetes HTTP server benchmark, Go had zero failures in Iterations 2 and 3, while Rust had a small number of timeouts/failures (though still low overall, especially after optimizations) [source](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).

## Developer Productivity

### Learning Curve & Ecosystem

*   **Go emphasizes rapid development, developer happiness, and pragmatic simplicity with a lower learning curve and mature cloud-native tooling.**
    *   Go has a low-to-moderate learning curve and fast iteration with mature cloud-native tooling [source](https://oscave.com/blog/rust-vs-go-for-microservices-architecture-trade-offs).
    *   Go's standard library, particularly `net/http`, is simpler and more pleasant for HTTP server setup [source](https://jmkopper.github.io/posts/2023/04/go-rust/).
    *   Go's simpler ecosystems often lead to faster iteration [source](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).
*   **Rust has an extremely steep learning curve due to concepts like ownership, lifetimes, and the Borrow Checker, and often requires third-party libraries for common tasks like HTTP servers.**
    *   Rust has an extremely steep learning curve and slower compilation times [source](https://oscave.com/blog/rust-vs-go-for-microservices-architecture-trade-offs).
    *   Rust often lacks a convenient standard HTTP server, requiring third-party libraries, which can add friction and variability [source](https://jmkopper.github.io/posts/2023/04/go-rust/).

### Compile Time

*   **Go generally offers faster compile times compared to Rust.**
    *   Go compiled in 6.1s, while Rust took 14.2s in a benchmark [source](https://johal.in/language-benchmark-rust-185-vs-go-123-vs).

## Trade-offs and Recommendations

*   **Go is often the preferred choice for rapid feature delivery, standard CRUD APIs, event-driven architectures, and data ingestion pipelines, especially where GC pauses are not a critical bottleneck.**
    *   Go offers the best balance of performance, latency, memory, and production readiness for 80% of use cases [source](https://johal.in/language-benchmark-rust-185-vs-go-123-vs).
    *   It is favored for many scalable systems where GC performance is acceptable and offers faster iteration [source](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).
    *   For overall Service Level Objectives (SLOs) covering the entire request, Go's added latency at P99 might be a small fraction of typical user-perceived latency [source](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/go-vs-rust-ai-inference-gateway-latency-memory/).
*   **Rust is ideal for foundational cloud infrastructure, networking proxies, distributed storage, cryptography, and real-time streaming, where absolute safety, deterministic memory management, ultra-low tail latency, and maximum efficiency are paramount.**
    *   Rust is best for latency-critical workloads and when memory safety with no GC is desired, despite its steeper learning curve [source](https://johal.in/language-benchmark-benchmark-rust-185-vs-go-123-vs).
    *   It is favored when avoiding GC pauses and achieving tighter memory control or lower latency [source](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).
    *   If the gateway's own SLO is strict or maximum throughput with lower memory is needed, Rust performs better in latency tail and uses far less memory [source](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/go-vs-rust-ai-inference-gateway-latency-memory/).

**Conclusion:** The choice between Rust and Go depends heavily on specific project requirements, existing team skills, and the nature of the workload. If rapid development, a gentler learning curve, and a robust standard library are priorities, Go excels. If ultra-low latency, deterministic performance, minimal memory footprint, and high-performance in core infrastructure components are critical, Rust is the stronger choice, provided the team is prepared for its steeper learning curve.

sources.summary:
Summary:
- A side-by-side test compared a Go gateway and a Rust gateway under 3,000 requests/s (4 vCPU) for an AI inference workflow.
- Latency (excluding backend token delays): Go p99 = 9.4 ms; Rust p99 = 2.7 ms; p99.9: Go 27.8 ms vs Rust 4.6 ms. Median gaps are small, but Go shows heavy tail with spikes tied to GC cycles.
- Memory usage (RSS at 3,000 req/s): Go ~148 MB; Rust ~34 MB (Rust is far more memory-efficient here).
- GC/Pause behavior (Go): most latency impact comes from mutator assist during GC; with tuning, Go’s p99 and p99.9 improve but at the cost of memory. Different Go GC tuning (GOGC values, GOMEMLIMIT) reduces pauses but increases RSS.
- Rust (with tuned settings) achieves similar or better latency with far lower memory use and fewer GC-related spikes.
- Throughput comparison: at 6,000 req/s, Go is CPU-saturated (3.9/4 cores) with p99 ~31.6 ms (node queueing, not GC); Rust reaches 6,000 req/s with ~2.7 cores and much lower p99 (4.8 ms). This implies Rust uses far fewer vCPUs per throughput at high load.
- Practical takeaways:
  - For overall SLOs that cover the entire request, Go’s added latency at p99 (~9.4 ms) is a small fraction of typical 90 ms-time-to-first-token, so Go often wins on user-perceived latency.
  - If the gateway’s own SLO is strict or you need maximum throughput with lower memory, Rust performs better in latency tail and uses far less memory, but at the cost of longer initial build times and more complex toolchain.
- Decision: They deployed Rust for the shared multi-tenant tier and kept Go for the internal, single-model tier, balancing latency, memory, and operational familiarity.

Summary:
- Setup: Head-to-head HTTP server benchmarks (Go vs Rust) under high load on Kubernetes. Each request performs 100 SHA-256 iterations.
- Iteration 1 (musl, baseline): Go had lower latency overall; Rust had higher throughput but worse tail latency. Go: lower P50/P99; Rust: higher throughput.
- Iteration 2 (glibc, more resources, dedicated load): Go improved further, achieving higher throughput and lower latency across more percentiles; Rust throughput rose but still lagged in latency tail.
- Iteration 3 (Rust heap allocations eliminated; fixed-size buffers; dedicated clients): Major shift for Rust. Rust achieved:
  - P50 latency: 0.203 ms (Rust) vs 0.255 ms (Go) — first time Rust wins on median.
  - P99 latency: Go still better tail latency (1.23–1.23 ms vs Rust ~2.29 ms in this iteration).
  - Throughput: Rust ~28.8M requests vs Go ~28.6M (nearly identical; Rust up ~74% from Iteration 2).
  - Memory: Rust uses 57% less memory (≈224 MB vs 521 MB); CPU slightly higher for Rust.
  - Reliability: Go zero failures; Rust had some timeouts (516).
- Key takeaway: Eliminating per-request heap allocations in Rust’s hot path dramatically boosted throughput and improved median latency, revealing Rust’s potential when allocations are avoided. Across all iterations, Go shows better tail latency and higher reliability, while Rust demonstrates superior memory efficiency and, after optimizations, competitive throughput.

runs.report:
# Rust vs. Go for Network Services: Performance and Developer Productivity Trade-offs

This report summarizes the trade-offs between Rust and Go for network services, focusing on performance, developer productivity, and suitable use cases.

## Performance Benchmarks

*   **Overall Performance & Latency:**
    *   For a high-throughput HTTP server sorting data, Go surprisingly outperformed Rust in average and max round-trip and server times across various request sizes [jmkopper.github.io](https://jmkopper.github.io/posts/2023/04/go-rust/).
    *   In a CPU-bound microservice (image processing), Rust consistently showed faster performance and significantly better tail latency (p90, p99, p99.9) compared to Go, with Rust being 20% to 2.8x faster at various percentiles [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
    *   When processing 100 SHA-256 iterations per request under high load, Go generally had better tail latency (P99) and higher reliability (zero failures), while Rust achieved superior memory efficiency and, after specific optimizations, competitive throughput [github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
    *   Optimizing Rust by eliminating per-request heap allocations dramatically improved its throughput and median latency [github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).

*   **Throughput & Resource Usage:**
    *   For CPU-bound tasks, Rust offered approximately 30% higher throughput per core and lower CPU usage compared to Go [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
    *   Rust consistently demonstrated lower memory usage across various benchmarks. For a CPU-bound service, Rust used 38 MB RSS after 3 minutes versus Go's 112 MB (Go ~2.9x more) [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
    *   In high-load HTTP server tests, Rust used 57% less memory (≈224 MB vs 521 MB) than Go, though CPU usage was slightly higher for Rust [github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
    *   With 100k concurrent connections, Rust used ~120MB memory with 3ms latency p99 and no GC pauses, whereas Go used ~850MB with 15ms latency and GC pauses [cloudbridge-research.ru](https://cloudbridge-research.ru/en/blog/go-rust-networking/).

*   **Garbage Collection (GC) Impact:**
    *   Go's default GC can lead to tail latency issues; aggressive memory tuning with `GOMEMLIMIT` and `GOGC` can mitigate this but often increases memory usage [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
    *   Rust benefits from having no GC, which contributes to its predictable latency and lower memory footprint [cloudbridge-research.ru](https://cloudbridge-research.ru/en/blog/go-rust-networking/).

## Developer Productivity & Ecosystem

*   **Development Speed & Learning Curve:**
    *   Go is generally favored for faster development, simpler syntax, and a lower learning curve, making it suitable for quick results and teams needing minimal adoption burden [deepengineering.net](https://deepengineering.net/p/issue51-rust-vs-go-service-level-backend-decisions), [cloudbridge-research.ru](https://cloudbridge-research.ru/en/blog/go-rust-networking/).
    *   Rust has a steeper learning curve and typically requires longer development times due to its focus on memory safety and explicit resource management [cloudbridge-research.ru](https://cloudbridge-research.ru/en/blog/go-rust-networking/).

*   **Ecosystem & Tooling:**
    *   Go boasts a strong, cohesive ecosystem, particularly for web services with its standard `net/http` library, and excellent integration with cloud infrastructure tools like Docker and Kubernetes [jmkopper.github.io](https://jmkopper.github.io/posts/2023/04/go-rust/), [deepengineering.net](https://deepengineering.net/p/issue51-rust-vs-go-service-level-backend-decisions).
    *   Rust's HTTP server ecosystem relies on third-party crates, lacking a standard library HTTP server API, which can lead to more boilerplate code and a less cohesive experience [jmkopper.github.io](https://jmkopper.github.io/posts/2023/04/go-rust/). While growing, its web-service ecosystem is considered less mature than Go's [flightaware.engineering](https://flightaware.engineering/the-best-tool-for-the-job-assessing-languages-for-microservice-development-at-flightaware-2/).

*   **Code Footprint:**
    *   One study observed a Go server with ~94 lines of code compared to a Rust server with ~65 lines, but noted Rust needed more boilerplate due to its HTTP ecosystem choices [jmkopper.github.io](https://jmkopper.github.io/posts/2023/04/go-rust/).

## Use Cases & Recommendations

*   **When to choose Go:**
    *   Rapid delivery, fast initial deployment, and quick iteration are priorities [deepengineering.net](https://deepengineering.net/p/issue51-rust-vs-go-service-level-backend-decisions), [cloudbridge-research.ru](https://cloudbridge-research.ru/en/blog/go-rust-networking/).
    *   I/O-bound workloads, control-plane tools, and REST APIs where development speed is critical [cloudbridge-research.ru](https://cloudbridge-research.ru/en/blog/go-rust-networking/).
    *   Teams with Go-centric expertise seeking a lower-risk, productive choice for general web services [flightaware.engineering](https://flightaware.engineering/the-best-tool-for-the-job-assessing-languages-for-microservice-development-at-flightaware-2/).
    *   Cloud infrastructure tooling and CLI tools [deepengineering.net](https://deepengineering.net/p/issue51-rust-vs-go-service-level-backend-decisions).

*   **When to choose Rust:**
    *   Services with strict latency predictability, low memory footprint, and high concurrency requirements [deepengineering.net](https://deepengineering.net/p/issue51-rust-vs-go-service-level-backend-decisions), [cloudbridge-research.ru](https://cloudbridge-research.ru/en/blog/go-rust-networking/).
    *   CPU-bound paths with tight p99 latency and best throughput [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
    *   Data-plane, high-throughput gateways/proxies, latency-critical services, and security-sensitive components [cloudbridge-research.ru](https://cloudbridge-research.ru/en/blog/go-rust-networking/).
    *   Workloads where removing runtime-related failures is critical (due to memory safety) [deepengineering.net](https://deepengineering.net/p/issue51-rust-vs-go-service-level-backend-decisions).

*   **Hybrid Approach:**
    *   A common recommendation is to use both languages: Go for control-plane/management services (fast iteration, ecosystem integration) and Rust for data-plane/performance-critical components (ultra-high performance, memory efficiency, predictable latency) [cloudbridge-research.ru](https://cloudbridge-research.ru/en/blog/go-rust-networking/), [deepengineering.net](https://deepengineering.net/p/issue51-rust-vs-go-service-level-backend-decisions).
    *   Focus on solving specific service constraints rather than treating Rust as a universal upgrade [deepengineering.net](https://deepengineering.net/p/issue51-rust-vs-go-service-level-backend-decisions).

Summary:
- Study: Pilot benchmark evaluating language-stack efficiency for self-hosted HTTP CRUD services on a Raspberry Pi 5.
- Stacks tested (SQLite-backed APIs): Go 1.26/net/http, Rust 1.95/Axum, Python 3.13/FastAPI+Granian, Fastify (Node.js), and .NET 10 Native AOT.
- Key findings:
  - Rust delivered the highest weighted throughput per RAM (310.25 req/s/MB) with a small peak RSS of 7.36 MB, outperforming Go by ~2.8x on this metric.
  - Raw throughput cluster (high concurrency) achieved: ~2,125–2,461 req/s across stacks; Python underperformed (~969 req/s) compared with others.
  - Concurrency scaling (GET /items/:id) varied:
    - .NET: very strong at high concurrency, reaching ~26,209 req/s at concurrency 240.
    - Go and Rust: plateau near 9,700 req/s (saturation point around c ≈ 120).
    - Python: remained under 2,300 req/s.
  - Memory behavior:
    - Rust maintained a flat RSS around 7.8 MB during tests.
    - Other stacks saw RSS growth up to ~117 MB without clear GC drops in some scenarios.
- Practical recommendations for RAM-constrained, self-hosted CRUD over SQLite on a Pi 5:
  - Rust is the most RAM-efficient measured stack.
  - .NET offers the strongest high-concurrency performance.
  - Go is a solid option when ecosystem breadth is important.
- Caveats: Results are from a single Raspberry Pi 5 unit; replication with additional devices and storage backends is recommended before generalizing.

  - Slack: Flannel edge cache implemented to reduce boot payloads (Go/Rust mix in the ecosystem).
- Practical takeaway: If you’re facing GC pauses or strict latency/memory constraints, Rust is a common choice. If you’re achieving scale with predictable latency on a familiar runtime, Go remains a solid, widely-used option.

runs.report:
# Rust vs. Go for Network Services: Performance and Developer Productivity Trade-offs

This report summarizes the trade-offs between Rust and Go for network services, focusing on performance metrics and developer productivity insights drawn from various benchmarks and real-world case studies.

## Performance

### Throughput & Latency

*   **Rust vs. Go (High Kubernetes Load - SHA256 iterations)**:
    *   In initial iterations, Go sometimes achieved lower latency and higher throughput, especially in P99 tail latency [source](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
    *   By eliminating per-request heap allocations in Rust, Rust significantly improved P50 latency (0.203 ms vs Go's 0.255 ms) and achieved nearly identical throughput (Rust ~28.8M vs Go ~28.6M requests). Go still maintained superior P99 tail latency (1.23 ms vs 2.29 ms) [source](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
*   **Rust vs. Go (CPU-Bound Microservice - p99 < 15ms target)**:
    *   Rust consistently demonstrated lower latency across P50, P90, P99, and P99.9 compared to Go. At 4,000 req/s, Rust's P99 was 6.8 ms vs Go's 12.7 ms [source](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
    *   Rust achieved higher maximum sustainable throughput (9,840 req/s) at the P99 < 15ms target, compared to Go's default 7,410 req/s (or 8,560 req/s with GC tuning) [source](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
    *   Rust provided significantly more requests per vCPU-second (2,460) compared to Go (1,850 default, up to 2,140 with GC tuning) [source](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
*   **Rust vs. Go (General Benchmarks)**:
    *   Rust 1.85 generally leads in raw throughput across TCP echo and HTTP/1.1 JSON and HTTP/2 multiplexed workloads (e.g., 142k req/s for TCP echo vs Go's 116k) [source](https://johal.in/language-benchmark-rust-185-vs-go-123-vs).
    *   Go 1.23 often delivers the lowest P99 latency on HTTP workloads (9–14 ms range) compared to Rust (12–18 ms) and Zig [source](https://johal.in/language-benchmark-rust-185-vs-go-123-vs).
*   **Rust vs. Go (Raspberry Pi 5 - Self-hosted HTTP CRUD)**:
    *   Both Go and Rust plateaued near 9,700 req/s at a saturation point around 120 concurrency when evaluating concurrency scaling for GET requests [source](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11932).

### Memory Usage

*   **Rust vs. Go (High Kubernetes Load - SHA256 iterations)**:
    *   Rust was significantly more memory-efficient when heap allocations were eliminated, using ~224 MB compared to Go's ~521 MB (a ~57% advantage) [source](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
*   **Rust vs. Go (CPU-Bound Microservice)**:
    *   Rust maintained lower RSS (38 MB) after 3 minutes compared to Go's 112 MB (~2.9x more) [source](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
*   **Rust vs. Go (Raspberry Pi 5 - Self-hosted HTTP CRUD)**:
    *   Rust delivered the highest weighted throughput per RAM (310.25 req/s/MB) with a small peak RSS of 7.36 MB, outperforming Go by ~2.8x on this metric [source](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11932).
    *   Rust maintained a flat RSS around 7.8 MB during tests, while other stacks including Go saw RSS growth up to ~117 MB [source](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11932).
*   **Rust vs. Go (General Benchmarks)**:
    *   Rust generally uses less memory than Go in some tests (e.g., HTTP/1.1 JSON). Idle memory for Rust ranged from ~48–112 MB, while Go was ~16–64 MB [source](https://johal.in/language-benchmark-rust-185-vs-go-123-vs).

### CPU Utilization

*   **Rust vs. Go (CPU-Bound Microservice)**:
    *   Rust showed lower CPU utilization (61%) compared to Go (78%), indicating greater efficiency [source](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).

### Other Performance Factors

*   **Garbage Collection (GC) Impact**: Go's GC pauses (approximately every 40 ms) are identified as a primary driver of tail latency spikes under load due to per-request allocations and GC stalls. Rust, with its deterministic frees, avoids GC pauses and yields tighter tail latencies [source](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
*   **Failures**: In some high-load benchmarks, Go had zero failures while Rust experienced a small percentage of timeouts or failures (e.g., 323 failures in one iteration, 516 timeouts in another) [source](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
*   **Compile Times**: Rust has longer compile times (14.2s for a 10k LOC binary) compared to Go (6.1s) [source](https://johal.in/language-benchmark-rust-185-vs-go-123-vs).

## Developer Productivity

### Practical Use Cases & Team Velocity

*   **Go's Strengths**:
    *   Often chosen for its production readiness, mature HTTP/2 stack, and generally being a well-balanced choice for most 80% high-concurrency network service scenarios [source](https://johal.in/language-benchmark-rust-185-vs-go-123-vs).
    *   Provides a solid option when ecosystem breadth and team velocity are important [source](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11932), [source](https://johal.in/language-benchmark-rust-185-vs-go-123-vs).
    *   Common in scalable systems where GC-triggered issues are not problematic [source](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).
*   **Rust's Strengths**:
    *   Favored for peak throughput, strict memory safety, and for future latency-critical systems [source](https://johal.in/language-benchmark-rust-185-vs-go-123-vs).
    *   A common choice when facing GC pauses or strict latency/memory constraints [source](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).
    *   Excellent FFI interop [source](https://johal.in/language-benchmark-rust-185-vs-go-123-vs).

### Real-world Adoption & Case Studies

*   **Rust Adoption Examples**:
    *   **Discord**: Switched from Go to Rust to eliminate GC latency spikes in a large in-memory cache and uses Rust in ScyllaDB tooling [source](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).
    *   **Cloudflare**: Uses Rust for Pingora, a proxy [source](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).
    *   **Datadog**: Uses Rust in timeseries indexing adjustments [source](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).
    *   **Blue**: Migrating its Node.js backend to Rust using a strangler fig pattern, achieving significant speedups and improved P95 times (e.g., userChanges 159ms→3ms) with high reliability (fewer than 1 in 500 calls fell back to Node) [source](https://blue.app/blog/rewriting-blues-backend-in-rust).
*   **Go Adoption Examples**:
    *   **Cloudflare**: Employs Go in its Quicksilver and HTTP analytics pipeline [source](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).
    *   **Datadog**: Uses Go for Husky [source](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).
*   **Mixed Environments**:
    *   Companies like Dropbox (Magic Pocket) and Slack (Flannel edge cache) utilize a mix of Rust and Go in their infrastructure [source](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).
    *   OpenAI scales to 70M+ requests/sec with Rust/Go integration [source](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).

### Tuning & Optimization

*   **Go GC Tuning**: Tuning Go's garbage collector (e.g., with GOMEMLIMIT) can improve P99 latency and maximum sustainable throughput, but often at the cost of higher memory usage (RSS increasing from 131 MB default to 346-782 MB) [source](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
*   **Rust Optimization**: Eliminating heap allocations in Rust's hot path is crucial for substantial throughput gains and beating Go's P50 latency [source](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).

### Verdicts

*   **For peak throughput and strict memory safety, especially for CPU-bound hot paths with strict P99 SLOs, Rust 1.85 is recommended** [source](https://johal.in/language-benchmark-rust-185-vs-go-123-vs), [source](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
*   **For team velocity, lower P99 latency (in some HTTP contexts), and memory efficiency (when Rust isn't heavily optimized), Go 1.23 is often the best balanced choice for most high-concurrency network service scenarios** [source](https://johal.in/language-benchmark-rust-185-vs-go-123-vs).
*   **If facing GC pauses or strict latency/memory constraints, Rust is a common and effective choice. If achieving scale with predictable latency on a familiar runtime, Go remains a solid, widely-used option** [source](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).

Key throughput and latency at 4,000 req/s (pSLO: p99 < 15 ms)
- Rust (axum) vs Go (net/http)
  - p50: Rust 2.1 ms vs Go 2.6 ms (Go +24%)
  - p90: Rust 3.4 ms vs Go 4.9 ms (Go +44%)
  - p99: Rust 6.8 ms vs Go 12.7 ms (Go +87%)
  - p99.9: Rust 11.2 ms vs Go 31.4 ms (Go 2.8x)
  - CPU utilization: Rust 61% vs Go 78% (Go +17 pts)
  - RSS after 3 min: Rust 38 MB vs Go 112 MB (Go ~2.9x)

What drives the tail latency gap
- Go’s GC pauses (~every 40 ms) cause tail latency spikes under load due to per-request allocations (~70 KB) and GC stalls.
- Rust uses deterministic frees, avoiding GC pauses and yielding tighter tails; p50 is faster in Rust, and p99/p99.9 gaps are driven mainly by GC behavior in Go, not code-level optimizations.

Maximum sustainable throughput (p99 < 15 ms target)
- Max req/s at p99 < 15 ms:
  - Rust: 9,840
  - Go (default): 7,410
  - Go with GC tuning: 8,120 (GOGC) or 8,560 (GOMEMLIMIT + GOGC off)
- Corresponding p99 at that rate (roughly ~15 ms) and p99.9:
  - Rust: p99 14.6 ms; p99.9 22.9 ms; RSS 41 MB
  - Go (default): p99 14.8 ms; p99.9 48.3 ms; RSS 131 MB
  - Go with tuning (GOGC/limit): p99 14.9 ms; p99.9 39.1 ms (GOMEMLIMIT) or 33.6 ms (GOMEMLIMIT + GOGC off); RSS 346 MB to 782 MB

Per-box throughput comparison
- Requests per vCPU-second:
  - Rust: 2,460
  - Go (default): 1,850

results.search_result:
Summary:
- Raft is a consensus algorithm for maintaining a replicated log, with results equivalent to Paxos but designed to be more understandable and easier to implement.
- Key design features that improve understandability and safety:
  - Strong leader: a single leader drives log replication, simplifying reasoning.
  - Leader election: randomized timers resolve conflicts quickly with minimal extra mechanism.
  - Membership changes: a joint consensus method overlaps majorities from two configurations to keep the cluster available during reconfiguration.
- Safety and performance:
  - Raft reduces nondeterminism in state space, aiding comprehension while achieving comparable efficiency to Paxos.
  - The approach yields a practical, coherent framework for building replicated state machines with support for reconfiguration.
- Empirical user study:
  - 43 students compared Raft and Paxos quizzes after watching respective material.
  - On average, Raft users scored 4.9 points higher (mean Raft ≈ 25.7 vs. mean Paxos ≈ 20.8 out of 60).
  - 33 of 43 participants performed better on Raft questions (points above the diagonal in the study’s scatter plot).
  - A paired t-test with 95% confidence indicates Raft scores are meaningfully higher; a regression model linked quiz performance to factors like prior Paxos experience and which quiz was taken first.
- Overall takeaway: Raft is designed to be easier to learn while providing a robust, practical consensus foundation, with empirical evidence suggesting higher comprehension than Paxos among students.

Summary:

- Raft is a consensus protocol for replicated logs that yield a replicated state machine: all servers execute the same commands in the same order. A group of 2f + 1 replicas tolerates f crashes.
- Core properties:
  - Safety: at most one leader per term; a server votes only once per term and votes are persisted. If a leader has committed an entry, that entry will appear in logs of all future leaders.
  - Liveness: some candidate eventually becomes leader. Elections use randomized timeouts to avoid split votes; typically one candidate wins before others start.
- Log and entries:
  - Log entry format: <index, term, command>, stored on stable storage (disk) and durable across crashes.
  - An entry is committed when it is known to be stored on a majority of servers; once committed, it will be applied to the state machine.
  - Leader appends new commands to its log and sends AppendEntries RPCs to followers. Committed entries are propagated to and applied by followers and clients receive results when their command is committed and executed.
  - If entries share the same index and term across servers, they contain the same command; prior entries are identical as well.
- Leader changes:
  - A new leader’s log is taken as the truth; no special sync steps are required beyond normal operation. The new leader’s log will converge followers’ logs over time.
  - Safety: if a log entry is committed by a leader, it will appear in all future leaders’ logs.
- Client interaction and idempotency:
  - Clients send commands to the leader; if the leader crashes, clients may be redirected to a new leader.
  - Exactly-once semantics are maintained by embedding a unique request ID in each command, which is checked against existing log entries to avoid duplicates.
- Configuration changes:
  - Raft supports configuration changes (e.g., adding/removing replicas) via joint consensus: both old and new configurations must reach majority during the transition.
  - A configuration change is logged as an entry; the system gradually transitions to the new configuration after the joint consensus is committed.
- Practical notes:
  - Raft resembles a single “virtual” leader that manages replication, similar to multi-Paxos or viewstamped replication, but designed to be easier to understand and implement.
  - Strong leader constraints (e.g., a leader’s log must be at least as up-to-date as followers’ logs) help keep logs consistent across the cluster.

Summary:
- The document outlines core operations and thread roles in the HashiCorp Raft implementation (docs/R).
- Leader writes include RequestConfigChange, Apply (committing log entries on a majority and applying to FSM), Barrier, LeadershipTransfer, Restore (snapshot), and VerifyLeader.
- Follower writes include BootstrapCluster (storing cluster config locally).
- Read operations are available from any state and cover: AppliedIndex, GetConfiguration, LastContact, LastIndex, Leader, Snapshot, State, and Stats.
- The runtime behavior is organized by roles and goroutines:
  - run: handles follower, candidate, and leader states with RPC processing, heartbeats, elections, leadership transfer, commits, verifications, snapshot and restore flows, and client Apply requests.
  - runFSM: exclusive access to the FSM for applying/mutating state and snapshot restoration.
  - runSnapshot: persists snapshots and compacts logs, triggered periodically or by user.
  - askPeerForVote: candidate-only, sends RequestVote to each voting peer.
  - replicate (leader-only): handles AppendEntries to peers, heartbeat management, and snapshot sending on failure.
  - heartbeat (leader-only) and pipelineDecode (leader-only): support leader replication/optimization.
- Key concepts: log entries are considered committed when replicated on a majority; various specialized operations manage config, leadership, snapshots, and FSM state.

Raft is a consensus algorithm designed to be easy to understand while delivering fault tolerance comparable to Paxos. It achieves agreement across a cluster of servers on a replicated state machine by coordinating leader election, log replication, and membership changes. Key ideas:

- Consensus goal: multiple servers agree on a sequence of commands (log entries) so all state machines apply identical logs and reach the same state.
- Fault tolerance: the system can continue operating as long as a majority of servers are available; it can tolerate failures within that majority.
- Raft subproblems: clearly separates leader election, log replication, safety, and configuration changes to make implementation and reasoning easier.
- Practical resources: includes interactive visuals (RaftScope) and guided explanations (The Secret Lives of Data) to illustrate how Raft works in real time.
- Publications and validation: primary paper “In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm” (Ongaro & Ousterhout) with extended version; related dissertations and formal specifications.
- Community and implementations: active discussion forums (raft-dev Google group) and multiple language implementations; a maintained table catalogues available projects (with notes on leadership, persistence, membership changes, and log compaction).

If you’re answering “what is Raft and what does it guarantee?”:
- Raft guarantees safe, consistent replication of a log across a majority of servers, enabling a deterministic, fault-tolerant replicated state machine.
- It remains able to make progress with a majority available; it does not sacrifice correctness for availability.

For deep dive: consider reading the Raft paper, exploring RaftScope and The Secret Lives of Data visualizations, and reviewing the implementation table to find a language/licensing option that fits your needs.

runs.report:
## Raft Consensus Algorithm: Leader Election and Log Replication

This report summarizes how the Raft consensus algorithm handles leader election and log replication, drawing from the provided search results. Raft is designed for understandability while achieving fault tolerance and performance comparable to Paxos.

### Overview and Core Properties

Raft is a consensus algorithm that maintains a replicated log across a cluster of servers, enabling a replicated state machine where all servers execute the same commands in the same order [https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf), [https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf). Its key design features focus on improving understandability and safety [https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf), [https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/atc14/atc14-paper-ongaro.pdf](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/atc14/atc14-paper-ongaro.pdf):

*   **Strong Leader:** A single leader manages all log replication, simplifying the protocol [https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf), [https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/atc14/atc14-paper-ongaro.pdf](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/atc14/atc14-paper-ongaro.pdf).
*   **Safety:** Guarantees at most one leader per term, and if a leader commits an entry, that entry will be present in the logs of all future leaders [https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf). Votes are persisted, and a server votes only once per term [https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
*   **Liveness:** Ensures that some candidate will eventually become the leader [https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
*   **Fault Tolerance:** The system remains operational as long as a majority of servers are available [https://raft.github.io/](https://raft.github.io/).

### Leader Election

Raft employs a robust leader election process to ensure a single, consistent leader:

*   **Randomized Timers:** Leader elections utilize randomized timeouts to quickly resolve conflicts and avoid split votes [https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf), [https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf), [https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/atc14/atc14-paper-ongaro.pdf](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/atc14/atc14-paper-ongaro.pdf). This typically allows one candidate to win before others start [https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
*   **RequestVote RPC:** When a server's election timeout expires, it transitions to a candidate state, increments its term, and sends `RequestVote` RPCs to other voting peers [https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md).
*   **Majority Rule:** A candidate becomes the leader if it receives votes from a majority of the servers in the cluster [https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
*   **Leadership Transfer:** Raft supports transferring leadership, allowing a current leader to relinquish its role to another server [https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md).

### Log Replication

Log replication in Raft is leader-driven and designed for consistency and safety:

*   **Log Entry Format:** Each log entry contains an index, the term in which it was created, and the command to be executed [https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf). These entries are stored on stable storage (disk) for durability across crashes [https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
*   **Leader-Only Appends:** Only the leader can append new commands to its log and then replicates these entries to its followers using `AppendEntries` RPCs [https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf), [https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/atc14/atc14-paper-ongaro.pdf](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/atc14/atc14-paper-ongaro.pdf).
*   **Commitment:** An entry is considered committed when it is known to be stored on a majority of servers [https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf), [https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md). Once committed, the entry is applied to the state machine by the leader and subsequently by followers [https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
*   **Log Consistency:** If two entries on different servers have the same index and term, they are guaranteed to contain the same command. Furthermore, their preceding entries are also identical [https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf). This strong consistency is maintained by the leader's log being at least as up-to-date as followers' logs [https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
*   **Leader Changes and Log Convergence:** When a new leader is elected, its log is taken as the source of truth. The new leader's log will converge followers' logs over time through normal operation, without requiring special synchronization steps [https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf). This ensures that if a log entry is committed by a leader, it will appear in all future leaders' logs [https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
*   **Client Interaction and Idempotency:** Clients send commands to the leader. To maintain exactly-once semantics, each command includes a unique request ID, which the leader checks against existing log entries to prevent duplicates [https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
*   **Snapshots and Log Compaction:** Raft implementations support snapshots to compact logs, which are triggered periodically or by user action, persisting the FSM state and removing older log entries [https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md).
