runs.report:
## Mercury Safety Report

### Executive Summary:
Mercury is a naturally occurring neurotoxin that poses significant health risks to humans and the environment. Exposure primarily occurs through inhaling vapors in industrial settings, consuming contaminated fish and shellfish (methylmercury), and contact with mercury-containing products. Health effects vary depending on the form of mercury, dose, and duration of exposure, with developing fetuses and young children being most vulnerable. Regulatory efforts globally aim to reduce mercury emissions, ban its use in certain products, and manage its waste to mitigate health and environmental impacts.

### Health Effects of Mercury Exposure

Mercury exists in several forms—elemental (metallic) mercury, inorganic mercury salts, and methylmercury—each with distinct toxic effects [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).

*   **General Health Concerns:**
    *   Mercury is one of the WHO's top ten chemicals of major public health concern [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).
    *   Health risks are broad and serious, especially for developing fetuses and young children [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   It can affect the nervous, digestive, immune systems, lungs, kidneys, skin, and eyes [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).
    *   Neurological and cognitive impairments are common after exposure [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).
    *   The health effects depend on the form, dose, duration, exposure route, age, and individual health [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).

*   **Elemental Mercury (Vapor):**
    *   **Exposure:** Primarily through inhaling mercury vapors (e.g., from spills or broken devices) [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury), [source](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxguides/toxguide-46.pdf).
    *   **Neurological Effects:** Tremor, vision issues, slowed nerve conduction, reduced motor speed/coordination, memory and cognitive changes, mood/irritability symptoms, insomnia, headaches, and sensory disturbances [source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/), [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   **Renal Effects:** Decreased glomerular/tubular function and nephrotoxicity [source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/), [source](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxguides/toxguide-46.pdf).
    *   **Respiratory Effects:** Severe inhalation can cause acute lung injury, pneumonitis, and respiratory failure [source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).

*   **Inorganic Mercury Salts:**
    *   **Exposure:** Absorbed via all routes, including GI tract, skin, and inhalation [source](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxguides/toxguide-46.pdf).
    *   **Neurological Effects:** Impaired motor function, memory, learning; overt neurotoxicity at higher exposures; mood swings, memory loss, and mental disturbances [source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/), [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   **Renal Effects:** Dose- and duration-dependent renal toxicity [source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
    *   **Other Effects:** Possible cardiovascular, immunological, reproductive effects, and some carcinogenic signals (in male rats) [source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/). High exposure can damage the GI tract and cause skin rashes/dermatitis [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).

*   **Methylmercury (MeHg):**
    *   **Exposure:** Primarily from eating contaminated fish and shellfish, which is the main dietary source [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury), [source](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxguides/toxguide-46.pdf).
    *   **Neurodevelopmental Effects (Prenatal Exposure):** Most significant risk is to developing fetuses, leading to harm to the brain and nervous system development, affecting cognitive, memory, attention, language, fine motor, and visual-spatial skills [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury), [source](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxguides/toxguide-46.pdf). Potential birth defects at high dietary MeHg [source](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxguides/toxguide-46.pdf).
    *   **Adult Neurological Effects:** Vision loss, sensory deficits, coordination problems, speech/hearing impairment, muscle weakness, and paresthesias [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   **Cardiovascular Effects:** Epidemiological studies link mercury biomarkers to various cardiovascular outcomes [source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
    *   **Excretion:** Primarily through hair [source](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxguides/toxguide-46.pdf).

*   **Ethylmercury:**
    *   Found in some vaccines (thiomersal) but does not pose a health risk [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).

### Sources of Exposure and Prevention

Mercury is a naturally occurring element, but human activities significantly contribute to its release and exposure [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).

*   **Primary Exposure Routes:**
    *   **Dietary:** Contaminated fish/seafood (Methylmercury) is the main source; rice may also contribute [source](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxguides/toxguide-46.pdf).
    *   **Inhalation:** Mercury vapors from industrial settings, coal combustion, or spills from broken mercury-containing items (e.g., thermometers, dental amalgams) [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [source](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxguides/toxguide-46.pdf).
    *   **Dermal:** From consumer products containing mercury (e.g., skin-lightening creams) [source](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxguides/toxguide-46.pdf).
    *   **Other:** Contaminated water (minor source), and elemental mercury from dental amalgams [source](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxguides/toxguide-46.pdf).

*   **Prevention and Mitigation Strategies:**
    *   **Industrial Practices:** Eliminate mercury mining and its use in gold mining; promote non-mercury gold extraction methods; shift to clean energy to avoid mercury from coal combustion; reduce exposure in workplaces [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).
    *   **Product Management:** Replace mercury-containing medical devices with safer alternatives; manage and minimize mercury in products such as batteries, thermometers, lamps, dental amalgam, cosmetics, and pharmaceuticals [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).
    *   **Public Health Guidance:** Consult a physician or poison control if concerned about mercury exposure [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).

### Regulatory Frameworks and Safety Guidelines

Global and national efforts are in place to regulate mercury to protect human health and the environment.

*   **International:**
    *   **Minamata Convention (2013):** The EU ratified this convention to curb global mercury emissions and releases [source](https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/chemicals/mercury_en).

*   **United States (EPA Regulations):**
    *   **Mercury Export Ban Act (2008):** Prohibits the export of metallic mercury and mandates long-term storage of mercury by federal agencies [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/environmental-laws-apply-mercury).
    *   **Mercury-Containing and Rechargeable Battery Management Act (1996):** Phases out mercury in batteries and establishes disposal requirements [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/environmental-laws-apply-mercury).
    *   **Clean Air Act:** Lists mercury as a hazardous air pollutant, with EPA setting technology-based emission standards [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/environmental-laws-apply-mercury).
    *   **Clean Water Act:** States set water quality standards for mercury, regulating discharges and warning about methylmercury in fish [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/environmental-laws-apply-mercury).
    *   **Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA):** Regulates mercury waste management from generation to disposal [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/environmental-laws-apply-mercury).
    *   **Safe Drinking Water Act:** EPA sets standards limiting mercury in drinking water [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/environmental-laws-apply-mercury).

*   **European Union (EU Regulations):**
    *   **Revised Mercury Regulation (Effective 30 July 2024):** Tightens restrictions on mercury uses within the EU [source](https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/chemicals/mercury_en).
    *   **Prohibitions:** Bans export, manufacture, and many mercury-containing products (MAPs); prohibits new industrial uses without demonstrated benefits and lack of alternatives [source](https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/chemicals/mercury_en).
    *   **Phase-Outs:**
        *   Dental amalgam: Phased out by January 1, 2025, with limited temporary derogations until June 30, 2026 [source](https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/chemicals/mercury_en).
        *   Mercury-containing lamps: Export banned and use limited for six types by December 31, 2025, or 2026 [source](https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/chemicals/mercury_en).
    *   **Industrial Processes:** Prohibits mercury use as catalysts/electrodes [source](https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/chemicals/mercury_en).
    *   **Waste Management:** Regulates mercury waste management under the Waste Framework Directive and Landfill Directive [source](https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/chemicals/mercury_en).
    *   **Integrated Approach:** Addresses mercury emissions from major industrial sources through IED 2.0, integrated with Water Framework Directive and EQSD for surface water, sediment, and biota mercury limits [source](https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/chemicals/mercury_en).

Summary:
- Mercury exposure across three chemical forms (elemental mercury, inorganic mercury salts, and methylmercury) consistently affects the nervous system and kidneys in humans and animals.
- Elemental mercury (vapor):
  - Neurological effects in humans: tremor, vision issues, slowed nerve conduction, reduced motor speed/coordination, memory and cognitive changes, mood/irritability symptoms.
  - Neurodevelopmental effects in animals; potential CNS damage and motor impairments in adults.
  - Renal effects: decreased glomerular/tubular function; nephrotoxicity in animals with dose/duration dependency.
  - Severe inhalation exposures can cause acute lung injury, pneumonitis, respiratory failure.
- Inorganic mercury salts:
  - Neurological and renal toxicity in animals (oral exposure) with consistent findings.
  - Possible cardiovascular, immunological, reproductive effects; some male-rat carcinogenic signals.
  - No human epidemiological studies identified for inorganic salts.
  - Neurodevelopmental effects in offspring and neurobehavioral signs in adults; impaired motor function, memory, and learning; overt neurotoxicity at higher exposures.
  - Renal toxicity is dose- and duration-dependent.
  - Some evidence of increased blood pressure and altered cardiac function (cardiovascular effects).
  - Reproductive toxicity (fertility impairment, reduced sperm motility/number).
  - Some cancer signals in male rats (forestomach/thyroid tumors).
- Methylmercury (not detailed in excerpt but implied as a major category):
  - Cardiovascular effects data exist; epidemiological studies link mercury biomarkers to various cardiovascular outcomes across occupational, dietary (fish), and general populations.
- Overall: For all mercury forms, neurological and renal effects are consistently observed; cardiovascular, immunological, reproductive, and some carcinogenic signals exist mainly from animal studies or limited human data.

Summary:

- Mercury can exist as gas, liquid, or solid; many mercury compounds are solid at room temperature. MeHg (methylmercury) and mercury vapor are odorless.
- Primary exposure routes:
  - Oral: contaminated fish/seafood (MeHg) is the main dietary source; rice may contribute. Minor: contaminated water and elemental mercury from dental amalgams.
  - Inhalation: from ambient air or mercury from broken/spilled items (amalgams, thermometers).
  - Dermal: from consumer products containing mercury (e.g., skin lightening creams).
- Absorption and distribution:
  - Elemental mercury: inhaled, also small absorption via skin/GI.
  - Inorganic mercury: absorbed via all routes; organics (MeHg) are nearly fully absorbed in the GI tract.
  - Mercury distributes to the brain and kidneys; can be found in cord blood, placenta, and breast milk, and can transfer to the fetus.
- Metabolism:
  - Elemental mercury oxidized to Hg2+; inorganic mercury can oxidize in gastric conditions; MeHg may demethylate to Hg2+.
- Excretion:
  - Exhalation (elemental Hg); urine/feces (Hg2+); hair (MeHg).
- Health effects (dependent on dose, duration, form, and exposure route):
  - Neuro effects (tremor, cognitive, sensory, motor impairments; mood changes), especially from inhalation of elemental mercury or MeHg exposure.
  - Prenatal exposure to MeHg associated with neurodevelopmental effects; potential birth defects at high dietary MeHg.
  - Renal effects from elemental mercury exposure; possible renal damage from inorganic/organic mercury.
  - Impaired fertility (animal data, oral exposure); high dietary MeHg linked to birth/health effects.
  - Possible immune alterations from inorganic/organic mercury exposure.

It is used in electronics, fluorescent lighting, chlorine-caustic soda production, and historically in dental fillings (phasing out) and some cultural practices. Exposures occur mainly indoors (e.g., broken CFLs or thermometers) and near old mines or mercury-using facilities. runs.report:
## Is Mercury Safe?

This report summarizes the safety of different forms of mercury exposure, drawing from various health organizations and research findings.

### Elemental Mercury (Hg0) Exposure

Elemental mercury is a highly toxic element that poses significant health risks, primarily affecting the nervous system. Exposure mainly occurs through inhalation of its vapors, particularly in occupational settings or from spills of mercury-containing products.

*   **Health Effects:** Inhaling elemental mercury vapors can lead to tremors, coordination problems, vision, hearing, and memory issues, headaches, and mood changes. Very high exposure can cause breathing problems or be fatal [https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxfaqs/tfacts46_metallic_mercury.pdf](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxfaqs/tfacts46_metallic_mercury.pdf), [https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/). Children are more vulnerable and may develop acrodynia with high exposures [https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxfaqs/tfacts46_metallic_mercury.pdf](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxfaqs/tfacts46_metallic_mercury.pdf).
*   **Exposure Limits:** The chronic inhalation Minimal Risk Level (MRL) for elemental mercury is 0.3 μg Hg/m3, based on tremors observed in occupational studies. This level considers a 10-fold uncertainty factor for human variability [https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxprofiles/tp46-a.pdf](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxprofiles/tp46-a.pdf).
*   **Sources of Exposure:** Common sources include occupational settings (e.g., chlor-alkali, fluorescent lamp, mining industries), broken compact fluorescent lamps (CFLs) or thermometers, and old mining or mercury-using facilities [https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxprofiles/tp46-a.pdf](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxfaqs/tfacts46_metallic_mercury.pdf), [https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxfaqs/tfacts46_metallic_mercury.pdf](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxfaqs/tfacts46_metallic_mercury.pdf).
*   **Public Health Concerns:** The WHO identifies mercury as one of its top ten chemicals of major public health concern, advocating for the elimination of mercury mining, reduction in industrial use, promotion of clean energy, and replacement of mercury-containing medical devices [https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).

### Methylmercury Exposure (Primarily from Fish)

Methylmercury is an organic form of mercury found primarily in fish and seafood. While fish provides essential nutrients, larger, predatory fish tend to accumulate higher levels of methylmercury, posing a risk, especially to vulnerable populations.

*   **Health Risks:** The fetus is particularly vulnerable to methylmercury, risking developmental harm [https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).
*   **Fish Consumption Guidelines:**
    *   **Lower Mercury Options:** Prioritize fish like salmon, shrimp, canned light (skipjack) tuna, sardines, pollock, or trout [https://hmapfoundation.org/heavy-metals-101/fish-mercury-smarter-choices/](https://hmapfoundation.org/heavy-metals-101/fish-mercury-smarter-choices/), [https://www.cdc.zj.cn/jksd/202610/t20261013_23345.shtml](https://www.cdc.zj.cn/jksd/202610/t20261013_23345.shtml).
    *   **Higher Mercury Fish to Limit/Avoid:** Large predatory deep-sea fish such as swordfish, king mackerel, shark, and albacore (white) tuna accumulate higher levels of methylmercury. Canned albacore tuna typically has about three times more mercury than canned light tuna [https://hmapfoundation.org/heavy-metals-101/fish-mercury-smarter-choices/](https://hmapfoundation.org/heavy-metals-101/fish-mercury-smarter-choices/), [https://www.cdc.zj.cn/jksd/202610/t20261013_23345.shtml](https://www.cdc.zj.cn/jksd/202610/t20261013_23345.shtml).
    *   **Serving Recommendations:** The FDA/EPA standard adult serving is 4 oz (about 113g). Pregnant or breastfeeding individuals are advised to consume 2-3 servings per week of "Best Choices" fish, 4 oz each, or one "Good Choices" serving with no other fish that week. Cooking does not reduce mercury content [https://hmapfoundation.org/heavy-metals-101/fish-mercury-smarter-choices/](https://hmapfoundation.org/heavy-metals-101/fish-mercury-smarter-choices/).
    *   **Infants and Young Children:** It is recommended to choose low-mercury fish and avoid raw or undercooked fish due to microbial and parasitic risks. Specialized infant auxiliary foods have significantly lower mercury limits compared to general aquatic products [https://www.cdc.zj.cn/jksd/202610/t20261013_23345.shtml](https://www.cdc.zj.cn/jksd/202610/t20261013_23345.shtml).
*   **Guideline Refinement:** Ongoing research assesses whether current fish consumption guidance adequately protects pregnant individuals from mercury exposure while preserving the benefits of essential fatty acids, suggesting a need for refined guidelines [https://doi.org/10.13140/rg.2.2.25717.95208](https://doi.org/10.13140/rg.2.2.25717.95208).

### Other Forms of Mercury

*   **Inorganic Mercury:** This form also has varying toxic effects [https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).
*   **Ethylmercury:** Found in thimerosal, it is not considered a health risk at current exposure levels [https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).

### General Recommendations

## Mercury Exposure: A Safety Report

This report summarizes key information regarding mercury's safety, health impacts, sources of exposure, and regulatory efforts.

### Health Effects of Mercury Exposure

Mercury is a naturally occurring toxic element that poses significant public health concerns due to its ability to damage various bodily systems [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health). The severity of health effects depends on the form of mercury, dose, duration, exposure route, age, and individual health [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).

*   **Vulnerable Populations:** Fetuses and young children are particularly vulnerable to mercury's harmful effects, especially concerning brain and nervous system development [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health), [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
*   **Systemic Damage:** Exposure can damage the nervous, digestive, and immune systems, as well as the lungs, kidneys, skin, and eyes. Neurological and behavioral disorders are common outcomes [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health).
*   **Forms of Mercury and Their Effects:**
    *   **Methylmercury:** Primarily encountered through consuming contaminated fish and shellfish. High levels can lead to neurotoxic effects such as loss of peripheral vision, tingling sensations, poor coordination, speech/hearing/walking impairment, and muscle weakness [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury). It is classified as possibly carcinogenic to humans [source](https://www.who.int/europe/publications/i/item/WHO-EURO-2023-8983-48755-72523).
    *   **Elemental/Metallic Mercury:** Exposure usually occurs through inhaling mercury vapor from spills or broken devices in industrial settings. Acute or chronic exposure can cause tremors, mood changes, insomnia, neuromuscular issues, headaches, sensory disturbances, and impaired mental function. Higher exposures can result in kidney damage, respiratory failure, or death [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health), [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   **Inorganic Mercury:** Can damage the gastrointestinal tract, nervous system, and kidneys. Symptoms include skin rash, mood swings, memory loss, mental disturbances, and muscle weakness. Prolonged exposure carries a risk of kidney damage [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   **Ethylmercury:** Found in thiomersal (used in vaccines) and does not pose health risks at the levels used [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health).
*   **Other Health Associations:** Epidemiological evidence links mercury to adverse cardiovascular, immunological, neurological, and reproductive effects [source](https://www.who.int/europe/publications/i/item/WHO-EURO-2023-8983-48755-72523).
*   **Medical Advice:** Individuals concerned about mercury exposure should consult a physician or poison control [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).

### Sources of Mercury Exposure

Mercury is ubiquitous in the environment, and human exposure arises from various sources:

*   **Environmental Release:** Coal burning, mining (especially artisanal gold mining), industrial processes, electricity generation, and fuel combustion release mercury into the air, water, and soil [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health), [source](https://www.who.int/europe/publications/i/item/WHO-EURO-2023-8983-48755-72523).
*   **Contaminated Food:** Consumption of contaminated fish and shellfish is the primary route of methylmercury exposure [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health), [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
*   **Mercury-Containing Products:** Common household and industrial items such as batteries, thermometers, barometers, switches, relays, lamps, and dental amalgams are sources of mercury. Improper disposal can lead to environmental release [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health).
*   **Occupational Exposure:** Inhalation of elemental mercury vapors is a significant risk in industrial settings [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health).

### Environmental Regulations and Safety Standards

Significant global and national efforts are underway to reduce mercury exposure and manage its risks:

*   **Minamata Convention on Mercury:** This international treaty aims to protect human health and the environment from anthropogenic emissions and releases of mercury and mercury compounds. Efforts include eliminating mercury mining, replacing mercury in industrial processes, and promoting safe work practices [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health), [source](https://www.unep.org/gef/news-and-stories/technical-highlight/pacific-island-countries-advance-regional-action-mercury).
    *   **Pacific Island Countries:** 14 Pacific Island countries are advancing regional cooperation, legislative development (including model legislation for mercury-containing products), and capacity building to implement the Minamata Convention [source](https://www.unep.org/gef/news-and-stories/technical-highlight/pacific-island-countries-advance-regional-action-mercury).
*   **Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS) in the US:** The EPA has established limits for mercury and other hazardous air pollutants from coal- and oil-fired electric utility steam generating units. These standards have led to significant reductions in mercury emissions, with approximately 86-90% reduction since 2010 levels [source](https://www.edgechat.ai/mercury-and-air-toxics-standards).
*   **Healthcare Sector Initiatives:** India aims to eliminate mercury-containing medical devices (thermometers and blood pressure monitors) from healthcare services by 2030. This involves replacing devices, strengthening safe mercury-waste management, and ensuring access to reliable non-mercury alternatives. Several states in India have already eliminated mercury-based devices in public health services [source](https://www.who.int/india/news-room/detail/22-10-2026-push-to-eliminate-mercury-based-devices-in-health-care).
*   **Public Health Protection:**
    *   Promoting mercury-free products and enforcing emissions controls are crucial [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health).
    *   The EPA sets drinking water Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) to protect health [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   Ongoing monitoring and refining of guidelines are necessary as new evidence emerges [source](https://www.who.int/europe/publications/i/item/WHO-EURO-2023-8983-48755-72523).

Summary:
- Hidden correspondence from the 1950s reveals that the Fields Medal was not designed to honor the absolute greatest mathematical genius, but to recognize promising, younger up-and-coming talents.
- Harald Bohr tended to steer selections toward younger, less “old” candidates and those who would benefit most from the recognition, rather than the most accomplished or famous mathematicians.
- 1950 medals went to Laurent Schwartz and Atle Selberg over stronger candidates like André Weil and Oscar Zariski, due to a preference for nurturing emerging talent.
- In 1958, Klaus Roth and René Thom were chosen, with John Nash ranking highly but not winning; committee members sought to highlight comparatively lesser-known recipients who needed the prize for career impact.
- The process, once opaque, shows personal agendas and strategic considerations shaping early Fields selections, contradicting the idea that the prize always aimed at recognizing the greatest genius.

runs.report:
## 2025 Nobel Prize in Mathematics: Masaki Kashiwara's Contributions

This report summarizes the contributions of Masaki Kashiwara, who was awarded the 2025 Abel Prize, often considered the equivalent of the Nobel Prize in Mathematics.

### I. Award and Recognition

*   **2025 Abel Prize Laureate:** Masaki Kashiwara was awarded the 2025 Abel Prize by the Norwegian King in Oslo for his foundational contributions to algebraic analysis and representation theory [source](https://www.imu-news.org/imu-news/archive/2025/imu-news-130-march-2025). This makes him the first Japanese recipient of the Abel Prize [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masaki_Kashiwara).
*   **Other Awards and Honors:** Kashiwara has received numerous other accolades throughout his career, including the Kyoto Prize (2018), Chern Medal (2018), Iyanaga Prize (1981), Asahi Prize (1988), Japan Academy Prize (1988), and the Order of the Sacred Treasure, Gold and Silver Star (2020) [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masaki_Kashiwara). He was also a plenary speaker at ICM 1978 and an invited speaker at ICM 1990 [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masaki_Kashiwara).
*   **The Nobel Prize in Mathematics Context:** It's important to note that there is no official Nobel Prize in Mathematics. The Abel Prize is widely regarded as its closest equivalent in prestige for mathematicians [source](https://www.imu-news.org/imu-news/archive/2025/imu-news-130-march-2025).

### II. Key Mathematical Contributions

Masaki Kashiwara's work has profoundly impacted algebraic analysis, representation theory, and related fields. His primary contributions cited for the Abel Prize include:

*   **Development of D-module Theory:** Kashiwara's foundational work on the theory of D-modules (also referred to as $\mathscr{D}$-modules) is a cornerstone of his contributions. This theory provides a crucial link between algebraic analysis and representation theory and has significant applications to partial differential equations [source](https://doi.org/10.1090/noti3306), [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masaki_Kashiwara).
    *   He developed the analytic side of D-module theory and applied it to linear partial differential equations with analytic coefficients, often in collaboration with Mikio Sato [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masaki_Kashiwara).
    *   D-modules played a crucial role in the proof of the Kazhdan–Lusztig conjecture [source](https://doi.org/10.1090/noti3306).
*   **Discovery of Crystal Bases:** Kashiwara discovered crystal bases (and crystal graphs) for quantum groups, offering a purely combinatorial framework to understand representations in the limit where *q* approaches 0. This significantly simplified the understanding of complex representation theory [source](https://doi.org/10.1090/noti3306).
*   **Riemann–Hilbert Correspondence:** He made significant contributions to the Riemann–Hilbert correspondence (1980), which establishes an equivalence between derived categories of D-modules and constructible sheaves [source](https://doi.org/10.1090/noti3306), [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masaki_Kashiwara). This work has connections to Deligne and Beilinson–Bernstein–Mebkhout's algebraic case [source](https://doi.org/10.1090/noti3306).
*   **Microlocal Analysis:** Kashiwara made important contributions to microlocal analysis, including the involutivity of characteristics of microdifferential systems and their classification at generic points [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masaki_Kashiwara).
*   **Bernstein–Sato (b-function) Theory:** His work includes proofs and results related to this theory, utilizing D-modules and the resolution of singularities [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masaki_Kashiwara).

### III. Broader Impact

Kashiwara's work has laid the groundwork for modern algebraic analysis and its interplay with algebraic geometry, representation theory, and mathematical physics [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masaki_Kashiwara). His innovations, such as crystal bases, provided conceptual simplification and combinatorial structure to complex mathematical problems [source](https://doi.org/10.1090/noti3306).

## Report: 2025 Nobel Prize in Mathematics

### Existence of a Nobel Prize in Mathematics

It is important to clarify that **there is no Nobel Prize in Mathematics**. The Nobel Prizes, established by Alfred Nobel's will, were created to recognize those who have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind in specific fields [source](https://www.nobelprize.org/frequently-asked-questions/).

*   **Established Categories:** The original Nobel Prize categories are Physics, Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine, Literature, and Peace [source](https://www.nobelprize.org/frequently-asked-questions/).
*   **Economics Prize:** The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel was added later in 1969 [source](https://www.nobelprize.org/about-the-nobel-prize/).
*   **Exclusion of Mathematics:** Alfred Nobel's will did not include mathematics as a prize category, and the exact reasons for this exclusion are unclear [source](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/etimes/trending/why-is-there-no-nobel-prize-for-mathematics-why-alfred-nobel-left-the-subject-out-of-his-famous-awards-the-truth-behind-the-love-rivalry-rumour-and-the-prestigious-prizes-that-recognise-mathematicians-today/photostory/134813902.cms).
*   **Debunked Rumors:** A popular rumor suggesting a romantic rivalry between Nobel and a mathematician influenced the omission is false; Nobel never married, and there is no evidence to support this claim [source](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/etimes/trending/why-is-there-no-nobel-prize-for-mathematics-why-alfred-nobel-left-the-subject-out-of-his-famous-awards-the-truth-behind-the-love-rivalry-rumour-and-the-prestigious-prizes-that-recognise-mathematicians-today/photostory/134813902.cms), [source](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/the-prizes-rite/).
*   **Nobel's Interests:** Likely reasons for the exclusion are tied to Nobel's personal interests, his focus on fields with clear practical impact, and the existence of other mathematics prizes in Sweden at the time [source](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/the-prizes-rite/).

### Recognition for Achievements in Mathematics

While there is no Nobel Prize in Mathematics, mathematicians are recognized through other highly prestigious awards that are considered the equivalent of Nobel-level honors in the field.

*   **Fields Medal:** Awarded every four years to mathematicians aged 40 or younger [source](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/etimes/trending/why-is-there-no-nobel-prize-for-mathematics-why-alfred-nobel-left-the-subject-out-of-his-famous-awards-the-truth-behind-the-love-rivalry-rumour-and-the-prestigious-prizes-that-recognise-mathematicians-today/photostory/134813902.cms).
    *   Speculation for the 2006 Fields Medal, mentioning individuals like Terence Tao and Grigori Perelman, highlights the significance of this award [source](http://demairena.blogspot.com/2006/02/1091-congreso-de-futurologia.html).
*   **Abel Prize:** Awarded annually, with no age limit [source](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/etimes/trending/why-is-there-no-nobel-prize-for-mathematics-why-alfred-nobel-left-the-subject-out-of-his-famous-awards-the-truth-behind-the-love-rivalry-rumour-and-the-prestigious-prizes-that-recognise-mathematicians-today/photostory/134813902.cms).
*   **Breakthrough Prize in Mathematics:** Honors top achievements across diverse areas of mathematics, awarded annually since 2015 [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakthrough_Prize_in_Mathematics).
    *   **Notable Laureates and Contributions:**
        *   **2015:** Simon Donaldson (new invariants for 4-manifolds), Maxim Kontsevich (broad impact across various mathematical fields), Jacob Lurie (higher category theory and derived algebraic geometry), Terence Tao (harmonic analysis, PDEs, analytic number theory), Richard Taylor (automorphic forms) [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakthrough_Prize_in_Mathematics).
        *   **2016:** Ian Agol (low-dimensional topology and geometric group theory) [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakthrough_Prize_in_Mathematics).
        *   **2017:** Jean Bourgain (transformative work in analysis, combinatorics, PDEs, geometry, number theory) [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakthrough_Prize_in_Mathematics).
        *   **2018:** Christopher Hacon and James McKernan (birational algebraic geometry; minimal model program) [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakthrough_Prize_in_Mathematics).
        *   **2019:** Vincent Lafforgue (Langlands program in function fields) [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakthrough_Prize_in_Mathematics).
        *   **2020:** Alex Eskin (dynamics/geometry of moduli spaces of Abelian differentials) [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakthrough_Prize_in_Mathematics).
        *   **2021:** Martin Hairer (stochastic analysis; regularity structures theory) [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakthrough_Prize_in_Mathematics).
        *   **2022:** Takurō Mochizuki (theory of flat connections on algebraic varieties) [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakthrough_Prize_in_Mathematics).
        *   **2023:** Daniel Spielman (theoretical CS and math; spectral graph theory, Kadison–Singer problem, numerical linear algebra, optimization, coding theory) [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakthrough_Prize_in_Mathematics).

sources.summary:
- The Nobel Prize was created from Alfred Nobel’s will, funding prizes for those “who shall have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind.” The prizes were first awarded in 1901 and have been awarded annually, with some gaps during WWI and WWII.
- Prize categories: Physics, Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine, Literature, Peace. Economics (Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel) was added in 1968.
- Prize rules: Up to three individuals can share a prize; organizations can receive the Peace Prize. Prizes cannot be awarded posthumously, except if the recipient dies after the announcement (since 1974). Self-nomination is not allowed; nominations are by invitation or eligibility criteria, depending on the prize.
- Nomination and selection: Eligible nominators submit nominations, which prize-awarding bodies evaluate to determine laureates according to Nobel’s will.
- Other points: The Nobel Foundation statutes restrict appeals against prize decisions; the Nobel Day is December 10, commemorating Nobel’s death and the award ceremony.
